question_text:
A 23-year-old student presents to his new GP in the UK to arrange ongoing follow-up for a genetic condition. The patient states that his father died from bowel cancer in his 30s.

The patient states that genetic testing was performed whilst he was a child which led to yearly colonoscopies starting aged 10 and eventually, he had a total colectomy and ileoanal pouch formation 2 years ago in the US. He states that he now has upper endoscopies yearly.

What gene mutation is associated with the most likely underlying diagnosis?
options_json: ["Adenomatous polyposis coli oncogene", "Adenomatous polyposis coli tumour suppressor gene", "Deleted in colorectal cancer tumour suppressor gene", "MutS Homolog 2 tumour suppressor gene", "Protein P53 tumour suppressor gene"]
answer_text: Adenomatous polyposis coli tumour suppressor gene
explanation_text:
Familial adenomatous polyposis is due to a mutation in a tumour suppressor gene called adenomatous polyposis coli gene (APC)

This is a typical history of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP), a rare autosomal dominant condition resulting from the inheritance of a mutated

adenomatous polyposis coli tumour suppressor gene

(APC). Children may be identified as carriers of this gene via genetic testing which is carried out due to strong family history of cancer. Once identified, children have regular sigmoidoscopies or colonoscopies from age 10-12 and once polyps are identified, a total colectomy is planned and normally happens in the patient's early 20s. Up to 100% of patients with FAP will develop colorectal cancer if polyps are not removed. FAP is also associated with stomach cancer and therefore patients also require regular upper GI endoscopy.

Adenomatous polyposis coli oncogene

is incorrect because APC is a tumour suppressor gene, meaning that it is the loss of function of the gene that results in an increased risk of cancer.

Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal carcinoma (HNPCC) is a slightly more common cause of colorectal cancer caused by autosomal dominant inheritance of mutated

MutS Homolog 2 gene

(MSH2) or MLH1 genes. Once diagnosed, HNPCC does not normally require screening with colonoscopy until at least aged 20. Regular upper endoscopy is required due to the risk of stomach cancer and regular pelvic ultrasound is also required in women due to the risk of ovarian cancer. The lifetime risk of colorectal cancer is 20-80% and therefore patients with HNPCC may eventually require colectomy, although at a later stage than FAP.

Sporadic colon cancer is more likely in patients with certain genetic mutations including allelic loss of the APC gene, deletion of the

protein P53 tumour suppressor gene

(p53), deletion of

deleted in colorectal cancer tumour suppressor gene

(DCC) and activation of K-ras. This scenario is not consistent with sporadic colon cancer due to the regular screening and early colectomy.

question_text:
A 55-year-old gentleman was brought into the emergency department with a 4-day history worsening right-sided abdominal pain, vomiting, fever and chills. He had vomited twice this morning with reduced eating and drinking. His background involves poorly controlled type-2 diabetes controlled by multiple medications, high blood pressure and alcoholism. His observations were a respiratory rate of 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure of 109/76 mmHg, heart rate of 101 beats per minute and temperature of 38.4ºC degrees. A subsequent liver ultrasound scan showed the presence of a deep-walled abscess within the liver.

What is the definitive management of this liver abscess?
options_json: ["Admit and monitor", "Emergency laparotomy", "Drainage and antibiotics", "Antibiotics and CT liver triple phase", "Discharge home with antibiotics"]
explanation_text:
Liver abscesses are generally managed with a combination of antibiotics & drainage

Liver abscesses can be a potentially life-threatening condition especially if left untreated as can develop into sepsis and result in end-organ damage. In this scenario, the patient is already showing early signs of haemodynamic instability with some abnormality in his vital signs. Therefore, he will require immediate intervention and treatment with close monitoring.

Computed tomography (CT) liver triple phase is scan used to evaluate liver lesion. Whilst it may be of benefit in this situation by giving further information about the actual abscess, it could delay the actual management.

Drainage with either a percutaneous or laparoscopic approach is the optimal management of the abscess with subsequent treatment with intravenous/oral antibiotics for 4-6 weeks. This would be guided by the sensitivities obtained from the fluid culture obtained from the drained abscess.

An emergency laparotomy would be too invasive and is not the best approach for abscess particularly when deeper within the liver.

Admit and monitor or discharging home with antibiotics would not be safe approaches and puts the patient at harm. More importantly, increases the risk of the patient developing sepsis from the underlying liver abscess if left untreated.

question_text:
A 25-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with episodic bleeding from the rectum. He describes it as fresh red blood. He is quite concerned as he reports his mother died from colorectal cancer aged 45. He has no significant past medical history.

Physical examination is unremarkable. He is referred for urgent investigations, including a colonoscopy, which shows approximately 150 polyps. No other lesions are noted on scans.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Annual surveillance colonoscopy", "Chemotherapy", "Proctocolectomy", "Radiotherapy", "Repeated polypectomy"]
explanation_text:
Familial adenomatous polyposis - once diagnosed patients typically have a total proctocolectomy with ileal pouch anal anastomosis due to the extremely high risk of developing colorectal cancer

This patient's presentation is highly suggestive of familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP). This is a rare inherited condition that leads to the formation of hundreds of polyps by the age of 30-40. Patients inevitably develop colorectal cancer. To prevent this, in almost all cases, patients undergo a total

proctocolectomy

with ileal pouch-anal anastomosis once the condition is diagnosed.

Annual surveillance colonoscopy

is inappropriate here, given the significant polyp burden. Proctocolectomy is more appropriate. If the patient instead has a very low polyp burden, regular surveillance colonoscopy with polypectomy may be suitable.

Chemotherapy

is incorrect. FAP is also associated with desmoid tumours - locally aggressive tumours that arise from connective tissue. Chemotherapy may be warranted for this. However, the scans do not indicate any such tumours.

Radiotherapy

may also be used to treat desmoid tumours. However, the scans here do not report any indication of tumours. Proctocolectomy is most appropriate here.

Repeated polypectomy

is incorrect. In a patient with a very low polyp burden, regular surveillance colonoscopy with polypectomy may be sufficient to manage the condition. However, given this patient's extensive polyp burden, proctocolectomy is more appropriate.

question_text:
A 86-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with ongoing fatigue. Over the past year, he has been investigated for persistent iron deficiency anaemia. He has not noticed any blood in his stool but has had two positive faecal immunochemical tests (FIT). A colonoscopy and upper gastrointestinal (GI) endoscopy were both unremarkable.

On examination, which heart murmur is most likely to be identified?
options_json: ["Early diastolic", "Ejection systolic heard louder on expiration", "Ejection systolic heard louder on inspiration", "Mid diastolic", "Pansystolic"]
answer_text: Ejection systolic heard louder on expiration
explanation_text:
Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis

The correct answer is

ejection systolic murmur heard loudest on expiration

due to aortic stenosis. The patient presents with iron deficiency anaemia and has returned two positive faecal immunochemical tests (FIT), indicative of gastrointestinal haemorrhage. Angiodysplasia, when situated in the small intestine beyond the detection range of standard upper-GI endoscopy and colonoscopy, necessitates the use of capsule endoscopy for identification. It is important to note that angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis, which is characterised by an ejection systolic murmur that can be heard radiating towards the carotid arteries and is loudest on expiration.

An

early diastolic murmur

commonly suggests aortic regurgitation. There is no established correlation between aortic regurgitation and angiodysplasia. While pulmonary regurgitation may also present with an early diastolic murmur, it is less frequently encountered than aortic regurgitation and similarly does not associate with angiodysplasia.

An

ejection systolic murmur heard louder on inspiration

is characteristic of pulmonary stenosis or an atrial septal defect. Neither are associated with angiodysplasia.

Mid diastolic

murmurs are frequently associated with mitral stenosis, often due to rheumatic heart disease ' a condition that has seen a decline in prevalence within the UK. Mitral stenosis does not have a connection to angiodysplasia.

Pansystolic

murmurs are indicative of mitral or tricuspid regurgitation; neither condition has an association with angiodysplasia. Tricuspid regurgitation often occurs in association with infective endocarditis. Although mitral regurgitation can also result from endocarditis, it more commonly arises due to degenerative mitral valve disease (including mitral valve prolapse).

is not correct, it is a cause of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis however it is not the most common.

Her concerned partner tells you that she has no other significant past medical history and that she has attended all of her pregnancy checks. These have all been normal. On examination she is tender in the epigastrium. Her reflexes are mildly brisk and she does not have any clonus. Her blood pressure is 124/55 mmHg. question_text: Which one of the following is not associated with villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy?
options_json: ["Tropical sprue", "Coeliac disease", "Hypogammaglobulinaemia", "Familial Mediterranean Fever", "Whipple's disease"]
explanation_text:
Causes of villous atrophy (other than coeliacs): tropical sprue, Whipple's, lymphoma, hypogammaglobulinaemia

The correct answer is

Familial Mediterranean Fever (FMF)

. Familial Mediterranean Fever is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by recurrent episodes of fever and inflammation in the peritoneum, synovium, or pleura. It does not involve the small intestine directly and therefore would not cause villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy.

Tropical sprue

is an incorrect answer because it is indeed associated with villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy. Tropical sprue is a malabsorption disease commonly found in tropical regions, marked with abnormal flattening of the villi and inflammation of the lining of the small intestine.

Coeliac disease

also causes villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy, making it another incorrect option. Coeliac disease is a chronic immune-mediated disorder resulting from exposure to gluten in genetically susceptible individuals. The immune response leads to inflammation and damage to the lining of the small intestine, particularly loss of villi - hence 'villous atrophy'.

Another incorrect answer choice is

Hypogammaglobulinaemia

. Hypogammaglobulinaemia refers to a set of immunodeficiency disorders characterised by a decrease in levels of gamma globulins including antibodies, leading to an increased risk of infections. Certain types such as common variable immunodeficiency can lead to gastrointestinal manifestations including malabsorption due to villous atrophy.

Lastly,

Whipple's disease

too can cause villous atrophy on jejunal biopsy, thus making it an incorrect option as well. Whipple's disease is a rare systemic infectious disease caused by the bacterium

Tropheryma whipplei

, which can affect any part of the body but most often affects the gastrointestinal system. The infection leads to thickening and malabsorption in the small intestine due to inflammatory infiltration and resultant villous atrophy.

question_text: You are reviewing a 55-year-old man who has recently been diagnosed with Barrett's oesophagus. This was diagnosed after the patient was referred due to difficult to control symptoms. No evidence of dysplasia was found on biopsies. In terms of risk factor modification, which one of the following has been shown to be most strongly linked to the development of Barrett's oesophagus?
options_json: ["Use of NSAIDs", "Eating smoked fish", "Alcohol", "Smoking", "Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease"]
explanation_text:
GORD is the single strongest risk factor for the development of Barrett's oesophagus

The correct answer is

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

. Barrett's oesophagus is a condition in which the normal squamous epithelium of the oesophagus is replaced by columnar epithelium, typically as a result of chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). GORD exposes the oesophagus to gastric acid and bile, causing inflammation and injury to the oesophageal mucosa. Over time, this can lead to metaplastic changes and the development of Barrett's oesophagus. According to UK guidelines, patients with Barrett's oesophagus should receive appropriate management for their GORD symptoms.

Use of NSAIDs

: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) are known to cause gastrointestinal side effects such as dyspepsia and peptic ulcer disease. However, there is no strong evidence linking NSAID use to the development of Barrett's oesophagus specifically.

Eating smoked fish

: While some studies have suggested that certain dietary factors may be associated with an increased risk of developing Barrett's oesophagus or oesophageal adenocarcinoma, there is no consistent evidence that eating smoked fish has a significant impact on the risk of developing Barrett's oesophagus.

Alcohol

: Alcohol consumption has been linked to various gastrointestinal conditions, including GORD and oesophageal cancer. However, its association with Barrett's oesophagus remains unclear. Some studies suggest that alcohol may increase the risk while others report no significant association between alcohol intake and Barrett's oesophagus.

Smoking

: Smoking is a well-established risk factor for many diseases, including several types of cancer. While smoking has been shown to increase the risk of developing GORD and oesophageal adenocarcinoma, its association with Barrett's oesophagus is not as strong as that of GORD. Nevertheless, smoking cessation should still be recommended to patients with Barrett's oesophagus due to its numerous health benefits.

In summary, GORD is the most strongly linked risk factor for the development of Barrett's oesophagus. While other factors such as NSAID use, diet, alcohol, and smoking may contribute to the overall risk profile, they do not have as significant an impact on the development of this condition as GORD does.

question_text: A 56-year-old man with a history of alcohol-related cirrhosis attends the hepatology clinic for surveillance endoscopy. He has medium-sized oesophageal varices but has never had a gastrointestinal bleed. His blood pressure is stable and he has no contraindications to medication. Which is the most appropriate first-line intervention to reduce his risk of future variceal bleeding?
options_json: ["Non-cardioselective beta-blocker", "Endoscopic sclerotherapy", "Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt", "Prophylactic antibiotics", "Sengstaken-Blakemore tube"]
explanation_text:
A non-cardioselective B-blocker (NSBB) is used for the prophylaxis of oesophageal bleeding

Non-cardioselective beta-blocker

therapy (such as propranolol) is recommended as a first-line option for primary prophylaxis of variceal bleeding in patients with medium or large oesophageal varices who have not yet bled, according to UK and NICE guidelines. Non-cardioselective beta-blockers reduce portal venous pressure by decreasing cardiac output and causing splanchnic vasoconstriction, thereby lowering the risk of first variceal haemorrhage. They are preferred if there are no contraindications, and their use has been shown to improve survival.

Endoscopic sclerotherapy

is not recommended for primary prophylaxis due to higher complication rates compared to band ligation or non-cardioselective beta-blockers. Sclerotherapy may be considered only when other options are unavailable or unsuccessful, but it is not first-line in this scenario.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS)

is reserved for patients who have recurrent or uncontrolled variceal bleeding despite optimal medical and endoscopic management. It is invasive and carries significant risks such as hepatic encephalopathy, so it would not be used for primary prevention in someone who has never bled.

Prophylactic antibiotics

are indicated in acute upper gastrointestinal bleeding episodes in cirrhotic patients to prevent bacterial infections and improve outcomes. They do not play any role in primary prophylaxis before any episode of bleeding occurs.

Sengstaken-Blakemore tube

is an emergency measure used only in cases of active, uncontrolled variceal haemorrhage where endoscopic therapies have failed or are unavailable. It does not have any role in preventing a first episode of bleeding.

question_text: A 27-year-old man with multiple pigmented freckles on his lips and face is investigated for iron-deficiency anaemia. A diagnosis of Peutz-Jeghers syndrome is suspected. What is the mode of inheritance?
options_json: ["Autosomal recessive", "Mitochondrial inheritance", "X-linked dominant", "Autosomal dominant", "X-linked recessive"]
explanation_text:
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome - autosomal dominant

The correct answer is

Autosomal dominant

. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is a rare hereditary condition that follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. This means that an individual only needs to inherit one copy of the faulty gene from either parent to develop the condition. In this mode of inheritance, both males and females can be equally affected and have a 50% chance of passing on the gene to their offspring.

Autosomal recessive

is incorrect as this would require both parents to carry a copy of the faulty gene, with a 25% chance for each child to inherit the disease. Autosomal recessive conditions are often seen in consanguineous families or isolated populations, which does not fit with PJS.

Mitochondrial inheritance

, also known as maternal inheritance, is incorrect because it refers to conditions caused by mutations in the mitochondrial DNA. These conditions are exclusively passed down from the mother to all her children but not by fathers. PJS is caused by mutations in nuclear genes (specifically STK11/LKB1), not mitochondrial genes.

The options

X-linked dominant

and

X-linked recessive

are also incorrect as they refer to genetic disorders caused by mutations on the X chromosome. Males with X-linked dominant disorders pass the condition onto all their daughters but none of their sons, while females can pass it on to both sons and daughters depending on whether they are heterozygous or homozygous for the trait. For X-linked recessive disorders, males are more frequently affected than females. Females carrying one copy of the mutation are carriers and can pass it on to their sons or daughters. However, PJS is not linked to any sex chromosomes but rather an autosomal chromosome.

question_text: Which one of the following genetic conditions is the most prevalent in a Caucasian population?
options_json: ["Wilson's disease", "Sickle cell anaemia", "Cystic fibrosis", "Alpha-1 antitrypsin", "Haemochromatosis"]
explanation_text:
Haemochromatosis is more common than cystic fibrosis

Haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder with a carrier rate of 1 in 10 and is present in about 1 in 200-400 people. Cystic fibrosis (CF) has a carrier rate of 1 in 25 and is present in about 1 in 2,500 births. CF is often quoted as being the most common lethal inherited condition in Caucasians

question_text:
A 43-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus presents with lethargy. His current medications include metformin and gliclazide, although the gliclazide may soon be stopped due to his obesity. A number of blood tests are ordered which reveal the following:


HbA1c	66 mmol/mol	(< 48)
Ferritin	204 ng/mL	(25 - 350)
Bilirubin	23 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	162 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	120 u/L	(3 - 40)
AST	109 u/L	(3 - 40)

On discussing these results he states that he does not drink alcohol.

What is the most likely cause of these abnormal results?
options_json: ["Metformin-induced steatohepatitis", "Haemochromatosis", "Acute hepatitis secondary to gliclazide", "Cryptogenic cirrhosis", "Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease"]
explanation_text:
T2DM with abnormal LFTs - ? non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

By far the most likely diagnosis in an obese type 2 diabetic is non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. This patient will require a liver screen, ultrasound and liver biopsy to confirm the diagnosis.

A normal ferritin makes a diagnosis of haemochromatosis unlikely, although it should always be considered in patients with both abnormal LFTs and diabetes.

question_text:
A 29-year-old man has recently noticed that his movements were becoming stiffer and slower and has consequently had several falls. He has also noticed intermittent involuntary twisting movements in his body and his speech has become more slurred.

He was diagnosed with depression last year and has been tried on various antidepressants and psychological therapy with little benefit. He is currently taking venlafaxine and drinks 14 units of alcohol per week.

His liver function test results are as follows:


Bilirubin	9 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	88 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	106 u/L	(3 - 40)
Albumin	46 g/L	(35 - 50)

The results of a comprehensive liver screen are pending.

Based on the above information, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Alcohol-induced transaminitis", "Drug-induced transaminitis", "Haemochromatosis", "Huntington's chorea", "Wilson's disease"]
explanation_text:
Wilson's disease: in the brain, most copper is deposited in the basal ganglia

The combination of neuropsychiatric symptoms with abnormal liver function tests (LFTs) in a young adult should raise the possibility of Wilson's disease.

Excess copper accumulation and deposition in various organs result in its clinical manifestations. In the brain, most copper is deposited in the basal ganglia (particularly the putamen and globus pallidus), resulting in symptoms of Parkinsonism such as rigidity, tremor and bradykinesia. Deposition in the liver results in hepatic impairment, which can range from asymptomatic LFT derangement to cirrhosis and liver failure.

His alcohol intake is not high enough to account for these clinical findings.

While venlafaxine can sometimes cause neurological side-effects, this is comparatively rare and would be lower on the list of differential diagnoses.

Haemochromatosis can cause abnormal LFTs in this age group due to iron overload but is not commonly associated with neuropsychiatric features.

Huntington's chorea can certainly cause involuntary movements, but the prominent Parkinsonian features are more suggestive of Wilson's disease.

question_text:
A 22-year-old man presents with 4 episodes of non-bloody diarrhoea in a 24-hour period. He has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis. Observations are within normal limits. He is started on rectal aminosalicylates however there is no improvement.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	145 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
WBC	8.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.4 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	6.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	74 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	8 mg/L	(< 5)
ESR	12 mm/hr	Men: < (age / 2)
Women: < ((age + 10) / 2)

A colonoscopy is performed:


Colonoscopy	Diffuse superficial ulceration from the rectum to the hepatic flexure

What treatment is indicated?
options_json: ["Intravenous ciclosporin", "Intravenous steroids", "Methotrexate", "Oral aminosalicylates", "Rectal mesalazine"]
explanation_text:
In a mild-moderate flare of ulcerative colitis extending past the left-sided colon, oral aminosalicylates should be added to rectal aminosalicylates, as enemas only reach so far

Oral aminosalicylates

is correct. As the patient has a mild flare-up of ulcerative colitis with demonstrable disease extending past the left-sided colon, oral aminosalicylates are the agent of choice as enemas only reach the splenic flexure.

Intravenous ciclosporin

is incorrect. Intravenous ciclosporin may be used in severe colitis if steroids are contraindicated.

Intravenous steroids

is incorrect. Intravenous steroids are usually given first-line for severe colitis. Features of severe disease include >6 bowel movements per day with systemic upset, visible blood, pyrexia, tachycardia (>90 beats per minute), anaemia, and an ESR >30mm/hour.

Methotrexate

is incorrect. Research on the use of methotrexate for ulcerative colitis has shown that it is not generally effective and it is therefore not a recommended treatment.

Rectal mesalazine

is incorrect. As the patient has demonstrable disease extending past the left-sided colon, oral aminosalicylates are the agent of choice as enemas only reach so far.

question_text:
A 32-year-old presents with an exacerbation of their ulcerative colitis reporting 6-8 bloody stools per day for 3 days. On exam, they had a mild fever at 38 oC and mild tachycardia with a heart rate of 105bpm. All other observations were within normal range and blood results found increased raised inflammatory markers only.

The patient was admitted, and remission of the flair achieved with steroid therapy. This is her second admission, with the last being 6 months ago when she presented with similar symptoms and examination/investigation findings.

On discharge what medication, if any, should be trialled?
options_json: ["No regular treatment required at this point", "Oral aminosalicylate", "Oral azathioprine", "Oral methotrexate", "Topical (rectal) aminosalicylate"]
explanation_text:
If a patient with ulcerative colitis has had a severe relapse or >=2 exacerbations in the past year they should be given either oral azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine to maintain remission

This patient has presented with her second severe exacerbation of ulcerative colitis (UC) within a year, with 6-8 bloody stools a day, fever, tachycardia and raised inflammatory markers. As such

oral azathioprine

or oral mercaptopurine should be commenced to maintain remission. This drug act as an immunosuppressant and has been shown to reduce the number and severity of UC exacerbations.

Given this is the patient's second severe exacerbation of their UC within a year treatment should be offered to reduce the risk of further episodes and therefore

no regular treatment required at this point

is incorrect.

Oral aminosalicylate

can be used in patients suffering mild to moderate exacerbations of UC, however, it is normally used with a topic form of the medication (unless a patient has isolated left-sided disease). This patient has presented with their second severe exacerbation and therefore a more potent therapy is required.

Unlike in Crohn's disease,

oral methotrexate

is not recommended in the management of UC as its use is associated with lower remission rates and higher complication rates when compared to its use in the other forms of inflammatory bowel disease.

Again

topical (rectal) aminosalicylate

can be considered to maintain remission in mild disease but once patients have severe exacerbations as in this case an oral immunosuppressant is required.

question_text:
A 20-year-old female with known Crohn's disease presents in gastroenterology clinic for review of her management. She is currently being treated with oral prednisolone. She has experienced 3 mild flare ups of her Crohn's disease in the past 12 months, each occurring when oral steroid dose has been tapered. You consider adding azathioprine to her management.

Which of the following should be assessed before commencing azathioprine in this patient?
options_json: ["Liver function", "Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) activity", "Body mass index (BMI)", "Renal function", "Coagulation"]
explanation_text:
TPMT activity should be assessed before offering azathioprine or mercaptopurine therapy in Crohn's disease

Thiopurine methyltransferase (TPMT) is an enzyme involved in the metabolism of azathioprine and mercaptopurine. Some people have a deficiency of TPMT due to genetic mutations, and these people are at a greater risk of experiencing severe side effects from conventional doses of azathioprine or mercaptopurine. TPMT activity should therefore be assessed before offering azathioprine or mercaptopurine therapy. Such medications should not be commenced if TPMT is very low or absent. If TPMT activity is below normal, but not deficient, azathioprine or mercaptopurine can be commenced at a lower dose.

question_text: Which one of the following conditions is most associated with angiodysplasia?
options_json: ["Aortic regurgitation", "Ventricular septal defect", "Aortic stenosis", "Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy", "Mitral regurgitation"]
explanation_text:
Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis

The association between angiodysplasia and aortic stenosis is thought to be caused by von Willebrand factor (vWF) being proteolysed in the turbulent blood flow around the aortic valve.

vWF is most active in vascular beds with high shear stress, such as angiodysplasia, and deficiency of vWF increases the bleeding risk from such lesions.

The diagnosis is explained to her, and that further investigations will need to take place.

For local staging, which investigation would be most appropriate?

explanation_text:
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion

The correct answer is endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). EUS is better than computed tomography (CT), and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans at assessing mural invasion in oesophageal and gastric cancer. Several studies have demonstrated the accuracy of staging with EUS is significantly higher than staging with CT or MRI.

CT scanning is also useful and carried out for patients with oesophageal or gastric cancer. However, with regards to local staging (mural invasion), it is not as good as EUS.

Laparoscopy may be used in those with negative imaging before definitive therapy. For mural invasion, it is not useful.

MRI scanning is useful to assess metastases and spread. As with CT, it is not as accurate as EUS.

Positron emission tomography scanning is used for pre-operative staging and is more sensitive than CT in picking up distant metastases. EUS is still better than this for local staging.

question_text:
A 35-year-old woman is seen in the gastroenterology clinic with a several-month history of weight loss and loose stool. Her initial investigations suggest a malabsorptive syndrome. Following several tests, the gastroenterologist plans for her to undergo a secretin stimulation test.

What would be the expected outcome of the test in a healthy participant?
options_json: ["Increased secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells", "Increased secretion of gastric acid", "Increased secretion of gastrin", "Reduced secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells", "Reduced secretion of gastrin"]
answer_text: Increased secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells
explanation_text:
Secretin increases secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreas and hepatic duct cells

Secretin is a digestive hormone secreted by S cells in the upper small intestine in response to acidic chyme and fatty acids. Its main actions are to

increase the secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells

, decrease gastric acid secretion and promote the growth of pancreatic acinar cells. It can be used as a stimulation test to investigate the cause of pancreatic malabsorption.

Other gastric hormones such as cholecystokinin and vasoactive intestinal peptide also act to increase the secretion of pancreatic fluid.

As such, the answer of

reduced secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells

is incorrect since secretin has the opposite effect in healthy people.

Secretin acts to reduce gastric acid secretion. Gastrin

increases gastric acid secretion

. As such, this answer would not be expected of the test in this context so is incorrect.

Gastrin secretion is increased by stimuli such as distension of the stomach, vagal tone (mediated by gastrin-releasing peptide) and luminal peptides/amino acids. Secretin does not

increase gastrin secretion

so this answer is incorrect.

Gastrin secretion is reduced

by low antral pH and stimulation by somatostatin. Secretin does not directly affect gastrin secretion and hence this answer is incorrect.

Observations show a heart rate of 105bpm, and blood pressure 76mmHg systolic. On examination, he appears pale. Cardiovascular, respiratory and abdominal examinations are otherwise unremarkable.

His blood tests are shown below:


Hb	72 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	23.3 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	111 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	7 mg/L	(< 5)
Lactate	1.3 mmol/L	(0.4-2.2)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Colorectal cancer", "Diverticulitis", "Perforated duodenal ulcer", "Haemorrhoids", "Ischaemic colitis"]
explanation_text:
High urea levels can indicate an upper GI bleed versus lower GI bleed

Perforated duodenal ulcer

is correct. The haemoglobin drop and urea rise out of proportion to the creatinine suggest upper gastrointestinal bleeding. A perforated duodenal ulcer is the most likely option of those listed to cause upper gastrointestinal bleeding.

Colorectal cancer

is incorrect. If rectal bleeding occurs it is most often occult and would not present as rapid onset haemodynamic instability, and the urea rise would not be seen as the bleeding would be in the lower gastrointestinal tract.

Diverticulitis

is incorrect. Although the patient has a history of diverticulosis, the normal abdominal examination and the normal inflammatory markers point away from an infectious/inflammatory process. The bleeding in diverticulitis would be lower gastrointestinal, so the urea rise would not be seen.

Haemorrhoids

is incorrect. This would cause small volumes of fresh red bleeding and is unlikely to cause enough bleeding to present as haemodynamic instability and collapse. The urea rise would not be seen as the bleeding would be in the lower gastrointestinal tract.

Ischaemic colitis

is incorrect. The normal abdominal examination, normal lactate and normal inflammatory markers point away from this diagnosis. The bleeding in ischaemic colitis would also be more likely to be lower gastrointestinal, so would be fresh red bleeding without the urea rise.

question_text:
A 47-year-old man with a history of alcohol liver disease is admitted to the gastroenterology ward. He has developed tense ascites again and a plan is made to site an ascitic drain. His renal function after 2 days is as follows:


Na+	131 mmol/l
K+	3.8 mmol/l
Urea	12.2 mmol/l
Creatinine	205 µmol/l

Which of the following pathophysiological changes is most likely to be responsible for the declining renal function?
options_json: ["Splanchnic vasoconstriction", "Splanchnic vasodilation", "Ammonia-induced nephropathy", "Intrahepatic portosystemic shunting of blood", "Renal artery vasodilation"]
explanation_text:
Hepatorenal syndrome is primarily caused by splanchnic vasodilation

The correct answer for this question is

splanchnic vasodilation

. In patients with liver cirrhosis and tense ascites, splanchnic vasodilation is the primary pathophysiological change responsible for declining renal function. This occurs due to the release of vasodilatory substances such as nitric oxide and prostaglandins in response to portal hypertension. The resultant splanchnic vasodilation leads to a decrease in effective arterial blood volume, which in turn triggers activation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) and antidiuretic hormone (ADH) secretion. These compensatory mechanisms cause renal vasoconstriction and sodium retention, leading to worsening renal function.

Splanchnic vasoconstriction

is not the correct answer because it would result in increased effective arterial blood volume rather than decreased volume. This would not lead to activation of RAAS or ADH secretion, and therefore would not contribute to declining renal function.

Ammonia-induced nephropathy

is also incorrect as this condition typically presents with acute kidney injury following an episode of severe hyperammonemia, often secondary to gastrointestinal bleeding or infection. While ammonia can be elevated in patients with liver disease, it is unlikely that this patient's renal dysfunction is solely attributable to ammonia-induced nephropathy.

Intrahepatic portosystemic shunting of blood

refers to the formation of collateral vessels that bypass the liver parenchyma due to portal hypertension. Although these shunts may contribute to complications such as hepatic encephalopathy, they do not directly cause a decline in renal function.

Finally,

renal artery vasodilation

is an incorrect option because it would increase renal perfusion and improve glomerular filtration rate (GFR). This would be expected to improve renal function rather than cause a decline. In this patient's case, activation of RAAS and ADH secretion as a result of splanchnic vasodilation leads to renal vasoconstriction, which contributes to the worsening renal function.

Hypocalcaemia occurs in pancreatitis due to the saponification of fats. As lipase leaks out of the damaged pancreas, it breakdown fat into triglycerides and fatty acids. He was visibly jaundiced on end-of-the-bed inspection. On examination the abdomen was generally tender, distended with shifting dullness and scars from previous ascitic drains in the right iliac fossa. Bowels sounds were present and normal.

ECG showed sinus tachycardia.

Bloods:

Lymphs 2.0 * 109/l		Albumin 29 g/l
CRP 130 mg/l

Chest X-ray shows no acute abnormality.

The patient was admitted and has been started on IV normal saline and broad-spectrum antibiotics. Blood cultures have been sent. During the evening handover, the consultant requests that as the evening on-call you investigate for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) and start IV cefotaxime if SBP is confirmed.

Which of the following would confirm a diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)?
options_json: ["Blood cultures showing mixed growth.", "Paracentesis. Glucose >2.8 mmol/L in ascitic fluid", "Paracentesis. Neutrophil count >250 cells/µL in ascitic fluid", "Paracentesis. Organisms seen on Gram-stain of ascitic fluid", "Paracentesis. Neutrophil count >100 cells/µL in ascitic fluid"]
answer_text: Paracentesis. Neutrophil count >250 cells/µL in ascitic fluid
explanation_text:
In suspected SBP- diagnosis is by paracentesis. Confirmed by neutrophil count >250 cells/ul

Diagnosis of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) is by paracentesis with a neutrophil count >250 cells/µL in the ascitic fluid.

1. Incorrect. Blood cultures are positive for the offending organism in SBP in up to 1/3 of patients and can help guide antibiotic regime. However, by the same token, blood cultures will be negative in more than 2/3 of cases of SBP. All patients with suspected SBP should have blood cultures done but they do not form part of the diagnostic criteria.

2. Incorrect. Glucose levels in the ascitic fluid do not form part of diagnostic criteria for SBP. Neutrophils in the ascitic fluid actually consume glucose and so the concentration is often low (<2.8 mmol/L)

3. Correct. SBP is confirmed by a paracentesis showing a neutrophil count >250 cells/µL. Based on this result a diagnosis can be made and the antibiotic of choice would be IV cefotaxime (as advised by your consultant).

4. Incorrect. Though Gram-stain of the ascitic fluid will often show organisms in SBP it is not reliable as a diagnostic test.

5. Incorrect. The neutrophil count is the key measure but the threshold for diagnosis of SBP is >250 cells/µL not 100.

question_text:
A 75-year-old man has recently been diagnosed with carcinoid syndrome caused by a gastrointestinal neuroendocrine tumour after experiencing diarrhoea and flushing for the last 6 months.

In order to manage his symptoms, he has been commenced on a subcutaneous injection which acts by inhibiting the release of serotonin from this tumour. It has been explained that this is a synthetic analogue of a hormone that is naturally produced in the body.

Which part of the body is this hormone normally produced?
options_json: ["Anterior pituitary gland", "D cells in pancreas and stomach", "G cells in antrum of stomach", "Parietal cells of stomach", "S cells in upper small intestine"]
answer_text: D cells in pancreas and stomach
explanation_text:
Somatostatin is produced by D cells in the pancreas & stomach

The medication that this man has been given most likely refers to octreotide, a synthetic somatostatin analogue that is licensed to treat symptoms associated with carcinoid tumours with features of carcinoid syndrome, particularly flushing and diarrhoea. It reduces the secretion of serotonin which is responsible for these symptoms. This peptide hormone is naturally produced by D (delta) cells in the pancreas and stomach and is thought to act to reduce acid secretion from gastric parietal cells.

The anterior pituitary gland is incorrect. As well as the delta cells in the gastrointestinal system, somatostatin is also released from the hypothalamus where it inhibits the release of growth hormone from the anterior pituitary. However, somatostatin is not synthesised in the pituitary gland itself.

Gastrin is secreted from the G cells in the antrum of the stomach and is not the correct answer here.

The gastric parietal cells are responsible for secreting hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor and is, therefore, an incorrect option.

The S cells in the small intestine is an incorrect option. These cells release secretin, which promotes the release of bicarbonate from the pancreas into the intestinal lumen.

explanation_text:
HPV infection  (especially HPV 16 subtype) is the strongest risk factor for anal cancer

Anal cancer is a relatively rare diagnosis, commoner in women, with most patients presenting in later life with symptoms of anal pain, bleeding and a lesion. There are several risk factors that increase a patient's risk of developing anal cancer but the rising levels of

HPV infections

have been attributed to the increased incidence of the malignancy. HPV infection is established as the strongest risk factor for anal cancer with approximately 80-85% of squamous cell carcinoma (which accounts for 80% of all anal cancers) being caused by the viral infection.

Being on immunosuppressive drugs

has been shown to increase an individual's risk of anal cancer but like most other risk factors it is thought to be a result of the increased risk of HPV infection which drives the increased incidence of the malignancy.

HIV infection

has been associated with anal cancer however the association is thought mainly to be a result of immunodepression caused by HIV increasing the risk of HPV infection and reducing the body's ability to keep the HPV infection under control.

Men who have sex with men

have a higher risk of anal cancer but again this is thought to be due to an increased risk of HPV infection.

Multiple sexual partners

, if barrier protection is not used, can increase the risk of sexually transmitted diseases such as HPV which in turn is associated with anal cancer however this alone is a weaker risk factor than HPV infection.

explanation_text:
Budd-Chiari syndrome - ultrasound with Doppler flow studies is very sensitive and should be the initial radiological investigation

This is a case of deranged liver function tests associated with hepatosplenomegaly and ascites in a young person. A triad of ascites, abdominal pain, and hepatomegaly should raise suspicions for Budd-Chiari Syndrome.

Budd-Chiari Syndrome is caused by thrombosis of the hepatic veins. Pregnancy and being recently postpartum are common causes in young women. However, the history mentions her use of the combined oral contraceptive pill, another known risk factor.

The correct answer is

abdominal ultrasound with doppler flow

. This is non-invasive and a cheap investigation that can identify occlusion of the hepatic veins and thus provide a diagnosis.

CT of the abdomen

may identify small changes to the lung parenchyma along with an inability to visualise the hepatic veins, however, it is not as sensitive and therefore not the correct answer.

Liver biopsies

are rarely performed as a diagnostic procedure but may be performed if shunting (transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt - TIPSS) or transplant.

MRCP

is not usually performed to diagnose Budd-Chiari but may be used to investigate the cause of it after a diagnosis is made.

On examination, he has significant weight loss and jaundice. His abdomen is generally tender and a non-tender mass can be felt in the epigastric/right upper quadrant region. Observation and bedside tests are all within normal range except a blood glucose finger prick test which is found to be raised.

What is the investigation of choice for the patient's likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography", "Faecal elastase", "High-resolution CT", "Serum CA19-9 marker", "Ultrasound pancreas"]
explanation_text:
High-resolution CT scanning is the diagnostic investigation of choice for pancreatic cancer

This patient has presented with features most in keeping with pancreatic cancer with the classical triad of abdominal discomfort, jaundice and weight loss as well as possible new-onset diabetes mellitus indicated by a raised glucose level. The patient also has Courvoisier sign with jaundice and a painless abdominal mass again indicating an obstructive pancreatic or biliary neoplasm.

High-resolution CT

is the diagnostic investigation of choice for pancreatic cancer due to its relative availability and high sensitivity.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography

(ERCP) is typically indicated to relieve biliary obstruction caused by stones, strictures or malignancy however it is most commonly utilised once a diagnosis has been confirmed. This procedure is relatively timely, costly and invasive when compared to CT and therefore is not the diagnostic test of choice.

Faecal elastase

testing is used for the detection of exocrine pancreatic dysfunction and not to diagnose pancreatic cancer.

Abdominal ultrasound

(US) may show some signs in keeping with pancreatic cancer such as liver metastasis and ascites however these are normal late features of advanced cancer. US is less sensitive than CT and can miss smaller tumours.

Serum CA19-9

is a tumour marker frequently found to be elevated in pancreatic cancer and therefore may sometimes be used for screening purposes. However, it lacks sensitivity and specificity when compared to other investigations with approximately 5% of the general population being unable to produce CA19-9.

Penicillamine

It binds copper, increasing urinary excretion and reducing tissue deposition. The scenario describes a young patient with hepatic and neurological features, low caeruloplasmin, and Kayser-Fleischer rings—classic for Wilson’s disease. Early initiation of penicillamine can prevent progression and improve symptoms.

Lactulose

On examination, mild peripheral oedema is noted. A soft mid-diastolic murmur is heard on auscultation. Observations are within normal limits except for a slightly low blood pressure of 107/64 mmHg.

explanation_text:
Flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, tricuspid stenosis, pellagra → carcinoid with liver mets - diagnosis: urinary 5-HIAA

This patient's presentation is suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. This is most commonly due to liver metastases, although can also occur due to neuroendocrine tumours of the gut and bronchi. The secretion of serotonin, kinins and amines leads to flushing - the earliest symptom - along with unexplained diarrhoea. This patient's heart murmur is suggestive of tricuspid stenosis, which may also occur and lead to signs of right heart failure. Diagnosis typically involves the 24-hour collection of

urinary 5-HIAA

, which is elevated. Treatment of the underlying malignancy will aid resolution of symptoms.

Serum follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH)

is incorrect. This may play a role in the diagnosis of menopause, which can also present with flushing. However, the other signs and symptoms here point toward carcinoid syndrome.

Serum thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH)

Urinary catecholamines

is incorrect. These are typically used in the diagnosis of phaeochromocytoma (although have now largely been superseded by urinary metanephrines). Whilst this may also present with palpitations, patients typically have hypertension and tachyarrhythmias rather than the signs and symptoms seen here.

A 23-year-old female with a history of diarrhoea and weight loss has a colonoscopy to investigate her symptoms. A biopsy is taken and reported as follows:


Pigment laden macrophages

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Intestinal melanoma", "Haemochromatosis", "Ulcerative colitis", "Laxative abuse", "Colorectal cancer"]
explanation_text:
Diarrhoea - biospy shows pigment laden macrophages = laxative abuse

The correct answer is

Laxative abuse

. The histological finding of pigment-laden macrophages in the colon, often referred to as 'pseudomelanosis coli', is indicative of chronic laxative use. Anthraquinone laxatives such as senna and cascara are culprits, leading to a brown-black discolouration of the colonic mucosa due to the accumulation of lipofuscin pigment in macrophages within the lamina propria.

Intestinal melanoma

is incorrect because it is a rare malignancy that would present with more specific findings on biopsy, such as atypical melanocytes and the presence of melanin pigment within these cells. Melanomas can metastasize to the gastrointestinal tract but primary intestinal melanomas are extremely rare.

Haemochromatosis

is also incorrect. This condition leads to iron overload and deposition throughout the body due to increased intestinal absorption. However, this does not typically cause diarrhoea or weight loss and the iron deposits would be found in parenchymal cells (like hepatocytes), not macrophages.

The option

Ulcerative colitis

is incorrect because it is an inflammatory bowel disease that would present with different histological findings such as crypt abscesses, goblet cell depletion and continuous inflammation starting from the rectum. Pigment-laden macrophages are not a feature of ulcerative colitis.

Finally,

Colorectal cancer

is also incorrect. While colorectal cancer may present with symptoms like diarrhoea and weight loss, its histological findings would likely include dysplastic glandular structures or adenocarcinoma cells rather than pigment-laden macrophages.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man is referred to gastroenterology with dyspepsia and diarrhoea. He has been treated for presumed Helicobacter pylori infection by his general practitioner with no improvement in symptoms. He has no past medical history. He takes regular omeprazole 20mg once daily. He does not smoke or drink alcohol and works in IT.

Abdominal examination reveals mild tenderness in the epigastrium with no guarding or rebound tenderness. Bowel sounds are present. There is no organomegaly.

Blood results are as follows:



Hb	133 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	8.4 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.1 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	7.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	89 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	4 mg/L	(< 5)
Bilirubin	11 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	87 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	37 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	54 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	37 g/L	(35 - 50)
Calcium	2.31 mmol/L	(2.20 - 2.60)
Parathyroid hormone	2.3 pmol/L	(1.6-6.9)
Prolactin	222 miU/L	(<700)

Stool MCS and faecal calprotectin are normal.

An upper GI endoscopy is undertaken, which demonstrates numerous duodenal ulcers. A colonoscopy is normal.

A CT chest, abdomen and pelvis is arranged, which demonstrates a single 1.5cm lesion in the distal duodenum.

Given the likely diagnosis, which hormone level is likely to be abnormal?
options_json: ["Cholecystokinin", "Gastrin", "Secretin", "Somatostatin", "Vasoactive intestinal peptide"]
explanation_text:
Gastrin increases H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells

Gastrin is the correct answer. This patient who presents with refractory dyspepsia, diarrhoea, multiple duodenal ulcerations and CT evidence of a possible primary malignancy is likely to have Zollinger-Ellinson syndrome caused by a gastrin-secreting tumour (gastrinoma). The multiple duodenal ulcers are caused by increased acid secretion by gastric parietal cells as a consequence of hypergastrinemia. Levels of serum gastrin, if measured, will be very elevated. It is sometimes associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (type 1) but normal levels of PTH, calcium and prolactin make this unlikely in this case.

Secretin, somatostatin and vasoactive intestinal peptide are all hormones that inhibit H+ secretion among their other effects and are therefore not the likely cause of numerous duodenal ulcers.

Cholecystokinin does not stimulate or inhibit acid secretion but rather causes the release of digestive enzymes from the pancreas and contraction of the gallbladder.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with three months of black stools and shortness of breath. She has a past medical history of knee osteoarthritis. She drinks 10 units of alcohol per week.

On examination, there is an ejection systolic murmur in the aortic area radiating to the carotids. The blood pressure is 110/90 mmHg. The abdominal examination is unremarkable. She has conjunctival pallor.

What is a unifying explanation for the presentation?
options_json: ["Angiodysplasia", "Colorectal cancer", "Duodenal ulcer", "Gastric ulcer", "Oesophageal varices"]
explanation_text:
Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis

Angiodysplasia

is correct. The patient presents with shortness of breath and black stools. She has clinical evidence of aortic stenosis and there is a suggestion of anaemia (conjunctival pallor). Aortic stenosis may cause shortness of breath and this may be exacerbated by anaemia. Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis and can cause gastrointestinal bleeding. The combination of these two conditions is known as Heyde's syndrome.

Colorectal cancer

is incorrect. Melena is suggestive of an upper gastrointestinal bleed. Cancer tends to cause either rectal bleeding or blood mixed with stool i.e. symptoms of a lower gastrointestinal bleed.

Duodenal ulcer

is incorrect. This may cause an upper GI bleed but there would usually be a history of abdominal pain and there may be abdominal tenderness on examination. It is not classically associated with aortic stenosis and is therefore a less likely explanation.

Gastric ulcer

is incorrect. Again, abdominal pain is typically a feature of gastric ulcers and its absence makes the diagnosis less likely. It is not associated with aortic stenosis.

Oesophageal varices

is incorrect. This tends to be associated with alcoholic liver disease. Drinking 10 units of alcohol weekly is relatively unlikely to result in significant liver disease and cirrhosis.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man presented to the emergency department with nausea and vomiting that started 2 hours ago. The vomiting contains some food content but there is no blood. He also complains of abdominal pain but is unable to point to a specific location for the pain on his abdomen. On examination, he has a heart rate of 88 beats per minute, a respiratory rate of 18 breaths per minute and blood pressure of 143/90 mmHg. The emergency physician notices that he has very red palms and his abdomen shows ascites. The blood results are as shown below.


Hb	130 g/l
AST	82 u/l
ALT	38 u/l

Upon further questioning, the man reveals that he used to engage in binge drinking and he currently consumes more than 60 units of alcohol every week since he got divorced 15 years ago and recently lost his job. Upon liver biopsy, which of the following pathological features is likely to be observed?

answer_text: Excess collagen and extracellular matrix deposition in periportal and pericentral zones leading to the formation of regenerative nodules

question_text:
A 43-year-old woman is seen in the gastroenterology clinic with a four-month history of fatigue and intermittent right upper quadrant pain. Her wife noticed yellowing of her sclerae. The patient drinks two units of alcohol per week.

The patient's GP requested an abdominal ultrasound which was unremarkable. Blood tests were sent:


Hb	123 g/L	(115 - 160)
Platelets	242 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


APTT	30s	(25-35s)
PT	12s	(10-14s)


Bilirubin	30µmol/L	(3-17)
ALP	320u/L	(30-100)
ALT	32u/L	(3-40)
Î³GT	130u/L	(8-60)


IgA	2.3g/L	(0.8-3.0)
IgG	10.0g/L	(6.0-16.0)
IgM	6.0g/L	(0.4-2.5)

What is the most appropriate treatment?
options_json: ["Advice on alcohol cessation", "Colestyramine", "Elective cholecystectomy", "Liver transplant", "Ursodeoxycholic acid"]
explanation_text:
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis

Ursodeoxycholic acid

is the correct answer. This patient has primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Fatigue, jaundice, and right upper quadrant pain are all in keeping with this diagnosis. The raised IgM is highly suggestive of PBC. Additionally, PBC tends to affect middle-aged women such as this patient. Ursodeoxycholic acid is the initial treatment for PBC. In PBC, there is autoimmune-medicated progressive destruction of intrahepatic bile ducts, resulting in chronic cholestasis. Ursodeoxycholic acid increases the transportation of intracellular bile acids across the liver cell and into the canaliculus, therefore reducing liver damage in patients with PBC.

Advice on alcohol cessation

is the incorrect answer. Alcohol consumption of two units per week is unlikely to cause liver damage and there was no evidence of liver cirrhosis on the abdominal ultrasound. Given this patient has PBC, alcohol cessation might nonetheless be considered given this patient is at high risk for liver damage. However, alcohol cessation will not treat PBC and therefore ursodeoxycholic acid is the more appropriate answer.

Colestyramine

is the incorrect answer. Colestyramine is a bile-acid sequestrant that is useful to treat pruritus secondary to jaundice. This patient is not complaining of an itch and therefore colestyramine is not required at present - it would be reasonable to start should an itch develop. Colestyramine does not treat PBC.

Elective cholecystectomy

is the incorrect answer. Gallstones could explain intermittent right upper quadrant pain and an obstructing gallstone could cause jaundice. However, there is no evidence of gallstones or biliary dilatation on the abdominal ultrasound, making this very unlikely. Gallstones would not explain the raised IgM.

Liver transplant

is the incorrect answer. A liver transplant would be considered if PBC progresses to cirrhosis, or if there is clinical deterioration with no response to ursodeoxycholic acid. The patient's abdominal ultrasound showed no evidence of cirrhosis and the blood tests show no evidence of decompensated liver disease (normal platelets and clotting) - therefore a liver transplant would not be considered at present.

A 40-year-old man is referred to gastroenterology with severe itching.

His past medical history is significant for ulcerative colitis which is currently well controlled.

On examination, he has jaundiced sclera and widespread excoriation marks.

Relevant blood tests are shown below:


Bilirubin	43 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	368 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	33 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	227 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	38 g/L	(35 - 50)

What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
options_json: ["Antimitochondrial antibody titres", "Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titres", "CT abdomen", "MRCP", "Ultrasound abdomen"]
explanation_text:
MRCP is the investigations of choice in primary sclerosing cholangitis

MRCP

is correct. This investigation is the preferred diagnostic test in suspected primary sclerosing cholangitis: the most likely diagnosis in this question given the cholestatic liver function tests, patient demographics, and strong association between ulcerative colitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis.

Antimitochondrial antibody titres

is incorrect. The M2 antibody is highly specific for primary biliary cholangitis. The patient demographics and history of ulcerative colitis strongly favour primary sclerosing cholangitis rather than primary biliary cholangitis, so this answer is incorrect.

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titres

is incorrect. This may be raised in primary sclerosing cholangitis but is not specific.

CT abdomen

is incorrect. CT may show bile duct thickening/dilatation, but diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis requires MRCP or ERCP. Primary sclerosing cholangitis in this case is strongly suggested by the patient demographics, cholestatic liver function, and history of ulcerative colitis.

Ultrasound abdomen

is incorrect. This is a good test to investigate initially for bile duct abnormalities but does not provide enough information to make a diagnosis of primary sclerosing cholangitis. This requires MRCP or ERCP.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with multiple symptoms. He reports a six-month history of diarrhoea, with stools that are pale and float, abdominal pain, migrating polyarthralgia, intermittent fevers and photosensitive rashes. He had a single episode of uveitis previously and was found to be HLA-B27 positive at the time.

On examination, there is mild peripheral oedema. There are small petechiae on the torso and abdomen. The skin is subtly hyperpigmented.

The patient undergoes an upper GI endoscopy.

Given the likely diagnosis, what would be the expected findings of a jejunal biopsy?
options_json: ["Caseating granulomata", "Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes", "Macrophages containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules", "Non caseating granulomata", "Villous atrophy"]
explanation_text:
Whipple's disease: jejunal biopsy shows deposition of macrophages containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules

Macrophages containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules is correct. This patient presents with a multisystem disease with symptoms of abdominal pain, diarrhoea, steatorrhoea, migrating polyarthralgia, photosensitivity, skin hyperpigmentation, petechiae and peripheral oedema. This constellation of findings suggests Whipple's disease as the diagnosis. This is a multi-system disorder caused by infection with

Tropheryma whipplei

, which is a gram-positive rod bacteria. It is diagnosed by demonstrating macrophages containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules on jejunal biopsy. It is more common in males and those who are HLA-B27 positive. The bruising and oedema is due to malabsorption of protein, vitamin K and vitamin C. The hyperpigmentation is typically due to vitamin B3 malabsorption and subsequent deficiency.

Caseating granuloma is incorrect. This would be a typical finding of tuberculosis. While abdominal TB can cause abdominal pain and fevers, it often causes ascites and intestinal obstruction in addition. It is not associated with skin hyperpigmentation or photosensitivity and is less likely to cause a migrating polyarthralgia.

Non-caseating granuloma is incorrect. This could be reflective or sarcoidosis of crohn's disease. Neither condition is classically associated with hyperpigmentation or photosensitivity.

Villous atrophy is incorrect. This a the characteristic finding of coeliac disease. This could cause abdominal pain and diarrhoea. It can also cause a rash (dermatitis herpetiformis), which may be aggravated by sunlight. However, it is not typically associated with fevers, skin hyperpigmentation or migratory polyarthralgia and therefore Whipple's disease is more likely.

Increased intraepithelial lymphocytes is incorrect. This a the characteristic finding of coeliac disease. This could cause abdominal pain and diarrhoea. It can also cause a rash (dermatitis herpetiformis), which may be aggravated by sunlight. However, it is not typically associated with fevers, skin hyperpigmentation or migratory polyarthralgia and therefore Whipple's disease is more likely.
