options_json: ["Smoking", "Blood group O", "Nitrates in diet", "Pernicious anaemia", "H. pylori infection"]

question_text:
A 55-year-old man presents to the emergency department with progressive abdominal swelling and no significant past medical history. On examination, his abdomen is distended and shifting dullness is present. Fluid aspiration from his abdomen and subsequent blood tests reveal the following results:


Serum albumin	31 g/L
Ascites albumin	11 g/L

What is the most likely cause of his presentation?
options_json: ["Hypoalbuminaemia", "Peritoneal TB", "Peritoneal carcinomatosis", "Portal hypertension", "Severe malnutrition"]
explanation_text:
Ascites: a high SAAG gradient (> 11g/L) indicates portal hypertension

Portal hypertension

is the correct diagnosis. The patient presents with progressive abdominal distension, and clinical examination reveals ascites, as indicated by shifting dullness. To investigate this further, serum and ascitic fluid albumin levels are measured. The serum-ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) is calculated by subtracting the ascitic albumin concentration from the serum albumin concentration; in this case, it is 31 - 11 = 20 g/L. A SAAG exceeding 11 g/L suggests portal hypertension as the underlying cause of the ascites. It is crucial to understand that portal hypertension may arise from a variety of pathologies, rendering it an unspecific indicator.

Hypoalbuminaemia

does not explain this patient's presentation. Although slightly low serum albumin levels are noted, hypoalbuminaemia-induced ascites typically present with a SAAG below 11 g/L. Hypoalbuminaemia can occur due to multiple causes such as liver disease, renal disease, malnutrition, sepsis, and burns among others.

Peritoneal TB

is not a likely diagnosis in this case. Peritoneal tuberculosis generally results in a SAAG lower than 11 g/L and its diagnosis can be challenging, often necessitating peritoneal biopsy for confirmation rather than relying solely on fluid analysis. Additionally, symptoms such as fever, night sweats or weight loss would be expected in cases of peritoneal TB; these are not present in this patient.

Peritoneal carcinomatosis

is also inconsistent with the findings since malignant ascites typically yield a SAAG below 11 g/L. This indicates that such forms of ascites are not associated with increased hydrostatic pressure within the portal system.

Lastly,

severe malnutrition

does not correspond with the clinical presentation as it also leads to a SAAG less than 11 g/L when associated with ascites.

question_text:
A 59-year-old woman presented with painful dysphagia, poor appetite and weight loss over the past nine months. She is a heavy chain smoker with a 30 pack year history. She admits to consuming alcohol excessively. An urgent barium swallow was arranged and shows the presence of a suspicious malignant oesophageal stricture.

What is the best investigation to assess for mural invasion?
options_json: ["Contrast-enhanced CT", "T2-weighted MRI scan", "Endoscopic ultrasound", "Conventional side-viewing duodenoscopy", "Positron-emission tomography (PET) scan"]
explanation_text:
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion

The endoscopic ultrasound aids the visualisation of local invasion as it can display all the layers of the wall of the oesophagus and should routinely be performed with CT or MRI scans.

Overall, endoscopic ultrasound is far superior to CT or MRI when assessing mural invasion.

The positron-emission tomography (PET) scan is increasingly being employed by oncologists in detecting and following up the tumour progression.

Duodenoscopes are essentially specialised endoscopes that are used primarily for endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). They are side-viewing (rather than forward-viewing) endoscopes that have an advantage in being able to view the major duodenal papilla.

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with colicky right upper quadrant pain. She ate a fatty meal earlier. She has a raised body mass index (32 kg/m²) but no other past medical history.

On examination, there is right upper quadrant tenderness but she is afebrile.


Hb	136 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	412* 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	8.9 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.4 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	4 mg/L	(< 5)
Bilirubin	12 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	44 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	34 u/L	(3 - 40)

What cells are responsible for the secretion of the hormone implicated in the cause of the underlying pathology?
options_json: ["Beta cells", "D cells", "G cells", "I cells", "S cells"]
explanation_text:
CCK - I cells in upper small intestine

I cells

is the correct answer. The patient presents with colicky right upper quadrant pain after eating a fatty meal in the background of a raised body mass index. The likely diagnosis is biliary colic. CCK is released in response to a fatty meal and is the major hormonal stimulator of biliary contraction. It is the contraction of the gallbladder against a gallstone impacted in the bladder neck that causes the pain of biliary colic. I cells secrete CCK.

Beta cells

are incorrect. Beta cells in the pancreas secrete insulin. While insulin may be secreted in response to a fatty meal, it does not cause contraction of the gallbladder in contrast to CCK.

D cells

are incorrect. These cells secrete somatostatin. This decreases acid and pepsin secretion, decreases gastrin secretion, decreases pancreatic enzyme secretion, decreases insulin and glucagon secretion, inhibits trophic effects of gastrin and stimulates gastric mucous production.

G cells

are incorrect. The cells are located in the stomach and release gastrin. This is caused by distension of the stomach and exposure to luminal peptides and amino acids. While it can increase gastric motility it does not cause gallbladder contraction.

S cells

are incorrect. These cells secrete a bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic cells and are stimulated by fatty acids. However, it does not cause contraction of the gallbladder.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man presents to the GP with a 3-month history of diarrhoea. The patient states that he has lost weight and his clothes feel baggier, although he is not sure how much he has lost. On further questioning, he discloses that he has had pain in both of his knees for a similar period of time, and for the last couple of days he has suffered blurred vision on the extremes of his vision. On examination, widespread lymphadenopathy is noted.

What is the most likely underlying cause?
options_json: ["Campylobacter jejuni", "Cryptosporidium", "Neisseria gonorrhoea", "Treponema pallidum", "Tropheryma whipplei"]
explanation_text:
Diarrhoea, weight, arthralgia, lymphadenopathy, ophthalmoplegia ?Whipple's disease

This presentation, although rare, should raise suspicion of

Tropheryma whipplei

infection, also known as Whipple's disease. The infection is chronic and classically causes intestinal malabsorption. As the disease progresses, symptoms become more systemic with large joint arthralgia and lymphadenopathy often occurring. Less commonly, neurological manifestations such as ophthalmoplegia, confusion and facial muscle deficits can occur. Treatment is with a protracted course of antibiotics; penicillins and co-trimoxazole are often first-line.

Campylobacter jejuni

is a cause of bloody diarrhoea, however lymphadenopathy, arthralgia and ophthalmoplegia would be highly atypical. Although the infection is strongly associated with Guillain Barre syndrome, ophthalmoplegia would not be a typical manifestation of this.

Cryptosporidium

causes watery diarrhoea but is not associated with joint or neurological involvement. This parasitic infection typically is spread via contaminated water sources.

Disseminated

Neisseria gonorrhoea

is not associated with malabsorption or diarrhoea. Arthralgia and arthritis can be expected, however, any neurological involvement is likely to manifest as a meningitis picture rather than ophthalmoplegia.

Treponema pallidum

, or syphilis, can cause weight loss and lymphadenopathy in the secondary stage. In its extreme form, neurosyphilis can cause cranial nerve palsy's, but this is often secondary to syphilis meningitis. Arthralgia is less associated with

Treponema pallidum

.

question_text: Which one of the following features of haemochromatosis may be reversible with treatment?
options_json: ["Cardiomyopathy", "Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism", "Diabetes mellitus", "Arthropathy", "Liver cirrhosis"]
explanation_text:
In haemochromatosis, cardiomyopathy and skin pigmentation are reversible with treatment

The correct answer is

Cardiomyopathy

. Haemochromatosis is a genetic disorder that results in excessive absorption of dietary iron, leading to its deposition in various organs. The heart is one of the organs affected, and iron deposition can lead to cardiomyopathy. However, with early diagnosis and treatment through regular phlebotomies or chelation therapy, the myocardial iron overload can be reduced and cardiac function can improve, making this feature potentially reversible.

Discussing the incorrect options:

Hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism

occurs due to pituitary gland involvement in haemochromatosis. Iron deposits within the pituitary gland impair its ability to secrete gonadotropins, which leads to hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism. This condition typically presents as impotence in men and amenorrhea in women. Unfortunately, this endocrine dysfunction is not usually reversible with treatment as it's due to permanent damage of the pituitary gland.

Diabetes mellitus

develops when pancreatic beta cells are damaged by iron deposits, resulting in insulin deficiency. Despite treatment for haemochromatosis, diabetes mellitus may not be reversible because of irreversible damage to pancreatic beta cells.

Arthropathy

, specifically a degenerative arthritis affecting the metacarpophalangeal joints (most commonly the second and third), is another common manifestation of haemochromatosis. This arthropathy results from direct joint damage caused by iron deposition and is not generally reversible with treatment.

Finally,

Liver cirrhosis

occurs due to hepatic iron overload causing fibrosis and eventually cirrhosis if left untreated. Once cirrhosis has developed it cannot be reversed even after successful de-ironing treatments for haemochromatosis; however progression can be halted or slowed significantly with appropriate management.

question_text: A 62-year-old man is called for review after a positive faecal occult blood test done as part of the national screening programme. During counselling for colonoscopy he asks what percentage of patients with a positive faecal occult blood test have colorectal cancer. What is the most accurate answer?
explanation_text:
Colorectal cancer screening - PPV of FOB = 5 - 15%

The correct answer is

5 - 15%

. According to the UK National Health Service, approximately 10% of individuals with a positive faecal occult blood test (FOBT) will be found to have colorectal cancer on subsequent colonoscopy. This percentage falls within the range of 5 - 15%, making it the most accurate answer.

The option of

0.5 - 2%

is incorrect as it significantly underestimates the prevalence of colorectal cancer in individuals with a positive FOBT. While not every individual with a positive test will have cancer, the likelihood is higher than this range suggests.

Similarly,

20 - 30%

,

30 - 50%

, and

55 - 75%

all overestimate the prevalence of colorectal cancer following a positive FOBT. While a positive test does indicate an increased risk for colorectal cancer, most individuals will not have cancer. These options may reflect the prevalence rates in high-risk populations or those with additional symptoms suggestive of malignancy, but they do not accurately represent the general population screened through the national programme.

It's important to note that while only around 10% of people with a positive FOBT will have colorectal cancer, many others may have other significant findings such as polyps or inflammatory bowel disease which also require further management and treatment. Therefore, even if the chance of having cancer is relatively low, it's still crucial for patients to undergo further investigation if they receive a positive result from their screening test.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with pain in his hands. He has no significant past medical history.

On examination, there were osteoarthritic changes in the hands. The skin was noted to have a slate grey appearance.

Plain radiography of the hands demonstrated hook-like osteophytes at the 2nd and 3rd digits at the metacarpophalangeal joints.

Given the likely diagnosis, what are the best means of monitoring treatment response in this condition?
options_json: ["Hba1c", "Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)", "Serum iron", "Total iron binding capacity", "Transferrin saturation"]
explanation_text:
Ferritin and transferrin saturation are used to monitor treatment in haemochromatosis

Transferrin saturation

is correct. The patient has haemochromatosis. Typical clinical features of this condition include secondary osteoarthritis (with hook-like osteophytes at the 2nd and 3rd digits at the metacarpophalangeal joints being pathognomonic) and a slate-grey appearance of the skin. A transferrin saturation > 55% is typical in untreated disease and this is the best marker to monitor treatment response.

Hba1c

is incorrect. Haemochromatosis can cause diabetes due to iron deposition in the pancreas. This is a type 1 diabetes picture. The condition is also known as 'bronze diabetes' due to the colour of the skin. However, the patient will not definitely develop diabetes and therefore the best monitoring parameter for treatment response is transferrin saturation. Of course, if the patient did develop diabetes you may want to monitor the HbA1c.

Insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1)

is incorrect. This is a parameter used to measure disease activity in acromegaly. This condition can cause osteoarthritis. However, the slate grey appearance of the skin is not typical. Additionally, the other characteristic features of acromegaly are absent here.

Serum iron

is incorrect. This is a poor reflection of total body iron stores and is not used for monitoring.

Total iron-binding capacity

is incorrect. In haemochromatosis, this will be low. However, it is not used to monitor treatment response.

question_text:
A 47-year-old woman has recently had routine blood tests which have shown the following:


Bilirubin	12 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	88 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	103 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	74 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	49 g/L	(35 - 50)
Ferritin	404 ug/L	(20 - 230)
Iron	22 umol/L	(10-30)
Total iron-binding capacity	69 umol/L	(43-80)

She has a history of obstructive sleep apnoea, pre-diabetes and mild learning disability. She has a body mass index of 33 kg/m². She is taking vitamin D supplements but no other regular medication. She drinks 14 units of alcohol weekly.

On further exploration, she reports feeling well with no abdominal pain.

What is the likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Alcoholic hepatitis", "Gallstones", "Haemochromatosis", "Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease", "Primary biliary cholangitis"]
explanation_text:
Obesity with abnormal LFTs - ? non-alcoholic fatty liver disease

Raised transaminases in an obese individual who does not have a history of excessive alcohol consumption should raise the suspicion of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD). This disease is also closely linked to insulin resistance, hence her history of pre-diabetes is a further risk factor.

Alcoholic hepatitis is unlikely given her level of alcohol intake. NICE guidelines state that consumption of less than 20g (2.5 units) per day in women, and less than 30g (3.75 units) per day in men, is used as the cut-off to diagnose NAFLD.

Gallstones in isolation do not tend to cause raised transaminases unless associated with complications such as acute cholecystitis or ascending cholangitis. This patient is not exhibiting such symptoms.

While it is important to arrange further investigations (including autoantibodies) to check for other liver pathology, there is little indication of primary biliary cholangitis in this patient. This usually manifests either in symptoms of pruritus, or an incidental finding of a raised ALP in an asymptomatic patient.

While haemochromatosis can certainly manifest in abnormal liver function tests with a raised ferritin, the transferrin saturation - calculated as (iron / TIBC) x 100 - is well below the 40% threshold for females (based on British Society of Haematology guidelines) which would prompt consideration of iron overload. Furthermore we would normally expect ferritin to be even higher (>1000 ug/L) in haemochromatosis. Note that milder elevations of serum ferritin is commonly seen in NAFLD, as seen here.

question_text:
A patient is recovering in the gastroenterology ward after an upper gastrointestinal variceal bleed. He has ascites and jaundice as a result of a chronic hepatitis C infection. His routine blood tests come back showing impaired renal function. The results are shown below. They were normal 3 days ago when he was admitted. Urinalysis shows no protein or blood.


Na+	140 mmol/l
K+	3.8 mmol/l
Urea	11.2 mmol/l
Creatinine	302 µmol/l

Given this man's presentation, what is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Renal calculi", "Focal segmental glomerulonephritis", "Type-1 hepatorenal syndrome", "Type -2 hepatorenal syndrome", "Minimal change glomerulonephritis"]
explanation_text:
Speed of onset can help to differentiate the type of hepatorenal syndrome

This question is asking about a patient currently admitted to hospital following an upper GI bleed. The patient is suffering from chronic liver failure and then goes onto develop renal failure. This is the typical history of hepatorenal syndrome.

Hepatorenal syndrome is split into type 1 and 2. Type 1 is a rapid onset hepatorenal syndrome (less than two weeks). This typically occurs following an acute event such as an upper GI bleed. Type 2 is a more gradual decline in renal function and is generally associated with refractory ascites. Therefore as his blood tests were normal 3 days ago this is type 1.

Renal calculi would present with loin to groin pain as well as blood in the urine.

In focal segmental glomerulonephritis or minimal change glomerulonephritis, you would expect to see protein or blood in the urine and their absence helps to rule these out.

A 36-year-old man has abdominal pain, malaise, fatigue, and yellow skin discolouration. He has consumed 24 units of alcohol weekly for 4 years and binge drank 40 units over the last 6 days. He takes no regular medications.

He is jaundiced with tender hepatomegaly. There is no ascites, and his GCS is 15.

Investigations:


Hb	130 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	280 * 10 9/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.5 * 10 9/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Urea	4.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	98 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Bicarbonate	23 mmol/L	(22-28)


Bilirubin	83 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	89 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	92 u/L	(3 - 40)
γGT	145 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	34 g/L	(35 - 50)
Prothrombin time	26.2 secs	(10-14 secs)

Which option is the best next step in his management?
options_json: ["Liver transplant", "Pentoxifylline", "Prednisolone", "Rifaximin", "Vitamin E"]
explanation_text:
Corticosteroids are used in the management of severe alcoholic hepatitis

Prednisolone

is correct. The most likely diagnosis is acute alcoholic hepatitis, given the history of chronic alcohol use with recent binge drinking, clinical features of jaundice and tender hepatomegaly, and laboratory findings including elevated bilirubin, prolonged prothrombin time (PT), raised gamma-GT, and raised ALT. The markedly prolonged PT and high bilirubin result in a Maddrey’s Discriminant Function score > 32 (around 61 in this case), indicating severe disease with poor prognosis. Prednisolone is indicated because corticosteroids reduce inflammation and improve short-term survival in patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis.

Liver transplant

is incorrect. Liver transplantation is contraindicated in active alcohol consumption without demonstrated abstinence. In exceptional cases, after a multidisciplinary meeting, early liver transplantation may be considered if there is a low risk of relapse post-transplant and if strict abstinence and psychosocial criteria are met. However, this would be considered if the patient had failed to respond to medical therapy (e.g. corticosteroids), which is not the case here.

Pentoxifylline

is incorrect as the STOPAH trial demonstrated that it does not improve survival in acute alcoholic hepatitis when compared to prednisolone, which shows a short-term mortality benefit. It is no longer routinely recommended for the treatment of severe alcoholic hepatitis.

Rifaximin

is incorrect, as this is used in the prevention of hepatic encephalopathy in patients with established cirrhosis by reducing gut ammonia-producing bacteria. In this scenario, this patient has no evidence of hepatic encephalopathy (e.g. asterixis, confusion). It plays no role in the acute inflammatory phase of alcoholic hepatitis.

Vitamin E

is incorrect as this is not routinely used in alcoholic hepatitis. While it has demonstrated some anti-oxidant properties, it has mainly been studied in non-alcoholic fatty liver disease rather than alcoholic hepatitis.

explanation_text:
Torsades-des-pointes secondary to hypomagnesaemia can result as a consequence of refeeding syndrome

Refeeding syndrome is characterised by electrolyte abnormalities including hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia. Severe hypomagnesaemia and hypokalaemia can lead to the development of torsades-des-pointes, a variant of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with QT prolongation.

The other options are less likely to be precipitated by the electrolyte disturbances described in the question.

question_text:
A 70-year-old woman presented with difficulty swallowing, chronic cough associated with occasional swellings in the neck. She had a recent admission where she was treated with intravenous antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia. She was reviewed on this occasion by the gastroenterology team who were concerned about her symptoms and feel she is at risk of further aspiration. They decided to perform an urgent barium swallow investigation.

What is the barium swallow most likely to show?
options_json: ["Achalasia", "Barrett's oesophagus", "Diffuse oesophageal spasm", "Oesophageal stricture", "Pharyngeal pouch"]
explanation_text:
Dysphagia, aspiration pneumonia, halitosis → ?pharyngeal pouch

Pharyngeal pouch (also known as Zenker's diverticulum) is a small bulge, like a hernia, that occurs in the pharynx. This is most commonly in elderly patients (over 70 years) with symptoms such as dysphagia, regurgitation, chronic cough, aspiration and weight loss. It occurs through a weakness in the muscle layer called the Killian dehiscence. The diagnostic investigation of choice is a barium swallow.

Barrett's oesophagus is a where cells that line your oesophagus change and begin to look like the cells that make up your intestines. This occurs when cells are damaged by prolonged exposure to stomach acid. This often arises after years of experiencing gastroesophageal reflux (GORD). This commonly produces symptoms of heartburn and reflux which are not present in this case. The diagnostic investigation of choice is endoscopy with biopsy to enable histological analysis and not barium swallow.

Diffuse oesophageal spasm is where a patient experiences uncoordinated contractions of the oesophagus, which may result in difficulty swallowing or regurgitation. An endoscopy would typically demonstrate a corkscrew oesophagus.

Achalasia is primarily a neurogenic oesophageal motility disorder with impaired oesophageal peristalsis and a lack of lower oesophageal sphincter relaxation. It can cause symptoms of dysphagia and regurgitation of undigested food. A barium swallow investigation typically shows a 'bird beak' appearance.

An oesophageal stricture is an abnormal tightening or narrowing of the oesophagus making it difficult for food to travel down. This is usually investigated and managed endoscopically and not with barium swallow.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman presents to the gastroenterology clinic with a 2-year history of abdominal discomfort, bloating, and altered bowel habits characterized by constipation. She reports that her symptoms worsen with stress and are partially relieved by defecation. Despite trying over-the-counter laxatives and increasing her dietary fibre intake through bran cereals, she hasn't noticed significant improvement. Her physical examination is unremarkable.

Which dietary modification is most appropriate for this patient?
options_json: ["Increase intake of insoluble fibre such as bran", "Limit intake of wholemeal bread and cereals high in bran", "Reduce consumption of dairy products", "Increase fluid intake to at least 10 cups per day", "Adopt a gluten-free diet"]
answer_text: Limit intake of wholemeal bread and cereals high in bran
explanation_text:
Insoluble sources of fibre such as bran and wholemeal should be avoided in IBS

Limit intake of wholemeal bread and cereals high in bran

is the correct answer because insoluble fibres like those found in bran can exacerbate symptoms in patients with IBS, particularly those with constipation-predominant IBS. These fibres may increase gut motility but do not dissolve well in water, potentially leading to increased bloating and discomfort.

Increase intake of insoluble fibre such as bran

might seem plausible for constipation; however, it often worsens symptoms in IBS due to its potential to cause bloating and discomfort without effectively relieving constipation.

Reduce consumption of dairy products

could be considered if lactose intolerance was suspected or confirmed. However, there is no indication from the scenario that dairy is contributing to her symptoms.

Increase fluid intake to at least 10 cups per day

can be beneficial generally but focusing solely on fluid intake without addressing specific dietary triggers related to IBS may not provide adequate relief.

Adopt a gluten-free diet

would be relevant if coeliac disease or non-coeliac gluten sensitivity was suspected; however, these conditions are not suggested by the clinical scenario provided.

explanation_text:
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis

Ursodeoxycholic acid is the correct answer. question_text: The action of which one of the following brush border enzymes results in the formation of glucose and galactose?
options_json: ["Dipeptidase", "A-dextrinase", "Maltase", "Lactase", "Sucrase"]
explanation_text:
Brush border enzymes:

The correct answer is

Lactase

. Lactase is a brush border enzyme located in the small intestines. It hydrolyses lactose, a disaccharide found in milk and dairy products, into glucose and galactose. This allows for the absorption of these simple sugars into the bloodstream. A deficiency in lactase can lead to lactose intolerance, where undigested lactose passes into the colon causing symptoms such as bloating, diarrhoea and abdominal cramps.

Dipeptidase

is incorrect as this enzyme functions to break down dipeptides into individual amino acids. Dipeptides are molecules that contain two amino acids linked by a single peptide bond. Therefore, dipeptidases do not produce glucose or galactose.

A-dextrinase

(also known as isomaltase) is also an incorrect answer. This brush border enzyme acts on α-dextrins, which are intermediate products of starch digestion. It breaks α-1,6-glycosidic linkages producing glucose molecules but does not produce galactose.

Maltase

is another incorrect option. Maltase catalyses the hydrolysis of maltose (a disaccharide produced from starch) into two glucose units. While it produces glucose, it does not yield any galactose.

Finally,

Sucrase

is also not the correct answer. Sucrase breaks down sucrose (common table sugar) into glucose and fructose - not galactose. Like lactase, sucrase resides on the brush border membrane of the small intestine epithelial cells facilitating carbohydrate digestion.

question_text:
A 40-year-old woman with a family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 presents to her GP with upper abdominal pain. She reports that she has experienced worsening dyspepsia after meals for the last three months. On wider questioning, she reveals that for this period, her stools have been loose, and she has lost around a stone in weight unintentionally.

What is the normal physiological role of the hormone responsible for this patient's presentation?
options_json: ["Delay gastric emptying", "Increase H+ secretion by gastric chief cells", "Increase H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells", "Stimulate pancreatic bicarbonate secretion", "Suppress the release of pancreatic enzymes"]
answer_text: Increase H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells
explanation_text:
Gastrin increases H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells

The correct answer is

increase H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells

. This patient has a gastrinoma, causing the clinical presentation of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome. Here, excess gastrin production causes an overly acidic environment in the duodenum, causing dyspepsia and malabsorptive symptoms (in this case, diarrhoea and weight loss) as the intestinal pH is no longer optimised for its digestive enzymes to function. A further clue to the diagnosis is the family history of multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1, with which around one-quarter of gastrinomas are associated. The normal role of gastrin is to increase H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells.

Delay gastric emptying

is incorrect. Gastrin secretion is stimulated by stomach distension and the presence of undigested peptides in the stomach. As such, it promotes digestion and increases gastric emptying.

Increase H+ secretion by gastric chief cells

is incorrect, as the chief (or peptic) cells of the stomach secrete pepsinogen and gastric lipase to aid with the digestion of proteins and fats, rather than hydrochloric acid.

Stimulate pancreatic bicarbonate secretion

is incorrect. This function is carried out by secretin, produced by duodenal S-cells, rather than gastrin.

Suppress the release of pancreatic enzymes

is incorrect. This is performed by somatostatin, which is produced in the delta cells of the stomach, duodenum and pancreas.

question_text:
A 32-year-old man presents with several weeks of right-sided abdominal pain. He has recently migrated from Turkey and has no significant past medical history.

On examination, the abdomen is tender in the upper right quadrant. Significant hepatomegaly is evident. An urgent ultrasound scan is requested:


Liver ultrasound	Multiseptated, multivesicular cyst - several daughter cysts present. Thin-walled, approximately 7cm diameter overall.

What is the definitive treatment option for this condition?
options_json: ["Albendazole", "Dexamethasone", "Praziquantel", "Puncture, aspiration, injection and reaspiration (PAIR)", "Surgery"]
explanation_text:
Surgery is the mainstay of treatment for hydatid cysts

This patient's presentation and imaging findings are suggestive of a hydatid cyst. These occur due to infection due to the tapeworm parasite

Echinococcus granulosus

, most commonly in the Mediterranean and Middle East. An outer fibrous capsule forms, containing 'daughter' cysts as seen here. Most commonly, hydatid cysts form in the liver. Definitive treatment for the condition involves

surgery

to excise the cyst, ensuring not to rupture the cyst walls during the process.

Concurrent treatment with antiparasitic medication, such as

albendazole

, takes place preoperatively and postoperatively. However, this is not the definitive treatment option for the condition - surgery is necessary.

Dexamethasone

may be used in the management of allergic reactions in echinococcosis, especially following cyst rupture. It may also be administered as an adjunct to decrease perilesional oedema resulting from an intracranial hydatid cyst. The evidence supporting its use for oedema in hepatic hydatid cysts, however, is lacking. The definitive option here remains surgery.

Praziquantel

may be used in conjunction with albendazole, as some studies show the combination is more effective than albendazole monotherapy. These drugs, however, are used alongside surgery, not instead of it.

PAIR

is incorrect. This procedure may be suitable for patients with a simpler hydatid cyst (a unilocular cyst without 'daughter' cysts). However, as this patient's cyst is multiseptated, surgery is more appropriate.

A 21-year-old male presents to the Emergency Department after developing severe left iliac fossa pain, abdominal cramping and pyrexia. He has a past medical history of ulcerative colitis which has been previously well managed with oral mesalazine.

He describes a flare in his symptoms over the preceding 4 days, with the passage of 8 loose bowel motions daily which are each mixed with bright red blood.

On examination, his abdomen is soft, with generalized tenderness in all four quadrants and voluntary guarding in the left iliac fossa.

Other observations as follows:

heart rate 110 bpm
blood pressure 116/72 mmHg
temperature 37.9 degrees
oxygen saturations 97% on room air.

He has routine blood tests sent in the department


Hb	104 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	325 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	142 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.9 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	89 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	93 mg/L	(< 5)

An abdominal x-ray is requested which shows some thumbprinting of the large bowel mucosa.

Which of the following is the most suitable initial management?
options_json: ["Increase dose of oral mesalazine", "Methotrexate infusion", "Rectal mesalazine", "Oral azathioprine", "Intravenous hydrocortisone"]
explanation_text:
A severe flare of ulcerative colitis should be treated in hospital with IV corticosteroids

This patient is suffering from an acute exacerbation of his ulcerative colitis (UC). The severity of flares can be gauged using the Truelove and Witts criteria. This patient is passing >6 bloody stools/day, has a low-grade pyrexia and displays features of systemic upset and therefore is classed as severe UC. In order to induce remission, intravenous steroids (e.g hydrocortisone 100mg QDS) to be given in hospital are recommended as first-line therapy.

Oral mesalazine can be used to induce remission in a mild-moderate flare of ulcerative colitis, but is not suitable for induction of remission in severe cases.

Methotrexate is not recommended for use to induce or maintain remission in ulcerative colitis, but has benefit in Crohn's disease and therefore is not suitable in this case.

Rectal mesalazine can be used as an alternative or in addition to oral mesalazine to induce remission in mild-moderate flares. It is particularly efficacious in distal proctitis but it is not suitable for acute severe exacerbations.

Oral azathioprine is most useful to maintain remission after exacerbations of UC (usually 2 in 1 year) which have required steroids. However, it is not used as a sole agent to induce remission of the initial inflammatory process.

question_text: Which one of the following statements regarding gastrin is true?
options_json: ["Secreted by D cells in the stomach", "Secretion is inhibited by high antral pH", "Reduces acid secretion in the stomach", "Increases gastric motility", "Distension of the stomach inhibits secretion"]
explanation_text:
Gastrin - increases gastric motility

Increases gastric motility

is the correct answer. Gastrin is a peptide hormone primarily produced by G cells in the gastric antrum and duodenum. One of its key physiological actions is to increase gastric motility. Gastrin stimulates smooth muscle contraction in the stomach, which enhances gastric mixing and emptying. This effect is part of gastrin's overall role in promoting digestion. By increasing gastric motility, gastrin helps to mix food with gastric secretions and facilitates the movement of chyme from the stomach into the duodenum.

Secreted by D cells in the stomach

is incorrect. Gastrin is produced by G cells, not D cells, in the gastric antrum and duodenum. D cells in the gastrointestinal tract secrete somatostatin, which actually inhibits gastrin release and gastric acid secretion. This is an important regulatory mechanism in the stomach to prevent excessive acid production.

Secretion is inhibited by high antral pH

is incorrect. The opposite is true - gastrin secretion is inhibited by low antral pH (acidic environment) and stimulated by high antral pH (alkaline environment). This represents a negative feedback mechanism whereby gastrin stimulates acid secretion, and when the pH becomes sufficiently acidic, gastrin secretion is inhibited. This prevents excessive acid production that could damage the gastric mucosa.

Reduces acid secretion in the stomach

is incorrect. Gastrin actually stimulates acid secretion in the stomach. It acts on the parietal cells of the gastric glands, either directly or by stimulating histamine release from enterochromaffin-like (ECL) cells, to increase hydrochloric acid production. This is one of the primary functions of gastrin in the digestive process.

Distension of the stomach inhibits secretion

is incorrect. Gastric distension (stretching of the stomach wall) actually stimulates gastrin secretion rather than inhibiting it. This is part of the normal physiological response to food intake. When food enters the stomach causing distension, gastrin secretion increases to promote acid secretion and gastric motility, facilitating digestion.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman is admitted to the acute medical unit due to several days of watery diarrhoea. She is clinically dehydrated and febrile.

Blood and stool cultures return negative. However Clostridium difficile is detected in stool and toxin is also present.

What medication may have increased her risk of developing this condition?
options_json: ["Bendroflumethiazide", "Furosemide", "Omeprazole", "Peptac", "Prednisolone"]
explanation_text:
Omeprazole can increase your risk of severe diarrhoea (

Proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) such as

omeprazole

and lansoprazole are recognised to increase a person's risk of

C. difficile

diarrhoea. This risk increases further alongside other risk factors such as broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy. It is also recommended to stop PPIs once an episode is diagnosed, as this can reduce the risk of recurrence.

Bendroflumethiazide

can cause diarrhoea as an adverse effect alongside electrolyte disturbances such as hypokalaemia. It does not specifically increase the risk of

C. difficile

but obviously should be withheld where there are concerns about volume depletion.

Furosemide

is incorrect. This is a loop diuretic used in the management of fluid overload. Its main side effects include electrolyte imbalances and postural hypotension. It does not specifically increase the risk of

C. difficile

.

Peptac

is incorrect. This forms a protective layer over the stomach acid, preventing reflux. However, unlike PPIs, it does not reduce gastric acid production and therefore does not increase the risk of

C. difficile

.

Prednisolone

is incorrect. Although long-term corticosteroid therapy increases the risk of many infections, this has not been shown to be the case for

C. difficile

.

question_text:
You are looking after an 82-year-old woman who develops profuse diarrhoea. She recently completed a course of ciprofloxacin for a urinary tract infection. Two other patients in her bay also develop diarrhoea.

A stool culture is awaited.

What is the mechanism of transmission of the likely infectious agent?
options_json: ["Aerosol", "Droplet", "Faecal-oral route by ingestion of bacteria", "Faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores", "Waterborne"]
answer_text: Faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores
explanation_text:
Clostridioides difficile

Faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores

is correct. The patient most likely has

C. difficile

infection due to the recent history of ciprofloxacin.  This infection spreads via the faecal-oral route by ingestion of spores.

Aerosol

is incorrect.  Aerosol transmission is the transmission of an infectious disease through small particles suspended in the air. Examples include measles, varicella zoster, and influenza virus.

Droplet

is incorrect. Respiratory droplet transmission is the usual route for respiratory infections. Common pathogens spread by droplet transmission include influenza virus, rhinovirus, respiratory syncytial virus, enterovirus, and norovirus.

Faecal-oral route by ingestion of bacteria

is incorrect.

C.difficile

spreads via the ingestion of spores.

Waterborne

is incorrect. Cholera, typhoid fever, dysentery, and hepatitis A and E, are examples of waterborne diseases.

question_text:
A 70-year-old is seen on the ward after originally being admitted for a chest infection requiring several courses of antibiotics.

After the last course, the patient's respiratory symptoms improved however they developed diarrhoea with a stool sample testing positive for Clostridium difficile and so they were started on a course of oral vancomycin.

Today is day 10 of the vancomycin but the patient still reports diarrhoea and abdominal cramps. Observations and investigations today are:


Heart rate 102/min
BP 130/80 mmHg
Oxygen saturations 96% on air
Temperature 38.1 oC


WCC	15x109/L	4.5-11
Abdominal x-ray	Evidence of colitis	

What treatment should be started now?
options_json: ["Bezlotoxumab", "IV vancomycin", "Oral fidaxomicin", "Oral gentamicin", "Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole"]
explanation_text:
If

This patient has developed complications secondary to a

Clostridium difficile

infection most like a result of extensive broad-spectrum antibiotic use. The patient has evidence of severe infection with a raised white cell count and evidence of colitis on imaging. First-line therapy for

C. difficile

is oral vancomycin for 10 days however if no improvement is seen then second-line therapy, in the form of

oral fidaxomicin

should be trialled.

Bezlotoxumab

is a monoclonal antibody shown to target

C. difficile

toxin B, one of the main exotoxins produced by the bacteria causing intestinal damage and pseudomembranous colitis. Currently NICE do not support its use for the management of

C. difficile

as it is not cost-effective.

IV vancomycin

does not have a clear role in the management of

C. difficile

infections with the oral form of the antibiotic used as first-line before escalating to other therapeutic agents.

Oral gentamicin

has very limited use for infection management in general with the IV formula used mainly for urinary infections and topical formula in eye and ear infections. Oral gentamicin has no role in the management of

C. difficile

.

Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole

is reserved for third-line or life-threatening cases of

C. difficile

. This treatment regime should therefore only be used if oral fidaxomicin fails or the patient has features such as hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon.

question_text:
You are admitting a 68-year-old carpenter with a background history of alcoholic liver disease, gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD), and a 20 pack-year smoking history. He has come in complaining of dysphagia of both solids and liquids which both started about 3 months ago. He feels swallowing is painful and has lost nearly 10 kilos in the last 6 months.

You organise a chest radiograph, a barium swallow, an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy, and oesophageal manometry.

What are the likely investigation findings?
options_json: ["Dilated tapering oesophagus", "Corkscrew oesophagus", "Oesophageal stricture with apple core effect", "Candidiasis", "Hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter"]
answer_text: Oesophageal stricture with apple core effect
explanation_text:
Whilst dysphagia of solids and liquids is a classic history for achalasia, certain features such as significant weight loss are not consistent and suggest cancer - 'pseudoachalasia'

Despite dysphagia of solids and liquids starting simultaneously, this patient has lost a significant amount of weight in the past 6 months, and has several risk factors for oesophageal cancer including GORD, excessive smoking and alcohol use. This makes oesophageal cancer the more likely diagnosis.

Dilated tapering oesophagus is the finding on barium swallow for achalasia. Achalasia presents with dysphagia to both liquids and solids, regurgitation, cramps and weight loss. However, it is less likely in this situation due to the risk factors for oesophageal cancer coupled with excessive weight loss.

Corkscrew oesophagus is a finding on barium swallow for oesophagitis. Oesophagitis more often presents with intermittent dysphagia and chest pains. It is less likely in this situation due to the risk factors for oesophageal cancer coupled with excessive weight loss.

Oesophageal stricture with apple core effect is the correct answer, this is a barium swallow result for malignant oesophageal stricture.

While you can get candidiasis in malignancies, this is not likely to be the only finding. Oesophageal candidiasis more often occurs in immunocompromised patients and presents with dysphagia, dry mouth, nausea and chest pain.

Hypertensive lower oesophageal sphincter is a finding for achalasia. Achalasia presents with dysphagia to both liquids and solids, regurgitation, cramps and weight loss. However, it is less likely in this situation due to the risk factors for oesophageal cancer coupled with excessive weight loss.

question_text:
A 73-year-old man has recently been admitted to hospital following a fall at home.

He has a history of hypertension, type 2 diabetes and chronic kidney disease, for which he takes ramipril, metformin and atorvastatin.

His admission blood tests showed the following:


Hb	102 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	328 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.5 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
MCV	70 fl	(80-100)
Ferritin	12 ng/mL	(20 - 230)

He denies any change in bowel habit or weight loss and has not noticed any obvious bleeding elsewhere. On examination, he is noted to have an ejection systolic murmur that is loudest in the aortic area. Abdominal examination is normal and digital rectal examination does not reveal any abnormalities.

What is the most likely cause of his anaemia from the list below?
options_json: ["Anaemia of chronic disease", "Angiodysplasia", "Coeliac disease", "Haemolysis from valve disease", "B12 deficiency due to metformin"]
explanation_text:
Angiodysplasia is associated with aortic stenosis

This man has unexplained microcytic anaemia. There are a number of causes, of which angiodysplasia is the most likely option from the listed options. This is a common cause of iron deficiency anaemia and may present either with painless rectal bleeding or may be completely asymptomatic, as seen in this patient. It is thought to be associated with aortic stenosis, which is suggested by his ejection systolic murmur. Of course, it is essential to exclude more sinister pathologies such as colorectal cancer, hence further investigations would be required to confirm the cause of his anaemia.

Anaemia of chronic disease is a possibility given his chronic kidney disease, but this would typically cause normocytic anaemia with a ferritin level that is either normal or raised, hence this is an incorrect option.

Coeliac disease is incorrect. Although it is a common cause of iron deficiency anaemia in patients who may not necessarily display any gastrointestinal symptoms, it is less commonly diagnosed for the first time in this age group and angiodysplasia would be the more likely cause.

Haemolytic anaemia would usually cause normocytic or macrocytic anaemia. Patients who have prosthetic heart valves can undergo haemolysis due to mechanical trauma to red blood cells, but there is no mention of this man having previous valve surgery, hence this answer is incorrect.

Long-term metformin use is associated with B12 deficiency which can cause anaemia, but this usually results in macrocytosis, so would not be applicable to this patient.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis underwent a Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt (TIPSS) procedure 3 days ago for recurrent variceal bleeding. He now presents with confusion, disorientation, and asterixis. His ammonia level is elevated at 120 µmol/L (reference range: 11-32). He is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers.

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Administer intravenous antibiotics", "Commence lactulose and rifaximin", "Perform CT head scan", "Arrange urgent TIPSS revision", "Start intravenous thiamine"]
explanation_text:
Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt  commonly causes an exacerbation of hepatic encephalopathy

This patient is presenting with features consistent with hepatic encephalopathy following a TIPSS procedure. The clinical features of confusion, disorientation, and asterixis, along with elevated ammonia levels, strongly support this diagnosis. Hepatic encephalopathy is a common complication following TIPSS, occurring in approximately 20-30% of patients. This occurs because the shunt allows portal blood to bypass the liver, reducing the liver's ability to clear ammonia and other toxins from the bloodstream.

Commence lactulose and rifaximin

is the correct management approach. Lactulose works by acidifying the colonic contents, trapping ammonia as ammonium which cannot be absorbed, and by its cathartic effect which reduces bacterial ammonia production. Rifaximin is a non-absorbable antibiotic that reduces ammonia-producing bacteria in the gut. The combination of lactulose and rifaximin has been shown to be more effective than lactulose alone in treating hepatic encephalopathy. The initial management should focus on reducing ammonia levels through these medications while ensuring adequate hydration and correcting any precipitating factors.

Administer intravenous antibiotics

would be appropriate if there were signs of infection, which can precipitate hepatic encephalopathy. However, the patient is afebrile with normal inflammatory markers, making infection less likely as the primary cause. Empirical antibiotics are not indicated without evidence of infection.

Perform CT head scan

might be considered to rule out intracranial pathology, but the clinical picture strongly suggests hepatic encephalopathy as a complication of TIPSS. The timing of symptoms (3 days post-TIPSS), presence of asterixis, and elevated ammonia levels make other neurological causes less likely. A CT scan would be appropriate if there were focal neurological signs or if the patient failed to improve with standard hepatic encephalopathy treatment.

Arrange urgent TIPSS revision

is occasionally necessary for severe, refractory hepatic encephalopathy that doesn't respond to medical management. However, it's not the first-line approach and would only be considered after a trial of medical therapy has failed. TIPSS revision carries its own risks and should be reserved for cases where the benefits outweigh the risks.

Start intravenous thiamine

would be appropriate for a patient with suspected Wernicke's encephalopathy, which can occur in patients with alcohol use disorder. However, the clinical presentation (post-TIPSS, asterixis, elevated ammonia) is more consistent with hepatic encephalopathy rather than thiamine deficiency. While thiamine replacement is important in patients with alcohol-related liver disease, it's not the most urgent intervention in this scenario.

question_text: A 72-year-old woman is reviewed following a course of oral flucloxacillin for right lower limb cellulitis. The local protocol suggests oral clindamycin should be used next-line. Which one of the following side-effects of clindamycin is it most important to warn her about?
options_json: ["Heartburn or indigestion", "Jaundice", "Sore throat, bruising or lethargy", "Avoid any food or drink containing alcohol", "Diarrhoea"]
explanation_text:
Clindamycin treatment is associated with a high risk of

The correct answer in this case is

diarrhoea

. Clindamycin is an antibiotic belonging to the lincosamide class, and it is commonly used as a second-line treatment for cellulitis when patients are allergic to penicillins or when first-line treatments have failed. One of the most important side-effects to warn patients about when prescribing clindamycin is diarrhoea, which can range from mild to severe and may be associated with

Clostridium difficile

infection. This infection can lead to pseudomembranous colitis, a potentially life-threatening condition that requires prompt identification and management.

Regarding the other options:

Heartburn or indigestion

can occur with many medications, including antibiotics; however, it is not considered a major concern with clindamycin therapy. While it's important for patients to be aware of potential gastrointestinal side effects, diarrhoea remains the primary concern with this medication.

Jaundice

is not a common side effect of clindamycin. Jaundice may indicate liver dysfunction or damage, but clindamycin-associated hepatotoxicity is rare. It would not be necessary to specifically warn the patient about jaundice as a side effect of clindamycin.

Sore throat, bruising or lethargy

are not typical side effects associated with clindamycin use. These symptoms might suggest an underlying infection or another medical problem unrelated to the antibiotic treatment.

Avoid any food or drink containing alcohol

is not specific advice related to clindamycin use. Some antibiotics, such as metronidazole and tinidazole, have known interactions with alcohol that can cause unpleasant reactions like nausea, vomiting, flushing and headache (disulfiram-like reaction). However, there's no evidence suggesting that this reaction occurs with clindamycin.

question_text:
A pharmaceutical company is attempting to produce a new weight-loss medication to mimic the action of the natural peptide hormone cholecystokinin (CCK) in inducing satiety.

What cells naturally produce and release this hormone?
options_json: ["B cells in the large intestine", "D cells in the pancreas & stomach", "G cells in the antrum of the stomach", "I cells in the upper small intestine", "S cells in the upper small intestine"]
answer_text: I cells in the upper small intestine
explanation_text:
CCK - I cells in upper small intestine

CCK is a peptide hormone that increases the digestion of fats and proteins. It is synthesized and released from

I cells in the upper small intestine

in response to increased detection of partially digested proteins and fats. CCK results in several processes including the secretion of digestion enzymes from the pancreas, contraction of the gallbladder, relaxation of the sphincter of Oddi, decreased gastric emptying, and a trophic effect on pancreatic acinar cells all of which result in fat and protein breakdown as well as hunger suppression.

B cells

are part of the body's immune system, producing antibodies that serve as part of the B cell receptors. B cells are produced and released from the bone marrow before migrating to the spleen and lymphoid system. They can organise in the gastrointestinal lymphoid tissues and regional lymph nodes but play no role in satiety.

Somatostatin is a peptide regulator hormone released from

D cells in the pancreas and stomach

. It is stimulated by the presence of fat, bile salt, and glucose within the intestines and results in a decrease in the rate of gastric emptying and gastrointestinal hormone release.

Gastrin is another hormone that increases acid release from parietal cells in the stomach and aids with gastric motility. It is released from

G cells in the antrum of the stomach

on distension of the stomach, stimulus of the vagus nerves, and the presence of peptides/amino acids in the lumen.

Secretin regulates enzyme secretion of the stomach, pancreas, and liver. It is released from

S cells in the upper small intestine

on detection of acidic chyme and fatty acids and increases the pH of the duodenum.

question_text: A 46-year-old woman with 10 year history of Crohn's disease presents for review in the gastroenterology clinic. She complains of persistent diarrhoea despite being on maintenance therapy and having normal inflammatory markers. A diagnosis of bile acid malabsorption is being considered. What is the most appropriate test to investigate this?
options_json: ["Capsule endoscopy", "SeHCAT test", "14C-glycocholic breath test", "Ileal biopsy", "D-xylose test"]
explanation_text:
SeHCAT is the investigation of choice for bile acid malabsorption

The correct answer in this scenario is the

SeHCAT test

. Bile acid malabsorption (BAM) is a common cause of chronic diarrhoea, particularly in patients with Crohn's disease. The SeHCAT (Selenium-75-labelled homocholic acid taurine) test is considered the gold standard for diagnosing BAM. In this test, the patient ingests a capsule containing the radiolabelled bile acid analogue SeHCAT. After 7 days, whole-body gamma camera imaging is performed to assess the retention of SeHCAT. A low retention rate indicates bile acid malabsorption.

The

capsule endoscopy

allows for direct visualisation of the entire small bowel and can be useful in identifying mucosal abnormalities such as ulcers or strictures in patients with Crohn's disease. However, it does not provide any specific information regarding bile acid malabsorption and would not be appropriate in this case.

The

14C-glycocholic breath test

is another method that has been used to investigate bile acid malabsorption, but it is less accurate and less commonly used compared to the SeHCAT test. The 14C-glycocholic breath test involves oral administration of radiolabelled glycocholic acid followed by measurement of expired 14CO2. An increase in 14CO2 levels suggests bacterial overgrowth and deconjugation of bile acids, which can lead to malabsorption.

An

ileal biopsy

could potentially show histological changes associated with Crohn's disease but would not specifically diagnose bile acid malabsorption. Moreover, obtaining an ileal biopsy may require invasive procedures like enteroscopy or surgery, which are not necessary for investigating BAM.

Finally, the

D-xylose test

is used to evaluate the absorptive capacity of the small intestine for carbohydrates. It can help diagnose conditions like celiac disease or bacterial overgrowth, but it does not provide any information on bile acid malabsorption. Therefore, it would not be appropriate in this case.

question_text: A 24-year-old man is admitted to the gastroenterology ward with a 2-week history of bloody diarrhoea, urgency, and lower abdominal discomfort. He reports no previous gastrointestinal issues. Flexible sigmoidoscopy is performed, revealing continuous mucosal inflammation starting at the anal verge. Which anatomical site is most likely to be initially affected in this condition?
options_json: ["Rectum", "Ascending colon", "Terminal ileum", "Transverse colon", "Caecum"]
explanation_text:
Ulcerative colitis - the rectum is the most common site affected

Rectum

: The rectum is almost invariably the initial and most commonly affected site in ulcerative colitis (UC). UC characteristically starts at the rectum and extends proximally in a continuous fashion without skip lesions, which differentiates it from Crohn’s disease. Rectal involvement explains symptoms such as urgency and tenesmus seen in this patient. Recognising that inflammation begins at the rectum is fundamental both for diagnosis and understanding clinical features.

Ascending colon

: While the ascending colon can be involved as UC progresses proximally, it is not typically the initial or most common site of disease onset. Inflammation always commences at the rectum and only later involves more proximal segments if disease severity increases.

Terminal ileum

: Terminal ileal involvement suggests Crohn’s disease rather than ulcerative colitis. Although 'backwash ileitis' can occur rarely in severe pancolitis, it does not represent the primary or most common site of involvement in UC.

Transverse colon

: Like other proximal segments of the large bowel, transverse colon involvement occurs only after inflammation has extended from the rectum through contiguous sections of bowel. It would not be expected as an initial or isolated finding in UC.

Caecum

: The caecum may be affected by severe or extensive UC but never as an isolated or initial site; its involvement follows continuous spread from distal to proximal colon beginning at the rectum.

options_json: ["High carbohydrate diet", "Low protein diet", "Diarrhoea", "Constipation", "High fibre diet"]
explanation_text:
Constipation can be a trigger for liver decompensation in cirrhotic patients

This question is asking about a man with a cirrhotic liver following chronic hepatitis. In this case, he is showing signs of liver decompensation (jaundice and confusion). There are many causes of liver decompensation and you should make sure to find any underlying cause to ensure it is treated promptly.

From the list above constipation is a common cause of liver decompensation, this is due to the accumulation of toxic products within the body. In fact, some patients with liver decompensation and hepatic encephalopathy are treated with enemas to reduce the uptake of toxic products.

Other common causes include infection, electrolyte imbalances, dehydration, upper GI bleeds or increased alcohol intake.

explanation_text:
If a mild-moderate flare of ulcerative colitis does not respond to topical or oral aminosalicylates then oral corticosteroids are added

question_text:
A 39-year-old woman with known ulcerative colitis is reviewed in the gastroenterology clinic.

From recent imaging, it is known that her disease affects mainly the distal sigmoid colon.

In the clinic, she complains of increased stool frequency over the last couple of weeks. She notes 4-5 loose stools each day and is noticing increasing amounts of blood in them.

What is the most appropriate first-line management?
options_json: ["IV corticosteroids", "Oral aminosalicylate", "Oral corticosteroids", "Rectal aminosalicylate", "Rectal corticosteroids"]
explanation_text:
In a mild-moderate flare of distal ulcerative colitis, the first-line treatment is topical (rectal) aminosalicylates

Rectal aminosalicylate

is correct. This patient is suffering from a flare of her distal ulcerative colitis. Using the Truelove and Witts severity index for ulcerative colitis, this flare can be shown to be moderate. A rectal aminosalicylate is the first line in this instance.

Oral aminosalicylate

is incorrect. This patient's disease affects only the distal colon. For a mild to moderate flare of distal colitis, rectal aminosalicylates are the first line. If there is no improvement in 4 weeks, an oral aminosalicylate may be added.

IV corticosteroids

is incorrect. IV corticosteroids are indicated in the management of a severe ulcerative colitis flare. Using the Truelove and Witts severity index for ulcerative colitis, this flare can be shown to be moderate. Rectal aminosalicylates are therefore first-line.

Oral corticosteroids

is incorrect. Oral steroids are indicated in a mild to moderate flare of distal ulcerative colitis

if

topical treatments (aminosalicylates and steroids) have failed.

Rectal corticosteroids

is incorrect. Rectal steroids are indicated in the management of a mild to moderate flare of distal colitis

if

rectal aminosalicylates have been unsuccessful after 4 weeks.

question_text:
A 66-year-old man has been referred to the upper gastrointestinal (UGI) cancer multidisciplinary team meeting (MDT) after a recent admission for dysphagia, reflux and weight loss.

Barium swallow shows an apple core stricture of the distal oesophagus. Computed tomography (CT) scan of the thorax, abdomen, and pelvis shows a 2.5cm, circumferential mass in the distal third of the oesophagus which is concerning for malignancy. There was no evidence of lymphadenopathy or distant metastases.

Which further investigation is the most appropriate to help stage this cancer?
options_json: ["Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)", "High-resolution CT scan", "Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)", "Oesophago-gastro-duodenoscopy (OGD)", "Positron emission tomography (PET) scan"]
explanation_text:
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion

EUS is correct. If whole-body imaging has not shown any evidence of metastatic disease, EUS is the best investigation for tumour staging and can investigate for mural disease.

High-resolution CT is rarely required in cancer staging and is not beneficial in assessing for mural invasion.

MRI helps assess for metastatic disease but does not aid in assessing for mural invasion.

OGD is the first-line for assessment of suspected oesophageal and gastric cancers, however is not able to assess for mural invasion and therefore is not the correct answer.

PET scans are helpful in further identifying cancers and uptake in nodes and other tissues. It is, however, unhelpful in assessing for mural disease.

question_text:
A 50-year-old man with chronic gastro-oesophageal reflux presents with a several-month history of diarrhoea and weight loss. During the examination, he appears wasted and exhibits mild epigastric tenderness upon palpation. Multiple investigations, including a CT abdomen that revealed a suspicious mass, are conducted.

Fasting gastrin levels were performed and found to be elevated, confirming the diagnosis.

Where are the majority of these tumours typically located?
options_json: ["First part of the duodenum", "Ileum", "Jejunum", "Pylorus section of the stomach", "Third part of the duodenum"]
explanation_text:
The majority of gastrinomas are found in the first part of the duodenum

This patient has presented with features of Zollinger-Ellison syndrome, where increased levels of gastrin are secreted by gastrinomas. These neuroendocrine tumours primarily form in the

first part of the duodenum

due to it containing G cells, which naturally produce gastrin. Other areas where gastrinomas may develop include the pancreas and occasionally the gastrin-producing antrum section of the stomach.

Gastrinomas rarely develop in the

ileum

as this region lacks the specialised G cells responsible for natural gastrin production. Gastrinomas typically arise where G cells are present, such as the duodenum or pancreas. The absence of these cells in the ileum makes it an uncommon site for gastrinoma development.

Gastrinomas rarely develop in the

jejunum

due to the unique distribution of gastrin-producing cells. G cells, responsible for producing gastrin, are primarily located in the antrum of the stomach and the duodenum. Consequently, gastrinomas tend to form in these regions or in the pancreas where G cells are also present. The absence of G cells in the jejunum makes it an uncommon site for gastrinoma development.

Gastrinomas rarely develop in the

pylorus section of the stomach

because gastrin-producing G cells are predominantly found in the antrum and duodenum. The pylorus, responsible for regulating the passage of food from the stomach to the small intestine, lacks these specialised cells.

Gastrinomas rarely develop in the

third part of the duodenum

as, being more distal in location, this area lacks the presence of gastrin-producing G cells where these neuroendocrine tumours primarily develop.

question_text:
A 63-year-old male presents to the general practice with watery diarrhoea. The previous fortnight he was prescribed triple therapy consisting of omeprazole, clarithromycin and amoxicillin for a duodenal ulcer. Relevant past medical history includes a previous myocardial infarction, gastroesophageal reflux disease (GORD) and bipolar syndrome.

Which of the following in the patient's history increases the risk of a Clostridium difficile infection (CDI)?
options_json: ["Lithium therapy", "Omeprazole use", "Longstanding GORD", "Previous CABG >1 year ago", "Long term statin use"]
explanation_text:
PPIs are a risk factor for

CDI occurs from disruptions in the normal gut flora increasing the colonisation of

C. difficile

. The increased release of toxins leads to inflammation. Established risk factors include antibiotics, protein pump inhibitors, antidepressants and a vast array of conditions that affect the immune system and/or decrease gastric acid secretion.

Bowel and early emergency surgery have been associated with higher rates of CDI. There is not an established link between CDI and extraintestinal surgery though surrounding factors like antibiotic use may increase the risk more acutely.

GORD, T2DM and lithium are not specifically linked with higher rates of CDI. However, there is much literature showing an association of CDI with obesity which can be linked to many conditions and medications.

There are numerous studies showing that statins have a protective effect against CDI which is thought to be through alteration of the microbiota or reduction of inflammation in endothelial cells.

question_text: A 31-year-old woman who initially presented with abdominal pain and constipation is diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome. Which one of the following bits of dietary advice is it least suitable to give?
options_json: ["Avoid missing meals", "Restrict tea and coffee to 3 cups per day", "Increase the intake of fibre such as bran and wholemeal bread", "Reduce intake of alcohol", "Drink at least 8 cups of fluid per day"]
answer_text: Increase the intake of fibre such as bran and wholemeal bread
explanation_text:
Insoluble sources of fibre such as bran and wholemeal should be avoided in IBS

The correct answer is

Increase the intake of fibre such as bran and wholemeal bread

. Although increasing dietary fibre is generally recommended for patients with constipation, this advice might not be suitable for all patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, while some people with IBS may benefit from increasing their intake of soluble fibre (such as oats and barley), insoluble fibre like bran can exacerbate symptoms in some people. Therefore, it's important to individualise dietary advice based on a patient's symptoms.

The option

Avoid missing meals

is incorrect because regular meals can help control IBS symptoms. Eating regularly helps regulate bowel function and can prevent the onset of IBS symptoms. Skipping meals can lead to overeating later on, which can worsen IBS symptoms.

The option

Restrict tea and coffee to 3 cups per day

is also incorrect. Tea and coffee are known stimulants of gut motility and can exacerbate diarrhoea in individuals with IBS. Reducing their intake could potentially alleviate some of these symptoms.

Reduce intake of alcohol

is another incorrect answer choice. Alcohol is a known irritant of the gastrointestinal tract and can worsen IBS symptoms, so reducing its consumption would be beneficial for a patient with IBS.

Lastly,

Drink at least 8 cups of fluid per day

, especially water or other non-caffeinated drinks, is good advice for someone with IBS. Adequate hydration aids in normal bowel function and prevents constipation, one of the common features of IBS. It's particularly important when increasing fibre intake as it helps prevent bloating and gas associated with increased fibre consumption.

question_text:
A 56-year-old woman presents to the outpatient clinic with a 6-month history of intermittent facial flushing, watery diarrhoea, and occasional wheezing. She has lost 5kg in weight. Examination reveals a systolic murmur at the left sternal edge. A CT scan of the abdomen shows a 2cm lesion in the terminal ileum and multiple hypodense lesions in the liver.

What is the most appropriate next investigation?
options_json: ["Plasma chromogranin A", "Urinary 5-HIAA", "Serum ACTH", "Serum calcitonin", "Plasma metanephrines"]
explanation_text:
Urinary 5-HIAA is the investigation of choice for suspected carcinoid tumours

Urinary 5-HIAA

is the most appropriate investigation for this patient who has clinical features highly suggestive of carcinoid syndrome. The patient presents with the classic triad of flushing, diarrhoea, and bronchospasm (wheezing), along with weight loss. The CT findings of a terminal ileum lesion with liver metastases are typical of a metastatic carcinoid tumour. Carcinoid syndrome occurs when serotonin and other vasoactive substances produced by the tumour enter the systemic circulation, usually after liver metastases develop. Urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) is the main metabolite of serotonin and is the gold standard biochemical test for diagnosing carcinoid syndrome, with sensitivity of 70-90% and specificity >90%. The patient should avoid serotonin-rich foods (bananas, pineapples, walnuts, etc.) for 3 days before the test to avoid false positives.

Plasma chromogranin A

is a non-specific marker for neuroendocrine tumours, including carcinoid tumours. While it can be elevated in carcinoid syndrome and may be used as a complementary test, it is less specific than urinary 5-HIAA. False positives can occur with proton pump inhibitor use, renal failure, and other conditions. It would be a reasonable second-line investigation but is not the most specific first-line test for suspected carcinoid syndrome.

Serum ACTH

measurement would be appropriate if Cushing's syndrome was suspected. While some carcinoid tumours can secrete ACTH leading to ectopic Cushing's syndrome, this patient's presentation is classic for carcinoid syndrome without features of hypercortisolism (no mention of central obesity, striae, hypertension, or hyperglycaemia). Therefore, ACTH measurement is not the most appropriate initial investigation.

Serum calcitonin

is the tumour marker for medullary thyroid carcinoma, not carcinoid tumours. While medullary thyroid carcinoma can present with diarrhoea, it typically presents with a thyroid nodule and does not cause flushing or bronchospasm. The imaging findings in this case are not consistent with medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Plasma metanephrines

are used to diagnose phaeochromocytoma. While phaeochromocytoma can cause flushing and occasionally diarrhoea, it typically presents with paroxysmal hypertension, headache, and palpitations. The CT findings of a terminal ileum lesion with liver metastases are not consistent with phaeochromocytoma, which would typically appear as an adrenal mass.
