question_text:
A 43-year-old female was screened for haemochromatosis on a background of positive family history. She was found to have raised iron stores and further testing revealed she had the HFE gene mutation. She was diagnosed with diabetes mellitus recently and an echocardiogram (done due to symptoms of shortness of breath and ankle swelling) has shown a dilated cardiomyopathy with a moderate reduction in ejection fraction. She was reviewed by the hepatology team who arranged for venesection to be carried out as part of the management plan.

What would the most appropriate marker to monitor response to treatment?
options_json: ["Haemoglobin", "Ferritin", "Echocardiography", "HbA1c", "Liver function tests"]
explanation_text:
Ferritin and transferrin saturation are used to monitor treatment in haemochromatosis

Haemochromatosis is a condition characterised by increased iron absorption and consequently, iron is deposited in multiple organs such as the liver, pancreas and heart giving rise to problems such as liver cirrhosis, diabetes mellitus and cardiomyopathy. Monitoring for a response to venesection is done via measurement of ferritin and transferrin saturation as this correlates with iron stores.

While it will be important to monitor haemoglobin with repeated venesection, it will not give you an indication of iron stores and therefore will not be useful is monitoring haemochromatosis.

Serial echocardiography may be used for monitoring of the cardiomyopathy, but is not used for routine monitoring of haemochromatosis.

Similarly, HbA1c is used to monitor for diabetes that has likely resulted from haemochromatosis but will not directly monitor response to treatment with venesection.

Liver function tests are important to check as haemochromatosis can cause liver cirrhosis; however, do not correlate with response to treatment.

question_text: A 47-year-old female patient attends her GP with a one week history of nausea, upper abdominal discomfort and acid reflux. Four weeks earlier she had completed a Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori) eradication therapy, consisting of omeprazole, amoxicillin and clarithromycin. What is the most appropriate next step in the management of this patient?
options_json: ["Re-test for H. pylori using a carbon-13 urea breath test", "Refer the patient for an upper GI endoscopy", "Re-test for H. pylori using a stool antigen test", "Commence second-line treatment for H. pylori with omeprazole, amoxicillin and doxycycline", "Commence second-line treatment for H. pylori with omeprazole, amoxicillin and metronidazole"]
answer_text: Re-test for H. pylori using a carbon-13 urea breath test

question_text:
A 41-year-old male with a two-month history of retrosternal chest pain, dysphagia, weight loss and vomiting is referred for urgent endoscopy. The only past medical history of note is asthma.

Findings on endoscopy include reduced vasculature, thick mucosa, mucosal furrows, strictures and laryngeal oedema. A biopsy is taken, which shows a dense infiltrate of eosinophils in the epithelium.

He is prescribed omeprazole however this does not result in an improvement of his symptoms. Given the likely diagnosis, he is advised on dietary modification however his symptoms persist.

What treatment is used the first-line in the management of this condition?
options_json: ["Chlorphenamine", "Fluticasone", "Prednisolone", "Ranitidine", "Sodium alginate"]
explanation_text:
Dietary modification and topical steroids are used in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis

This man is suffering from eosinophilic oesophagitis. This is consistent with the findings on endoscopy as well as the presence of eosinophils on biopsy. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) would be a reasonable differential diagnosis, however, the lack of any response to omeprazole makes this less likely.

As eosinophilic oesophagitis is mediated by an allergic reaction, the first-line medical treatment is a topical steroid (eg. Fluticasone). None of the other answers is treatments for eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Chlorphenamine is an antihistamine and has no role in treating eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Oral steroids such as prednisolone are not used in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Ranitidine is an H2 receptor antagonist and can be prescribed for GORD, rather than eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Sodium alginate helps to prevent reflux rather than being a treatment for eosinophilic oesophagitis.

question_text: A 70-year-old man who is known to have atrial fibrillation presents with abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. A diagnosis of ischaemic colitis is suspected. Which part of the colon is most likely to be affected?
options_json: ["Hepatic flexure", "Descending colon", "Splenic flexure", "Ascending colon", "Rectum"]
explanation_text:
The splenic flexure is the most likely area to be affected by ischaemic colitis

The correct answer is the

Splenic flexure

. The splenic flexure, also known as the left colic flexure, is one of the watershed areas of the colon. A watershed area refers to a region that receives dual blood supply from the end arteries and therefore it is more vulnerable to ischaemia when systemic perfusion decreases or there's vascular occlusion. In atrial fibrillation, embolisation can occur leading to occlusion of these end arteries and hence ischemia.

The

Hepatic flexure

, also known as right colic flexure, is less likely to be affected by ischemia because it has a better blood supply compared with the splenic flexure. It is primarily supplied by the superior mesenteric artery (SMA). However, if SMA itself gets blocked then hepatic flexure could get involved but in comparison with splenic flexure, the incidence is lower.

The

Descending colon

has a rich blood supply from branches of Inferior Mesenteric Artery (IMA) making it less susceptible to ischemia than the splenic flexure.

The

Ascending colon

, like hepatic flexure, primarily gets its blood supply from Superior Mesenteric Artery (SMA). Hence it's less likely to be affected by ischemia unless SMA gets blocked.

Lastly, the

Rectum

has an abundant blood supply from both systemic and portal circulation via Superior Rectal Artery (from IMA), Middle Rectal Artery (from Internal Iliac Artery), and Inferior Rectal Artery (from Internal Pudendal Artery). Therefore, this makes rectum less prone to ischemia compared with splenic flexure.

question_text:
A 53-year-old man presents to the Medical Admissions Unit complaining of weight gain and increased fatigue. He is known to have cirrhosis secondary to alcoholic liver disease, and was admitted to hospital once last year for an episode of hepatic encephalopathy, which was treated successfully with phosphate enemas and rifaximin.

His regular medications include thiamine, lactulose and acamprosate, and he has no known drug allergies.

On inspection, he is not jaundiced. PR examination reveals an empty rectum. His JVP is not raised, and there is mild peripheral oedema up to the middle of his calves. His abdomen is soft and non-tender, with some shifting dullness.

His blood test results are as follows:


Hb	145 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	115 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Na+	127 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.0 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	6.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	65 µmol/L	(55 - 120)


Bilirubin	16 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	98 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	30 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	110 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	27 g/L	(35 - 50)

Bedside ultrasonography reveals the presence of moderate ascites, which is not tense.

Which of the following represents the most appropriate initial management option for his ascites?
options_json: ["Fluid restriction", "Spironolactone", "Abdominal paracentesis", "Furosemide", "20% human albumin solution (HAS)"]
explanation_text:
Patients with ascites secondary to liver cirrhosis should be given an aldosterone antagonist

This patient has presented with ascites in the context of decompensated alcoholic liver disease with cirrhosis. Patients with cirrhosis are prone to the development of ascites for a number of reasons, including hypoalbuminaemia due to an impairment of hepatic synthetic function, as well as fluid overload due to hyperaldosteronism. Spironolactone is the correct answer - as a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist, it acts to reverse the hyperaldosteronism underpinning the patient's ascites.

Fluid restriction may be indicated for patients with ascites with serum sodium < 125mmol/L, but would not be appropriate as a stand-alone intervention for this patient.

Abdominal paracentesis may be used to provide temporary symptomatic relief to patients with tense ascites. However, this patient's ascites is not tense, and it would be more appropriate to initiate him on a therapy which sustainably reverses his fluid overload.

Furosemide may be used as an adjunctive diuretic in ascites due to chronic liver disease, but is less effective than spironolactone as monotherapy.

20% human albumin solution (HAS) has a number of uses in chronic liver disease, including: volume replacement after large volume paracentesis; the treatment of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis; and the management of hepatorenal syndrome. However, is not used as primary treatment for ascites, even in the context of hypoalbuminaemia.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic due to persistently deranged liver function tests. She reports a several-month history of fatigue but denies any other symptoms of note. Her past medical history is significant for hypothyroidism only. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender with no palpable organomegaly. Liver function tests are abnormal and therefore further blood tests are performed.


AMA	positive

Given the likely underlying diagnosis, what first-line medication should this patient be offered?
options_json: ["Cholestyramine", "Fat soluble vitamin supplementation", "Liver transplant", "Prednisolone", "Ursodeoxycholic acid"]
explanation_text:
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis

The underlying diagnosis is primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). This is a chronic liver disease, which causes inflammation of the interlobular bile ducts. It is strongly associated with other autoimmune conditions and classically presents in middle-aged women with fatigue and pruritis. AMA M2 subtype antibodies are present in the majority of patients with the disease.

Ursodeoxycholic acid

is the correct answer. It is used first-line in the treatment of PBC to improve liver function, slow disease progression and delay the need for liver transplant.

Cholestyramine

is incorrect. Cholestyramine may be used for symptomatic relief of pruritis in PBC but is not a first-line treatment option.

Fat soluble vitamin supplementation

is incorrect. According to the Royal Society of Gastroenterology, there is a role for supplementation of specific vitamins including A, D, E and K, but only in patients with advanced icteric disease, and not in place of ursodeoxycholic acid.

Liver transplant

is incorrect. This question refers to a patient who is in the early stages of PBC. Whilst liver transplant is indicated in decompensated disease (e.g. bilirubin > 100), it would not be an appropriate first-line treatment option in this context.

Prednisolone

is incorrect. It may be considered in patients who do not adequately respond to ursodeoxycholic acid, or in those with advanced disease, but is not used as a first-line treatment option.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presented with cramping abdominal pain and watery diarrhoea. He reports the symptoms persisting for the last 4-weeks and denies any blood loss in his stool. He has been taking omeprazole for his gastro-oesophageal reflux disease for several years now.

What is the diagnostic investigation of choice in this case?
options_json: ["Abdominal x-ray", "Capsule endoscopy", "Colonoscopy and biopsy", "Computed-tomography (CT) scan", "Digital rectal examination"]
explanation_text:
PPIs are a cause of microscopic colitis, which can present with chronic diarrhoea, colonoscopy and biopsy should be considered when patients present in this way and are taking a PPI

Colonoscopy and biopsy is the diagnostic investigation of choice given the most likely diagnosis of microscopic colitis in this case caused by the long-term regular use of a proton-pump inhibitor. Histological examination of colonic biopsy tissue is necessary and performed by a pathologist to confirm the diagnosis.

An abdominal x-ray is of little value in this case and often performed in cases where there is a high suspicion of inflammatory bowel disease to rule out toxic megacolon in the acute setting.

Capsule endoscopy whilst may provide us with images of the bowel mucosa, in this case, we would need to obtain colonic tissue from a biopsy to make the histological diagnosis of microscopic colitis.

A CT scan may be performed but usually is seen to be normal and therefore does not help much in making the diagnosis apart from ruling out any acute intra-abdominal pathology.

Digital rectal examination is commonly performed as part of the abdominal examination and in this particular context will help to confirm the presence of blood loss per rectum, if suspected.

question_text:
A 74-year-old woman inpatient complains of abdominal pain over the last 6 hours. The nurses report she has opened her bowels 7 times in the last 12 hours with watery diarrhoea. She has recently completed a course of intravenous ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial meningitis.

Her blood pressure is 95/60 mmHg, heart rate 105/min, temperature 38.7 ºC.

Initial laboratory investigations are as follow:

What is the most appropriate antimicrobial treatment for this patient?

explanation_text:
In life-threatening

This patient is suffering from a life-threatening

She presents with characteristics signs and symptoms including abdominal pain, watery diarrhoea and a very high white cell count. Public Health England (PHE) guidelines updated in 2019, recommend oral vancomycin and intravenous metronidazole as the treatment of choice in life-threatening

question_text: Which one of the following is most suggestive of Wilson's disease?
options_json: ["Reduced hepatic copper concentration", "Reduced 24hr urinary copper excretion", "Increased skin pigmentation", "Reduced serum caeruloplasmin", "Increased serum copper"]
explanation_text:
Wilson's disease - serum caeruloplasmin is

The correct answer is

reduced serum caeruloplasmin

. Wilson's disease is an autosomal recessive disorder characterised by defective hepatic copper transport, leading to copper accumulation in various tissues. The most consistent laboratory finding in Wilson's disease is reduced serum caeruloplasmin concentration. Caeruloplasmin is a copper-carrying protein, and its synthesis is impaired in Wilson's disease due to intracellular copper overload.

Reduced hepatic copper concentration

is not suggestive of Wilson's disease. On the contrary, this condition is characterised by increased hepatic copper concentration as a result of impaired biliary excretion of copper.

Similarly,

reduced 24hr urinary copper excretion

would not be expected in Wilson's disease. In fact, 24-hour urinary copper excretion is often increased in untreated Wilson's disease because the kidneys attempt to compensate for the defective biliary excretion by increasing renal clearance of copper.

Increased skin pigmentation

, while it can occur in several systemic diseases, it isn't typically associated with Wilson's disease. It might suggest conditions such as Addison's disease or haemochromatosis where there is an increase in melanin production.

Lastly,

increased serum copper

levels are not characteristic of Wilson's disease either. Although there may be excess free (non-caeruloplasmin-bound) copper circulating in the late stages of the condition due to massive release from damaged hepatocytes, total serum copper levels are usually normal or even low because ceruloplasmin (which carries most of the body's copper) level is low.

question_text: A 46-year-old man is being investigated for indigestion. Jejunal biopsy shows deposition of macrophages containing PAS-positive granules. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Bacterial overgrowth", "Coeliac disease", "Tropical sprue", "Whipple's disease", "Small bowel lymphoma"]
explanation_text:
Whipple's disease: jejunal biopsy shows deposition of macrophages containing Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) granules

The correct diagnosis, in this case, is

Whipple's disease

. The presence of macrophages containing Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) positive granules in the jejunal biopsy is a classic histological finding in Whipple's disease. This rare systemic infectious disorder is caused by the bacterium

Tropheryma whipplei

. It primarily affects middle-aged men and can cause a variety of symptoms, including weight loss, diarrhoea, joint pain and abdominal discomfort.

Bacterial overgrowth

is an incorrect answer. While bacterial overgrowth syndrome does involve an abnormal increase in the number of bacteria in the small intestine, it doesn't lead to the deposition of PAS-positive granules within macrophages. Its symptoms may include bloating, gas, abdominal pain and diarrhoea but these are due to malabsorption caused by competition for nutrients between the patient and the excess bacteria.

Similarly,

Coeliac disease

, another condition associated with malabsorption, would not present with PAS-positive macrophages. Coeliac disease is an autoimmune condition where ingestion of gluten leads to damage in the small intestine. Histologically, it presents with villous atrophy and crypt hyperplasia on jejunal biopsy rather than PAS-positive granules.

Tropical sprue

is also incorrect as this condition refers to a syndrome characterised by acute or chronic diarrhoea and malabsorption that occurs in residents or visitors to tropical regions. Its exact cause remains unknown but it's thought to be related to bacterial or viral infection causing damage to the intestinal lining. Again, it does not feature PAS-positive granules within macrophages.

Finally,

Small bowel lymphoma

would typically present with different histological findings such as infiltration of lymphoid cells into intestinal tissue rather than PAS-positive granules within macrophages. Lymphomas are cancers that start in lymphocytes - part of our immune system - which do not contain these types of granules. Symptoms can be nonspecific and may include abdominal pain or discomfort due to tumour growth.

question_text: A 67-year-old man with a history of oesophageal cancer is reviewed on the ward. He has been treated previously with an oesophagectomy and has recently had a course of chemotherapy.Unfortunately he has been feeling increasingly unwell recently and has not eaten anything for the 7 days due to dysphagia. An nasogastric tube is passed and it is decided to start enteral feeding. What is the most appropriate course of action to avoid refeeding syndrome?
options_json: ["Provide 50% of normal energy and protein requirements for the first 2 days", "Start a saline infusion with 20 mmol of potassium for the first 8 hours", "Provide 75% of normal energy and protein requirements for the first 2 days", "Give furosemide 40mg IV at the mid-point of the first feed", "Give hydrocortisone 200mg IV at the mid-point of the first feed"]
answer_text: Provide 50% of normal energy and protein requirements for the first 2 days
explanation_text:
Give 50% of normal energy intake in starved patients (> 5 days) to avoid refeeding syndrome

The correct answer is to

provide 50% of normal energy and protein requirements for the first 2 days

. This approach helps to prevent refeeding syndrome, a potentially fatal complication that can occur when reintroducing nutrition to a severely malnourished patient. Refeeding syndrome is characterized by rapid shifts in electrolytes, particularly phosphate, potassium, and magnesium, which can lead to cardiac and neurological complications. By providing only 50% of the patient's normal energy and protein requirements initially, it allows their body to gradually adapt to the increased nutritional intake while minimizing the risk of refeeding syndrome.

The option

start a saline infusion with 20 mmol of potassium for the first 8 hours

is not the most appropriate course of action as it does not address the need for a gradual increase in caloric intake. While supplementing potassium may be necessary in some cases of refeeding syndrome, this alone will not prevent its occurrence.

Providing

75% of normal energy and protein requirements for the first 2 days

may still place the patient at risk of developing refeeding syndrome. A more conservative approach with 50% caloric intake is recommended per UK guidelines to minimize this risk.

Administering

furosemide 40mg IV at the mid-point of the first feed

is not appropriate in this situation. Furosemide is a diuretic that promotes fluid loss via increased urine output; however, it does not address refeeding syndrome's primary concern related to electrolyte imbalances caused by rapid reintroduction of nutrition.

Finally, giving

hydrocortisone 200mg IV at the mid-point of the first feed

would also be an inappropriate intervention. Hydrocortisone is a corticosteroid typically used to treat inflammatory conditions or adrenal insufficiency but has no direct role in preventing or managing refeeding syndrome.

question_text:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with sudden onset abdominal pain and nausea. She has no past medical history and takes the combined oral contraceptive pill regularly.

On examination, her observations are normal. Her abdomen is distended with tenderness in the right upper quadrant and a palpable liver edge. Shifting dullness is present.

Investigations:


Hb	123 g/L	(115 - 160)
Platelets	299 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Creatinine	90 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Bilirubin	30 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	150 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	248 u/L	(3 - 40)
Albumin	30 g/L	(35 - 50)

What is the next most appropriate investigation to order?
options_json: ["Alpha-fetoprotein", "Ascitic tap", "Computed tomography (CT) abdomen", "Doppler ultrasound liver", "Liver biopsy"]
explanation_text:
Budd-Chiari syndrome - ultrasound with Doppler flow studies is very sensitive and should be the initial radiological investigation

This woman has a diagnosis of Budd-Chiari syndrome. Budd-Chiari syndrome or hepatic vein thrombosis is more commonly associated with a hypercoagulable state (e.g. pregnancy, combined oral contraceptive pill use, malignancy and polycythaemia). Liver function tests tend to show a markedly raised ALT. Jaundice may be present but not always in the acute presentation. The investigation of choice is a

doppler ultrasound of the liver

to show the hepatic vein thrombus.

Alpha-fetoprotein

is a tumour marker used to aid the detection of malignancies such as hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). HCC presents late with features of liver cirrhosis including jaundice, ascites and right upper quadrant pain. Typically in patients with cirrhosis, liver enzymes remain relatively normal with the most prominent derangements being a raised INR, reduced blood sugar and reduced albumin levels.

An

ascitic tap

can be a useful investigation to determine the aetiology of the underlying condition and to rule out infectious causes such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. However, the lack of a significant inflammatory response makes infection less likely. Furthermore, an ascitic tap is not the investigation of choice in Budd-Chiari syndrome.

A

CT abdomen

can show signs of Budd-Chiari syndrome such as enhancement of the caudate lobe and central liver around the inferior vena cava but is not used in the first instance.

A

liver biopsy

is associated with multiple complications including infection and bleeding. It is less frequently used in the diagnosis of hepatic disorders and plays no role in the investigation of Budd-Chiari syndrome.

Imaging is required before making a diagnosis of PBC to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction

This is a patient with dry eyes and mouth, fatigue, pruritis, and obstructive hyperbilirubinaemia. With positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies, the likely diagnosis is primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). The dry eyes and mouth are common in Sjogren's syndrome, which is commonly associated with PBC.

question_text:
A 72-year-old woman is admitted to hospital with small bowel obstruction secondary to adhesions from previous surgery. She has lost 15kg over the past 3 months due to abdominal pain and vomiting. Her BMI is 17 kg/m². She undergoes laparotomy and adhesiolysis. Postoperatively, she is commenced on total parenteral nutrition (TPN) via a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC). Three days later, she becomes confused and short of breath. On examination, she has a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/minute and oxygen saturations of 92% on room air. Her blood results are as follows:


Na⁺	136 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K⁺	3.1 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	6.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	78 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Corrected Ca²⁺	2.28 mmol/L	(2.20 - 2.60)
Phosphate	0.4 mmol/L	(0.8 - 1.5)
Magnesium	0.6 mmol/L	(0.7 - 1.0)
Glucose	7.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.5)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Catheter-related bloodstream infection", "Pulmonary embolism", "Refeeding syndrome", "Sepsis secondary to anastomotic leak", "TPN-induced hyperglycaemia"]
explanation_text:
Refeeding syndrome is a recognised complication of TPN -  the hallmark feature is hypophosphataemia

Refeeding syndrome

is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. This patient has several risk factors for refeeding syndrome: significant weight loss (15kg over 3 months), low BMI (17 kg/m²), and a period of minimal nutritional intake due to small bowel obstruction. When TPN was initiated, there was a sudden shift from a catabolic to an anabolic state, causing rapid intracellular movement of phosphate, potassium, and magnesium. The hallmark laboratory finding in refeeding syndrome is hypophosphataemia, which is evident in this patient's blood results (phosphate 0.4 mmol/L, significantly below the reference range of 0.8-1.5 mmol/L). Additionally, she has hypokalaemia (3.1 mmol/L) and hypomagnesaemia (0.6 mmol/L), which are also characteristic of refeeding syndrome. Her clinical presentation of confusion and respiratory distress is consistent with the neurological and cardiopulmonary manifestations of severe hypophosphataemia. Management would include correcting electrolyte abnormalities, temporarily reducing or stopping the TPN, and then gradually reintroducing nutrition with careful monitoring of electrolytes.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection

is an important complication of TPN administration. However, this patient lacks the typical features of infection such as fever, rigors, or raised inflammatory markers. While confusion can occur in sepsis, the predominant biochemical abnormalities (hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia) are more consistent with refeeding syndrome than infection. Additionally, catheter-related infections typically develop after a longer duration of central venous access than the three days described in this scenario.

Pulmonary embolism

could explain the respiratory symptoms but would not account for the significant electrolyte abnormalities seen in this patient. While patients with recent surgery are at increased risk of venous thromboembolism, the combination of respiratory symptoms with profound hypophosphataemia and other electrolyte disturbances makes refeeding syndrome a more likely diagnosis. Pulmonary embolism would typically present with more specific respiratory symptoms such as pleuritic chest pain or haemoptysis, which are not mentioned in this case.

Sepsis secondary to anastomotic leak

is an important postoperative complication following bowel surgery. However, the patient underwent adhesiolysis rather than bowel resection with anastomosis, making this diagnosis less likely. Additionally, anastomotic leaks typically present with abdominal pain, peritonism, and signs of systemic inflammation, which are not described in this case. The electrolyte abnormalities are more consistent with refeeding syndrome than sepsis from an intra-abdominal source.

TPN-induced hyperglycaemia

is a common metabolic complication of TPN due to the high glucose content of the solution. However, this patient's glucose level is only mildly elevated at 7.2 mmol/L, which is unlikely to cause the described symptoms. Hyperglycaemia alone would not explain the profound hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia, and hypomagnesaemia seen in this case. While glucose intolerance can occur during refeeding, it is not the primary issue in this scenario.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a two-hour history of haematemesis. He has a history of ischaemic heart disease and denies any alcohol consumption.

Despite undergoing an endoscopy where a bleeding gastric ulcer is identified and injected with adrenaline, he vomits an additional 20ml of fresh red blood the following day. A further endoscopy is performed where clipping is attempted but unfortunately, it is unsuccessful and he has a reoccurrence of haematemesis an hour later.

What is the most appropriate next step?
options_json: ["Endoscopic adrenaline injection", "IV esomeprazole", "IV terlipressin", "Referral to general surgery", "Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt"]
explanation_text:
Surgery is indicated in patients with ongoing acute bleeding despite repeated endoscopic therapy

The patient presents with an upper gastrointestinal (GI) bleed secondary to a gastric ulcer that has shown resistance to multiple endoscopic interventions. Endoscopic techniques include the injection of adrenaline directly into the ulcer to promote vasoconstriction and achieve haemostasis, as well as the mechanical application of clips to arrest the bleeding. When such endoscopic measures fail despite repeated attempts,

referral to general surgery

is the next appropriate step in management.

This individual has been subjected to two separate endoscopies, including adrenaline being administered to the ulcer. Considering this context, additional

endoscopic adrenaline injections

are unlikely to provide further benefit. Instead, the patient should be referred to general surgery.

IV terlipressin

is given in cases of upper GI bleed caused by oesophageal varices rather than for peptic ulcers. Terlipressin acts by causing constriction of the splanchnic blood vessels, thereby reducing blood flow to the portal vein and decreasing pressure in the portal vein and the varices.

Following the identification of a gastric ulcer as the source of bleeding, the patient should have received treatment with

IV esomeprazole

. Nonetheless, in cases where an upper GI bleed proves refractory to standard treatments, IV esomeprazole does not constitute definitive management; surgical intervention is required.

A

transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt

(TIPS) procedure is typically reserved for managing intractable bleeding from oesophageal varices associated with alcoholic liver disease by diverting blood flow from the portal vein into the systemic circulation. This reduces portal hypertension and subsequently decreases pressure on the varices prone to bleeding. However, there is no indication that this patient suffers from portal hypertension; therefore, TIPS would not be a suitable therapeutic option in this scenario.

question_text: Which one of the following enzymes is mainly responsible for breaking starch down into sugars?
options_json: ["Amylase", "Sucrase", "Alpha-glucosidase", "Maltase", "Lactase"]
explanation_text:
Amylase: breaks starch down to sugars

The correct answer is

Amylase

. Amylase is an enzyme that is mainly responsible for breaking down starch, a complex carbohydrate, into simpler sugars. It is produced in the salivary glands and the pancreas, and it starts the digestion of starch in the mouth and continues it in the small intestine.

Sucrase

is incorrect because this enzyme breaks down sucrose into glucose and fructose. Sucrose is a disaccharide sugar that we commonly know as table sugar or saccharose. While sucrase does break down a type of sugar, it does not act on starch.

Alpha-glucosidase

is also incorrect. This enzyme breaks down complex carbohydrates into glucose, but it acts primarily on disaccharides and oligosaccharides rather than on polysaccharides like starch.

The option

Maltase

is another incorrect choice. Maltase breaks maltose (a disaccharide) into two units of glucose. Although maltose is one of the products of starch digestion by amylase, maltase itself doesn't act directly on starch.

Finally,

Lactase

is also not correct. Lactase's function in our body is to break lactose (the sugar found in milk) into glucose and galactose for absorption. It has no action on starch breakdown.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man presents with a progressive history of fatigue, joint, and abdominal pain, and a bronze, greying of his skin. Base-level blood tests are shown below.


Albumin	20 g/L	35-55
ALT	68 U/L	10-40
Alkaline phosphatase	160 U/L	25-100
INR	1.9	>1.1
HbA1c	8%	4-5.6

An element absorption and metabolism disorder is suspected and genetic testing confirms the presence of a specific mutation causing the condition. Venesection is started as a first-line treatment.

What measurement is used along with ferritin to monitor this patient's treatment?
options_json: ["Desferrioxamine", "Haemoglobin", "Serum iron", "Total iron-binding capacity", "Transferrin saturation"]
explanation_text:
Ferritin and transferrin saturation are used to monitor treatment in haemochromatosis

This patient has presented with the autosomal recessive iron absorption and metabolism disorder haemochromatosis. Patients normally develop complications of the condition after the age of 40 with common features including liver failure, type 2 diabetes, arthritis, and a bronze, greying of the skin. Diagnosis can be confirmed by identifying raised ferritin and transferrin saturation levels or via molecular genetic testing for the C282Y and H63D mutations. Venesection is the first-line treatment for the condition which is monitored via ferritin and

transferrin saturation

testing with target levels below 50ug/l and 50% respectively.

Desferrioxamine

is an iron chelator that can be used as an alternative treatment for haemochromatosis if venesection cannot be performed. It acts by binding to free iron in the bloodstream and increasing elimination in the urine. Desferrioxamine is a medication and is, therefore, a separate form of treatment from venesection.

Haemoglobin

(Hb) is an iron-containing protein found in red blood cells and, although reduced in iron deficits, a patient's Hb level is relatively unaffected in iron overload. For this reason, it should not be measured to monitor venesection treatment of haemochromatosis.

Serum iron

is a measurement of the total amount of circulating iron bound to both transferrin and ferritin. This level can be effect by several other factors such as haemoglobin levels and therefore the measurement has no value when attempting to diagnose haemochromatosis. It is the storage and excess of iron that is crucial to confirm the diagnosis and this is performed via ferritin and transferrin saturation.

Total iron-binding capacity

(TIBC) is a specific investigation that measures a patient's blood capacity to bind iron to transferrin. Although mainly used for establishing the cause of anaemia, TIBC levels are normally low in haemochromatosis which can assist in confirming the diagnosis. Again TIBC levels are not commonly used to monitor venesection treatment.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man re-presents to the Emergency Department with haematemesis. He was discharged two days earlier after receiving endoscopic band ligation twice for large bleeding oesophageal varices. The patient has a history of alcoholic liver disease.

He is tachycardic with a pulse of 118 bpm, blood pressure is 132/85 mmHg, and he is vomiting small amounts of fresh blood. On examination, he has hepatomegaly and ascites. Resuscitation measures including intravenous antibiotics and terlipressin have been initiated.

What is the most appropriate next definitive step in management?
options_json: ["Insert Sengstaken-Blakemore tube", "Refer for urgent surgical intervention", "Repeat endoscopic band ligation", "Repeat endoscopic sclerotherapy", "Start high-dose IV omeprazole"]
explanation_text:
Surgery is indicated in patients with ongoing acute bleeding despite repeated endoscopic therapy

The

referral for urgent surgical intervention

is correct. This patient has re-bleeding for oesophageal varices after undergoing endoscopic intervention twice, suggesting refractory bleeding. His history of alcoholic liver disease predisposes him to portal hypertension and the development of varices. While his blood pressure is holding, he is tachycardic, suggesting compensation for his underlying bleeding, which can deteriorate into haemorrhagic shock. Since this patient has had repeated unsuccessful endoscopic treatment, and is at risk of further instability, out of the options present, a referral for surgical intervention is warranted. Surgical options include an emergency portocaval shunt, direct surgical ligation, or varices resection.

Insert Sengstaken-Blakemore tube

is incorrect. This is a temporary measure involving the insertion of a balloon tamponade device to control variceal bleeding when intervention methods like endoscopy or surgery are not immediately available. This patient is not currently in haemodynamic shock, which would be suggested by features like severe hypotension (often < 90/60 mmHg) and altered consciousness, and resuscitation measures are in place to stabilise him for now. There is no indication in the stem that there is a delay in surgical assessment or management, hence, this step may not yet be necessary. A Sengstaken-Blakemore tube is not a definitive measure and prolonged use can cause pressure necrosis, which causes further bleeding and deterioration. If this patient were to be hypotensive or vomiting significant amounts of blood, or if there were delays in surgical assessment, then this option could be considered.

Repeat endoscopic band ligation

is incorrect. While this approach is first-line for oesophageal varices, this patient has already undergone band ligation twice without success. Repeating this is unlikely to yield any significant benefit. Additionally, further attempts at band ligation may increase the risk of complications such as perforation and oesophageal trauma. Instead, out of the options listed, a surgical assessment is the best next step.

Repeat endoscopic sclerotherapy

is incorrect as band ligation is preferred over sclerotherapy as it is more effective and carries fewer risks, and this patient has already undergone band ligation twice without success. Repeating endoscopy and performing sclerotherapy is unlikely to yield any significant benefit and may increase the risk of complications such as ulceration, strictures, and perforation. Out of the options listed, a referral for surgical assessment should be made to consider interventions to provide more definitive control of the patient's bleeding, such as portosystemic shunting or direct variceal ligation.

Start high-dose IV omeprazole

is incorrect as proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) are not used in acute variceal bleeding. PPIs are primarily used to reduce gastric acid secretion and prevent mucosal stress and disease, such as ulceration. In acute variceal bleeding, the focus is on controlling bleeding. They are instead used in non-variceal upper gastrointestinal bleeding if there is evidence of recent peptic ulcer disease at endoscopy. Alternatively, they may be used post-endoscopic variceal band ligation as haemorrhage prophylaxis. While this patient has undergone band ligation, the priority is stabilising his bleeding.

Albumin	28 g/L	(35 - 50)

What investigation should be performed to confirm the diagnosis?
options_json: ["Abdominal USS", "ERCP", "High resolution CT pancreas", "MRCP", "PET CT abdomen and pelvis"]
explanation_text:
High-resolution CT scanning is the diagnostic investigation of choice for pancreatic cancer

The patient's history (weight loss, jaundice, pruritis and steatorrhea), examination (palpable gallbladder - Courvoisier's sign) and blood tests (obstructive jaundice) are most suggestive of pancreatic cancer.

High resolution CT

is the diagnostic investigation of choice.

Abdominal USS

is indicated for the investigation of obstructive jaundice. However, it is less sensitive for pancreatic cancer than CT and therefore is not the investigation of choice.

ERCP

may be indicated later for stent insertion +/- tissue biopsy but is not the diagnostic test for pancreatic cancer.

MRCP

may be indicated for further visualisation of the biliary system but is not a first-line investigation for suspected pancreatic cancer.

PET CT

is not indicated for the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.

question_text: A 49-year-old woman who is known to have alcoholic liver disease is admitted to the ward following a decompensation. A diagnosis of grade II hepatic encephalopathy is made. She is confused and a screen looking for infection and other precipitants is performed. She is started on lactulose. What other medication may be used to prevent the hepatic encephalopathy if lactulose is ineffective?
options_json: ["Neomycin", "Senna", "Rifaximin", "Ciprofloxacin", "High-dose vitamin C"]
explanation_text:
Lactulose and rifaximin are used for the secondary prophylaxis of hepatic encephalopathy

The correct answer is

Rifaximin

. Rifaximin is a non-absorbable antibiotic that acts within the gastrointestinal tract to reduce the production and absorption of ammonia, which is a key factor in the development of hepatic encephalopathy. It is used as an add-on therapy to lactulose when lactulose alone is insufficient in controlling hepatic encephalopathy. Rifaximin has been shown to be effective in reducing recurrence rates and improving cognitive function in patients with hepatic encephalopathy.

The first incorrect option,

Neomycin

, was historically used as an alternative to lactulose for hepatic encephalopathy. However, it has fallen out of favor due to its nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, which can lead to renal impairment and hearing loss. Additionally, neomycin is less effective than rifaximin and has more side effects.

Senna

is a stimulant laxative that increases bowel motility but does not specifically target ammonia production or absorption. While it may help alleviate constipation, it would not be effective in preventing hepatic encephalopathy.

Ciprofloxacin

is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that may be used in treating infections that could precipitate hepatic encephalopathy (such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis), but it does not have a direct effect on ammonia levels or the management of hepatic encephalopathy itself.

Lastly,

High-dose vitamin C

has no proven role in the prevention or treatment of hepatic encephalopathy. While vitamin C has antioxidant properties and may have some general health benefits, there is no evidence supporting its use for this specific condition.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man with on-going constipation presents to his physician hoping to get some laxatives. He has been eating and drinking well, and apart from constipation, does not have any significant medical history. He does not drink alcohol but smokes occasionally when out with friends.

The physician wants to prescribe a laxative to help resolve the patient's constipation, however, laxatives like any other medication have adverse effects that should be considered before prescribing.

Which one of the following laxatives is shown to have to carcinogenic potential?
options_json: ["Lactulose", "Husk", "Senna", "Co-danthramer", "Bisacodyl"]
explanation_text:
Co-danthramer is genotoxic and should only be prescribed to palliative patients due to its carcinogenic potential

Co-danthramer has been shown be carcinogenic and therefore is not be prescribed normally. The only exception is in the case of palliative patients where it can be prescribed, especially if constipation is not improved by the other laxatives.

The use of co-danthramer and co-danthrusate is limited to constipation in terminally ill patients because of potential carcinogenicity (based on animal studies) and evidence of genotoxicity. (BNF)

The rest of the laxatives are not known to be carcinogenic. A thorough history will help dictate which laxative would be the best option for this patient.

In all patients with constipation, an increase in dietary fibre, adequate fluid intake and exercise is advised. Diet should be balanced and contain whole grains, fruits and vegetables. Fibre intake should be increased gradually (to minimise flatulence and bloating). The effects of a high-fibre diet may be seen in a few days although it can take as long as 4 weeks. Adequate fluid intake is important (particularly with a high-fibre diet or fibre supplements), but can be difficult for some people (for example, the frail or elderly). Fruits high in fibre and sorbitol, and fruit juices high in sorbitol can help prevent and treat constipation.

question_text:
A 64-year-old woman presents with profuse watery diarrhoea, vomiting and abdominal pain. She was recently treated for severe pneumonia with IV antibiotics.

She was hypotensive despite IV fluids and was quickly admitted to intensive care for vasopressors.

A CT abdomen and pelvis revealed the following:


Gross colonic dilatation, measuring up to 6.7cm in diameter.

Generalised circumferential wall thickening suggestive of pancolitis.

What is optimal management in the first instance?
options_json: ["Colonic decompression", "IV hydrocortisone", "IV vancomycin", "Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole", "Total colectomy"]
explanation_text:
In life-threatening

This question is alluding to

Clostridium difficile

infection (CDI), which should be suspected in all patients who have diarrhoea shortly following antibiotic therapy. This patient is haemodynamically unstable from insensible fluid loss and distributive sepsis. There is radiological evidence of colonic dilatation and inflammation suggestive of toxic megacolon.

The recommended medical therapy for life-threatening CDI is

oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole

. Oral vancomycin has low systemic absorption, making it effective at managing intestinal infections. It can also be given NG or as an enema if needed. Other recommendations include bowel rest, fluid and electrolyte replacement and cessation of medications that impair gut motility.

Colonic decompression

may play a role in the management of CDI, however, there is little significant data and poses a risk of perforation.

IV hydrocortisone

would be appropriate in the setting of suspected acute severe colitis secondary to inflammatory bowel disease. It would be justified if the patient had known ulcerative colitis or if there was bloody diarrhoea. In this instance, even though a

C. diff

toxin is not available, CDI is more likely.

IV vancomycin

is not recommended given the efficacy of local intestinal action in oral form.

Total colectomy

is something to be considered when managing toxic megacolon, however, poses its challenges including intra-operative risk and commitment to a lifelong ileostomy. It is typically recommended in complicated infections i.e. perforation, bleeding, and failure to respond to medical therapy after 48 hours.

question_text:
A 55-year-old-man presents to the acute medical unit with abdominal pain and diarrhoea. He is obese with a past medical history of hypertension, cholecystectomy, and ulcerative colitis.

He was admitted with a non-ST elevation myocardial infarction a few weeks ago and was started on aspirin, statins, ramipril, and bisoprolol. He decided to start exercising, eat a high fibre diet, stop smoking, and reduce alcohol intake.

The abdominal examination revealed a left-sided tenderness and red blood per rectum. ECG showed sinus tachycardia at 103 bpm. Venous blood gas was normal and abdominal x-ray showed some mural thickening of the descending colon.

What is the most likely cause for his presentation?
options_json: ["Aspirin", "Bowel cancer", "High fibre diet", "Ischaemic bowel", "Smoking cessation"]
explanation_text:
Cessation of smoking may trigger an ulcerative colitis flare

Abdominal pain, diarrhoea, and rectal bleeding in a patient with ulcerative colitis who recently stopped smoking suggest an exacerbation of ulcerative colitis. Smoking cessation is the likely cause of this. The mural thickening on a plain abdominal film is non-specific but, given the history of ulcerative colitis, a flare is a likely cause.

Despite aspirin increasing the likelihood of rectal bleeding, it does not cause abdominal pain and diarrhoea.

A high fibre diet could cause loose stools, and one could argue that patients with ulcerative colitis generally have rectal bleeding, but it does not explain the abdominal pain. This patient's presentation is suggestive of an exacerbation of ulcerative colitis.

Ischaemic bowel causes generalised abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, and diarrhoea in a patient with atrial fibrillation or peripheral vascular disease. Given that the ECG was sinus rhythm and VBG did not show elevated lactate, it is lower down on the differential.

Despite bowel cancer being on the differential, it is less likely to explain this patient's presentation.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man presents with 3 months of weight loss and, over the last few days, yellowing of the eyes and skin. He has no other symptoms. He has no medical history.

A biliary ultrasound is performed. The report describes simultaneous dilatation of the common bile and pancreatic ducts.

An endoscopic ultrasound +/- fine needle aspiration is requested.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Cholangiocarcinoma", "Choledocholithiasis", "Chronic pancreatitis", "Hepatocellular carcinoma", "Pancreatic cancer"]
explanation_text:
The 'double duct' sign may be seen in pancreatic cancer

Pancreatic cancer

is correct. Simultaneous dilatation of the common bile and pancreatic ducts is also known as the 'double duct' sign. It represents malignancy until proven otherwise. Tumours of the head of the pancreas are the most common cause of simultaneous dilatation of both the common bile and pancreatic ducts. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration is likely to be the next step for a tissue diagnosis.

Choledocholithiasis

is incorrect. This would typically cause abdominal pain. An impacted stone in the distal common bile duct may cause some pancreatic duct obstruction if there is significant oedema, but this would be less common than a malignant cause.

Cholangiocarcinoma

is incorrect. This is a less common cause of the 'double duct sign' than pancreatic cancer as cholangiocarcinoma does not always obstruct the pancreatic duct. It does frequently cause compression of the common bile duct, hence why it causes painless jaundice.

Chronic pancreatitis

is incorrect. This is a rare cause of the 'double duct sign'. Chronic pancreatitis is also unlikely in a patient with no medical history and no history of abdominal pain.

Hepatocellular carcinoma

(HCC) primarily affects the liver parenchyma and does not usually cause a 'double duct sign,' but it can cause bile duct obstruction if there is significant mass effect or invasion. The appearance of HCC on ultrasound is variable but may appear as a small hypoechoic liver lesion or a larger heterogeneous lesion due to fibrosis and calcification.

question_text:
A tertiary hospital centre heavily involved in gastroenterological research is currently recruiting participants for an upcoming study. During the double-blinded study, they will intravenously inject patients with a hormone that increases the release of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells and decreases gastric acid secretion. The study will analyse the effect of the therapy on patients with chronic pancreatitis.

What hormone is the study utilising?
options_json: ["Cholecystokinin (CCK)", "Gastrin", "Leptin", "Secretin", "Somatostatin"]
explanation_text:
Secretin increases secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreas and hepatic duct cells

The hormone being referred to in this study's description is

secretin

. This hormone is produced by the S cells of the upper small intestine, stimulated by acidic chyme and fatty acids. It acts to increase the secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from the pancreas and hepatic duct cells, while also decreasing gastric acid secretion.

CCK

is incorrect. This is produced by I cells of the upper small intestine and is stimulated by partially digested proteins and triglycerides. It instead acts to increase the secretion of enzyme-rich pancreatic fluid, causes gallbladder contraction and decreases gastric emptying.

Gastrin

is incorrect. This is produced by G cells in the antrum of the stomach and is stimulated by distension of the stomach and luminal peptides and amino acids. It increases acid, pepsinogen and intrinsic factor secretion and increases gastric motility.

Leptin

is incorrect. It is primarily secreted by adipose cells and promotes satiety.

Somatostatin

is incorrect. This is secreted by D cells in the pancreas and stomach and is stimulated by fat, bile salts and glucose in the intestinal lumen. It acts to decrease acid, pepsin and pancreatic enzyme secretion.

question_text: A 73-year-old man comes to the gastroenterology clinic for review. He has moderate aortic stenosis but is currently not keen to progress to valve replacement. He presents with persistent iron deficiency anaemia for which no cause has been found in spite of one upper GI endoscopy and two colonoscopies. What is the next most appropriate step?
options_json: ["CT abdomen", "Capsule endoscopy", "Intra-operative enteroscopy", "Labelled white cell scan", "Repeat upper GI endoscopy"]

question_text:
A 64-year-old man presents to his GP with several months of dysphagia, weight loss and vomiting. He has a background of gastric oesophageal reflux disease (GORD) and is a smoker. The symptoms prompt the GP to urgently refer the patient to the hospital, where endoscopy is performed and a biopsy taken. This demonstrates an adenocarcinoma of the oesophagus.

Which of the following investigations should be performed next, to assess mural invasion?
options_json: ["Computed tomography scan", "Endoscopic ultrasound", "Laparoscopy", "Magnetic resonance imaging scan", "Positron emission tomography scan"]
explanation_text:
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion

The correct answer is endoscopic ultrasound (EUS). With regards to oesophageal adenocarcinoma, EUS is better than computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scans at assessing mural invasion, and so is the investigation of choice at this stage. Several studies have demonstrated the accuracy of staging with EUS as being significantly higher than staging with CT or MRI.

CT scanning is incorrect. Whilst also useful, and indeed performed for all patients with oesophageal or gastric cancer, it is not as good at assessing mural invasion as EUS. It is performed to assess the extent of metastases.

Laparoscopy is incorrect. This may be considered in those with negative imaging before definitive therapy; to assess mural invasion, however, it is not useful.

MRI scanning, similarly to CT, is useful to assess spread and metastases, but again, EUS is better at assessing mural invasion.

Positron emission tomography scanning plays a role in pre-operative staging and is more sensitive than CT for detecting distant metastases. However, EUS is better for assessing mural invasion.

question_text:
A 40-year-old male presents to the emergency department with symptoms of epigastric pain and vomiting. On review of his medical records, you note he has had a number of admission with similar symptoms. You also note the patient has frequently attended the department with alcohol-related injuries.

On further questioning, the patient confirms he has frequent, oily foul-smelling bowel movements and has significant, unintentional weight loss. To aid with the prognosis and management of the patient's likely diagnosis you plan to assess his exocrine function.

The patient confirms he has no other medical conditions and is not on any regular medications.

Which of the following is the next most appropriate investigation?
options_json: ["Faecal 13C analysis", "Faecal elastase", "Gamma glutamyl transferase (GGT)", "Glucose tolerance test", "Serum amylase"]
explanation_text:
Faecal elastase is a useful test of exocrine function in chronic pancreatits

Given the symptoms seen here, the likely diagnosis is chronic pancreatitis. Faecal elastase can be measured both in the serum and stool and assesses for exocrine insufficiency seen in chronic pancreatitis. Faecal elastase is an exocrine product of the pancreas and is not broken down by gastrointestinal enzymes; therefore, its level can be detected and measured. These levels are decreased when the exocrine-producing tissue of the pancreas is damaged and therefore correlates with reduced function.

Faecal

13

C analysis is not an established test for the measurement of endocrine function. Indirect

13

C breath tests have been developed, involving the ingestion of

13

C labelled lipids and measuring the exhaled

13

C to calculate lipid breakdown.

Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT) is predominantly used as a diagnostic marker for liver disease and has been shown to be increased in both acute and chronic alcohol use. A raised GGT may add weight to the possibility of alcohol abuse in this patient but does not assess exocrine function.

Glucose tolerance test essentially measures the pancreas' ability to produce insulin so can be used to measure function; however, this is a measure of the pancreas' endocrine function, not exocrine.

Serum amylase is useful in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis and is normally raised in chronic pancreatitis; its level does not correlate with the severity of exocrine tissue damage or exocrine function.

question_text:
A 78-year-old woman attends with yellowing of her skin. A systematic enquiry was otherwise unremarkable. She has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation, rheumatoid arthritis, and cerebrovascular disease. She was recently treated for a urinary tract infection with a course of nitrofurantoin, and community-acquired pneumonia with a course of co-amoxiclav. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender and there is no organomegaly.

Blood results are as follows:


Bilirubin	68 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	660 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	38 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	842 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	35 g/L	(35 - 50)

What drug is most likely implicated?
options_json: ["Amiodarone", "Co-amoxiclav", "Methotrexate", "Nitrofurantoin", "Simvastatin"]
explanation_text:
Co-amoxiclav is a well recognised cause of cholestasis

The liver function tests demonstrate a cholestatic picture with a raised ALP/GGT and associated hyperbilirubinemia.

This is a classical presentation of drug-induced cholestasis.

Co-amoxiclav

is a well-recognised and common cause of cholestasis.

All the other drugs tend to cause a hepatitis-type picture.

However,

amiodarone

and

methotrexate

can also cause liver cirrhosis which should be excluded in this case with an abdominal ultrasound +/- Fibroscan.

question_text:
A 55-year-old woman with a history of alcoholic liver disease is reviewed in clinic. She has advanced cirrhosis and has started to accumulate ascites. An ascitic tap was recently performed and showed a protein concentration of 12 g/L but no evidence of any organisms.

What is the most appropriate management concerning the risk of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
options_json: ["No antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated", "Oral penicillin", "Oral ciprofloxacin", "Oral azithromycin", "Oral doxycycline"]
explanation_text:
Patients with ascites (and protein concentration <= 15 g/L) should be given oral ciprofloxacin or norfloxacin as prophylaxis against spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

The correct answer in this case is

Oral ciprofloxacin

. In patients with advanced cirrhosis and low ascitic fluid protein (<15 g/L), there is an increased risk of developing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). Oral ciprofloxacin is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic that provides broad-spectrum coverage against Gram-negative organisms, which are the most common cause of SBP. According to UK guidelines, long-term prophylaxis with oral ciprofloxacin (or norfloxacin) should be considered for patients at high risk for SBP, such as those with a previous episode of SBP or low ascitic fluid protein concentration.

Regarding the other options:

No antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated

would not be appropriate in this case due to the patient's increased risk for SBP based on her low ascitic fluid protein concentration and history of advanced cirrhosis.

Oral penicillin

is not an appropriate choice for SBP prophylaxis because it does not provide adequate coverage against Gram-negative organisms commonly implicated in SBP, such as

Escherichia coli

and

Klebsiella pneumoniae

.

Oral azithromycin

, a macrolide antibiotic, is also not suitable for SBP prophylaxis as it primarily targets Gram-positive bacteria and atypical organisms. It does not have sufficient activity against Gram-negative bacteria frequently associated with SBP.

Finally,

Oral doxycycline

, a tetracycline antibiotic, provides broader coverage than penicillin but still lacks optimal effectiveness against the typical causative organisms of SBP. Moreover, doxycycline has potential hepatotoxic effects which could further worsen liver function in a patient with advanced cirrhosis.

question_text: A 40-year-old female patient comes to see you in clinic with a recent diagnosis of hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC). Other than colorectal cancer, of which of these malignancies is she most at risk?
options_json: ["Vaginal cancer", "Breast cancer", "Cervical cancer", "Endometrial cancer", "Ovarian cancer"]

question_text:
A 63-year-old man is admitted to hospital with several days of severe diarrhoea, fever, malaise and abdominal pain. 12 days prior, he started a course of levofloxacin for community-acquired pneumonia. On examination, the abdomen is mildly tender and he has a fever of 38.3°C.

A stool sample is taken and comes back positive for Clostridium difficile toxin. Oral metronidazole does not improve his symptoms, so he is switched to oral vancomycin. Going through his past medical history, the doctor notes that he has had several Clostridium difficile infections previously.

Which of the following drugs may be beneficial in this patient's management?
options_json: ["Bezlotoxumab", "Infliximab", "Rituximab", "Suvratoxumab", "Trastuzumab"]
explanation_text:
Bezlotoxumab is a monoclonal antibody which targets

The correct answer here is bezlotoxumab - this is a relatively-new monoclonal antibody which binds to

Clostridium difficile

toxin B. It is licensed in Europe to reduce the risk of recurrence of

C. diff

infection in patients undergoing antibacterial treatment. It is not yet widely used.

The other options are also monoclonal antibodies, but are all incorrect as none of them are involved in the targeting or management of

C. diff

infection:

Infliximab is an anti-tumour necrosis factor antibody, used to manage rheumatoid arthritis and Crohn's disease.

Rituximab is an anti-CD20 antibody, used in the management of rheumatoid arthritis and non-Hodgkin's lymphoma.

Suvratoxumab is an anti-

Staphylococcus aureus

alpha toxin antibody, currently under investigation for the prevention of hospital-acquired pneumonia.

Trastuzumab, more commonly known by its brand name Herceptin, is a HER2/neu receptor antagonist, used in the management of metastatic breast cancer.

question_text: A 31-year-old man with a known history of alcoholic liver disease is reviewed following a suspected oesophageal variceal haemorrhage. He has been resuscitated and intravenous terlipressin has been given. His blood pressure is now 104/60 mmHg and his pulse is 84/min. What is the most appropriate intervention?
options_json: ["Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt", "Surgical referral", "Endoscopic variceal band ligation", "Sengstaken-Blakemore tube", "Endoscopic sclerotherapy"]

question_text:
A 42-year-old man presents a two-month history of steatorrhoea, abdominal discomfort, and diarrhoea. He is particularly worried, as three years ago, he required colonic resection following ischaemic colitis, leaving him with short bowel syndrome. He also reports paraesthesia and feeling unsteady on his feet. The endoscopic appearance of the small bowel is unremarkable. Biopsy samples show non-specific eosinophilia. Colonoscopy is also unremarkable. Abdominal examination is unremarkable, and his weight has remained stable.

What investigation is most likely to be diagnostic?
options_json: ["CT abdomen", "CT colonoscopy", "Faecal calprotectin", "Hydrogen breath test", "Serum lipase"]
explanation_text:
Hydrogen breath testing is an appropriate first line test for diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome

Hydrogen breath test

is the correct answer. This patient’s symptoms — steatorrhoea, abdominal discomfort, diarrhoea, and neurological features (paraesthesia and unsteadiness) — occurring in the context of short bowel syndrome following colonic resection, are highly suggestive of

small bowel bacterial overgrowth (SBBO)

.

Small bowel bacterial overgrowth (SBBO)

is a condition in which excessive microbes colonise the small intestine. Anatomical abnormalities that lead to intestinal stasis, such as previous bowel surgery, are well-recognised risk factors. The typical presentation includes bloating, steatorrhoea, and diarrhoea. Critically, SBBO can cause

vitamin B12 deficiency

, explaining this patient’s neurological symptoms. While small bowel mucosal biopsies may show modest villous blunting or lamina propria inflammation, they are often non-diagnostic. A

hydrogen breath test

is a non-invasive, first-line investigation that can confirm SBBO by detecting hydrogen or methane produced by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates in the small intestine.

CT abdomen

is incorrect. There is no clinical suspicion of intra-abdominal malignancy, obstruction, or acute pathology that would warrant ionising imaging at this stage. It would not identify SBBO and therefore would not guide further management.

CT colonoscopy

is incorrect. This investigation is unnecessary given that both upper GI endoscopy and colonoscopy were already performed and were unremarkable. It is also unlikely to identify mucosal abnormalities associated with SBBO.

Faecal calprotectin

is incorrect. This is a useful biomarker for active inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). However, the patient has no endoscopic signs of IBD, and his presentation — especially steatorrhoea and neurological features — is atypical for IBD. Moreover, faecal calprotectin is not useful in diagnosing SBBO.

Serum lipase

is incorrect. While steatorrhoea can be seen in pancreatic insufficiency, this patient’s history of colonic resection and neurological features point more strongly towards SBBO. There is no abdominal tenderness or other features to suggest acute pancreatitis, for which lipase would be appropriate.

question_text:
A 54-year-old man presents to his general practitioner with rectal bleeding. He has a past medical history of HIV and a renal transplant as a consequence of HIV-associated nephropathy. His regular medications include tacrolimus, prednisolone and Truvada. He is in a sexual relationship with a male partner. He smokes 20 cigarettes daily.

On examination, there is a craggy mass palpable on the lateral aspect of the anal canal.

What is the likely strongest risk factor that this man has for the probable diagnosis?
options_json: ["HIV", "HPV infection", "Immunosuppressive medication", "Sexual orientation", "Smoking"]
explanation_text:
HPV infection  (especially HPV 16 subtype) is the strongest risk factor for anal cancer

HPV infection

is the correct answer. The patient likely has anal cancer. 80-85% of anal cancer is caused by HPV infection. It is not commonly tested for and so while it is not explicitly mentioned in the clinical vignette, it is still the most likely risk factor for this patient developing anal cancer.

HIV

is incorrect. HIV is a risk factor for anal cancer but is not responsible for as many cases as HPV infection.

Immunosuppressive medication

is incorrect. This is another risk factor for anal cancer and the patient is on tacrolimus and prednisolone which are immunosuppressants. However, while this may be contributory it is less of a risk factor than HPV infection.

Sexual orientation

is incorrect. Men who have sex with men are at increased risk of anal cancer but HPV is a more significant risk factor.

Smoking

is incorrect. This is also a risk factor for anal cancer and many other cancers. Again, it is less significant in this context and less likely than HPV infection.

question_text:
A 52-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a 5-day history of abdominal pain. He reports a history of recurrent abdominal pain in the right upper abdomen but they have always been self-resolving. On examination, he is jaundiced. Tenderness is elicited on palpating the right upper quadrant. Murphy's sign is negative. His basic observations include temperature 38.7°C, heart rate 100 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, blood pressure 110/62 mmHg.

What is the first-line investigation for this patient?
options_json: ["Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)", "CT abdomen and pelvis", "Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)", "Ultrasound scan (USS)", "CT abdomen"]
explanation_text:
USS is the first line investigation for suspected cholangitis

This patient has the Charcot's triad of right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice. USS is the first line investigation for suspected cholangitis.

MRCP is helpful to visualise the biliary tree but not the first line investigation.

ERCP is helpful for the investigation of biliary pathology and therapeutic removal of gallstones but it is not the first line investigation for suspected cholangitis.

CT abdomen (and pelvis) is helpful to rule out other abdominal pathologies but ultrasound is usually the first line.

question_text:
A 55-year-old man presents with a 6 week history of dysphagia and heartburn. He has noticed dysphagia of both solids and liquids, and feels a burning sensation after eating, which is worse on lying flat at night. He says that despite this, he still has a good appetite and is eating well. He even regurgitated some steak whilst eating out at his favourite restaurant last weekend. On specific questioning, he admits to having to tighten his belt by two belt holes because his clothes feel looser.

Which of the above symptoms is least consistent with a diagnosis of achalasia?
options_json: ["Weight loss", "New heartburn", "Heartburn worse on lying flat", "Regurgitation", "Dysphagia to both solids and liquids"]
explanation_text:
Whilst dysphagia of solids and liquids is a classic history for achalasia, certain features such as significant weight loss are not consistent and suggest cancer - 'pseudoachalasia'

The correct answer is weight loss.

Achalasia is a condition in which the lower oesophageal sphincter fails to relax, resulting in symptoms of dysphagia to both solids and liquids and heartburn.

Weight loss is not usually associated with achalasia, and especially unintentional weight loss despite adequate dietary intake would suggest a more sinister diagnosis such as malignancy.

New heartburn is a concerning feature in a 55-year-old and paired with weight loss would warrant a two week wait referral. However, it is consistent with a diagnosis of achalasia.

Regurgitation and dysphagia to both solids and liquids are also both symptoms of achalasia.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman is diagnosed with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). She occasionally experiences spasms of pain in the left iliac fossa and has periods of both constipation and loose stools. You are considering drug therapy to provide her with symptomatic relief from the symptoms.

Which one of the following does NICE recommend that we avoid in patients with IBS?
options_json: ["Mebeverine", "Ispaghula", "Methylcellulose", "Sterculia", "Lactulose"]
explanation_text:
NICE recommend avoiding lactulose in the management of IBS

The correct answer in this case is

Lactulose

. According to the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines, lactulose should be avoided in patients with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS) as it can exacerbate symptoms. Lactulose is a synthetic disaccharide that works by drawing water into the bowel, softening stools and increasing bowel movements. However, it can also cause bloating, flatulence, and abdominal discomfort, which are common symptoms of IBS.

Mebeverine

is an antispasmodic medication that helps relieve muscle spasms in the gastrointestinal tract. It is commonly prescribed for IBS patients to alleviate abdominal pain and cramping associated with the condition. Therefore, mebeverine would not be contraindicated for use in IBS patients.

Ispaghula

, also known as psyllium husk, is a bulk-forming laxative derived from the seeds of the Plantago ovata plant. It works by absorbing water in the intestines, forming a gel-like substance that promotes softer stool consistency and easier passage through the colon. Ispaghula may help improve both constipation and diarrhea symptoms in IBS patients.

Methylcellulose

is another bulk-forming laxative similar to ispaghula. It absorbs water in the intestines and increases stool bulk, making it easier for stools to pass through the colon. Methylcellulose may help manage constipation-related symptoms of IBS without causing significant side effects or worsening other IBS symptoms.

Finally,

Sterculia

is a natural gum extracted from the Sterculia species of trees. It acts as a bulk-forming laxative by absorbing water and increasing fecal mass while softening stools. Sterculia can be used to manage constipation in IBS patients and is generally well-tolerated.

In summary, the NICE guidelines recommend avoiding lactulose in IBS patients due to its potential to exacerbate symptoms. The other options listed, such as mebeverine, ispaghula, methylcellulose, and sterculia, may provide symptomatic relief for IBS patients without causing significant adverse effects.

explanation_text:
Gastrin increases HCL production and gastrointestinal motility

question_text:
An 80-year-old man is admitted to the emergency department with acute onset abdominal pain and per rectum bleeding. His daughter mentions he is a smoker and has a past medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes. An abdominal X-ray is reported as showing 'thumbprinting'. A venous blood gas is taken with results shown below:


pH	7.21	(7.35 - 7.45)
PaCO2	4.8 kPa	(4.7 - 6.0)
HCO3-	17 mEq/L	(22 - 26)
Lactate	7.2 mmol/L	(0-2)

What area of the gastrointestinal tract is most commonly affected in the condition being described?
options_json: ["Caecum", "Hepatic flexure", "Ileocaecal junction", "Sigmoid", "Splenic flexure"]
explanation_text:
The splenic flexure is the most commonly affected site in ischaemic colitis

The condition being described is ischaemic colitis. This patient is at risk of vascular disease given his past medical history and smoking status. Ischaemic colitis occurs when there is reduced flow in vessels supplying the intestines, usually secondary to hypovolaemia or hypotension.

The most common site affected in ischaemic colitis is the

splenic flexure

. This is a 'watershed' area: it has a dual supply of blood from distal branches of both the superior  and inferior mesenteric arteries (the middle colic and left colic arteries, respectively). As such, in low-flow states, this area is the most vulnerable to inadequate perfusion and ischaemia.

All other areas in the question are supplied by a large single artery and so are incorrect as they are much less commonly affected in ischaemic colitis.

The ileocolic artery is the main termination of the superior mesenteric artery; it supplies the terminal ileum, the

ileocaecal junction

, the appendix, the

caecum

and the proximal ascending colon.

Another branch of the superior mesenteric artery, the right colic artery, supplies the ascending colon. Its ascending marginal branches supply the

hepatic flexure

and proximal transverse colon.

The

distal sigmoid

is supplied by the sigmoid arteries, branches of the inferior mesenteric artery.

The patient's symptoms had initially improved, however, they developed some diarrhoea and vomiting a few days ago and therefore were kept in hospital.

Today the patient appears to have deteriorated with worsening diarrhoea and new abdominal pain. Stool samples taken at the onset of the diarrhoea confirmed the presence of Clostridium difficile.

A CT abdomen is performed demonstrating a partial ileus and evidence of severe disease.

explanation_text:
In life-threatening

This patient has developed complications secondary to

Clostridium difficile

infection due to previous extensive broad-spectrum antibiotic use. The patient has evidence of a life-threatening infection with a partial ileus and severe disease demonstrated on CT imaging.

Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole

should be started immediately and a review for potential surgical intervention made early if there is no evidence of improvement.

IV fidaxomicin and IV vancomycin

are not used to treat

C difficile

infections with neither IV forms having a clear role in management. The oral forms of both may be used in different circumstances however vancomycin in combination with IV metronidazole is favoured in life-threatening infections.

IV metronidazole and IV vancomycin

is not commonly used in combination for the management of

C difficile

as even in life-threatening cases an oral form of antibiotic should be used to target existing gastrointestinal bacterial directly.

Oral fidaxomicin and IV vancomycin

is again not routinely used for
