Oral metronidazole and IV vancomycin

again is not the suggested combined antibiotic regime with neither oral metronidazole nor IV vancomycin having evidence of effectiveness in life-threatening

C difficile

infections. The combination of these two antibiotics in their alternative forms has however been shown to be effective with the oral vancomycin targeting the existing gastrointestinal bacteria and the more potent IV metronidazole (compared to its oral form) the infection systemically.

question_text: A 23-year-old man is investigated for chronic diarrhoea associated with raised inflammatory markers. A bowel biopsy is taken. Which one of the following findings is most suggestive of ulcerative colitis?
options_json: ["Multiple granulomas", "Goblet cell depletion", "Inflammation affecting the serosa", "Cobblestone appearance", "Skip lesions"]
explanation_text:
Ulcerative colitis - depletion of goblet cells

The correct answer is

Goblet cell depletion

. Ulcerative colitis (UC) is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterised by continuous mucosal inflammation starting from the rectum and extending proximally. One of the histological hallmarks of UC is goblet cell depletion, which refers to a decrease in the number of mucus-producing cells in the lining of the colon. This depletion contributes to a compromised intestinal barrier function, promoting ongoing inflammation.

Multiple granulomas

are more suggestive of Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis. Granulomas, which are clusters of immune cells, are not typically seen in UC. Their presence helps distinguish Crohn's disease from other forms of inflammatory bowel disease.

Inflammation affecting the serosa

also points towards Crohn's disease as opposed to ulcerative colitis. In UC, inflammation is usually limited to the mucosal layer while in Crohn's disease, it can affect all layers of the bowel wall including the serosa.

A

Cobblestone appearance

again suggests Crohn's disease rather than ulcerative colitis. This appearance results from deep ulcers that develop between areas of swollen intestinal lining, giving it a cobblestone-like look on imaging or endoscopy. This feature is not characteristic for UC where ulcers tend to be shallow and continuous.

Skip lesions

, which refer to areas of diseased intestine separated by healthy sections, are another characteristic finding in Crohn's disease but not in ulcerative colitis. In UC, inflammation typically starts at the rectum and extends continuously up the colon without skipping any parts.

question_text: A 55-year-old man with a history of gallstone disease presents with a two-day history of pain in the right upper quadrant. He feels 'like I have flu' and his wife reports he has had a fever for the past day. On examination his temperature is 38.1ºC, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg, pulse 102/min and he is tender in the right upper quadrant. His sclera have a yellow-tinge. What is the most likely diagnosis?

Charcot's cholangitis triad: fever, jaundice and right upper quadrant pain

This patient has Charcot's triad (right upper quadrant pain, fever and jaundice), which is classically linked to ascending cholangitis. The systemic upset and jaundice are less typical of acute cholecystitis.

A 35-year-old man presents to the Gastroenterology clinic due to a two-month history of dysphagia to solids and odynophagia, which has not responded to a trial of omeprazole. His weight is stable.

His medical history is significant for asthma and HIV infection, with a recent CD4 count of 520/mm³. He is taking salbutamol and beclometasone inhalers, as well as tenofovir and emtricitabine.

Blood test results are as follows:


Hb	149 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	226 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.3 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Neuts	4.1 * 109/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Lymphs	1.5 * 109/L	(1.0 - 3.5)
Mono	0.3 * 109/L	(0.2 - 0.8)
Eosin	1.4 * 109/L	(0.0 - 0.4)

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Achalasia", "Eosinophilic oesophagitis", "Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease", "Oesophageal cancer", "Oesophageal candidiasis"]
explanation_text:
Eosinophilic esophagitis typically presents in young men with symptoms of dysphagia and in patients with a history of food allergy, eczema and asthma

The correct answer is

eosinophilic oesophagitis

. This condition classically presents as dysphagia and/or odynophagia in young men. Features in the stem making eosinophilic oesophagitis more likely include the history of asthma and the raised blood eosinophil count.

Achalasia

is incorrect. Questions about achalasia classically give a history of dysphagia to both solids and liquids from the beginning of symptom onset, rather than the dysphagia to solids alone seen here. Achalasia would also not explain this patient's eosinophilia.

Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease

is incorrect. Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease would not cause eosinophilia and is more likely to respond at least partially to proton pump inhibitors.

Oesophageal cancer

is incorrect. Oesophageal cancer is not associated with eosinophilia; tends to be associated with weight loss; and is less likely to present in a patient of this age without a significant smoking or alcohol history, which is not provided.

Oesophageal candidiasis

is incorrect. Although this is a plausible cause of odynophagia in some patients with HIV, this patient has a CD4 count in the normal range and is therefore not especially susceptible to fungal infections. Candidiasis would also not explain this patient's eosinophilia.

I cells secrete CCK.

D cells secrete somatostatin.

There is no such cell as H cell in the stomach.

question_text:
A 35-year-old woman is referred to hospital. As part of a liver screen the following results are obtained:


Anti-HBs	Negative
Anti-HBc	Positive
HBs antigen	Positive
IgM anti-HBc	Negative

Anti-HBs = Hepatitis B Surface Antibody; Anti-HBc = Hepatitis B Core Antibody; HBs antigen = Hepatitis B Surface Antigen
What is the patient's hepatitis B status?
options_json: ["Probable hepatitis D infection", "Acute hepatitis B infection", "Previous immunisation to hepatitis B", "Chronic hepatitis B", "Previous hepatitis B infection, not a carrier"]
explanation_text:
Positive anti-HBc IgG, negative anti-HBc IgM and negative anti-HBc in the presence of HBsAg implies chronic HBV infection

The correct answer is

Chronic hepatitis B

. This diagnosis is made based on the presence of HBs antigen and anti-HBc, with the absence of IgM anti-HBc. In chronic Hepatitis B infection, the Hepatitis B surface antigen (HBsAg) remains positive for more than six months (which differentiates it from acute infection), and IgM antibodies to the core antigen are typically absent. The presence of Anti-HBc indicates past or ongoing infection with the hepatitis B virus in an undefined time frame.

The option

Probable hepatitis D infection

is incorrect because there is no evidence here to suggest a co-infection with Hepatitis D. Hepatitis D only occurs in those infected with Hepatitis B, but specific testing would be needed to confirm this diagnosis.

The option

Acute hepatitis B infection

is also incorrect as during an acute infection, IgM anti-HBc would be present which is not the case here.

Previous immunisation to hepatitis B

would result in a positive Anti-HBs, indicating immunity to Hepatitis B either through vaccination or natural infection. However, in this scenario, Anti-HBs is negative which rules out this option.

Finally,

Previous hepatitis B infection, not a carrier

, would be indicated by a positive Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc, and negative HBs antigen which again does not match our patient's results. This pattern suggests recovery and immunity from past infection rather than active disease.

question_text:
A 53-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner with a three-month history of non-bloody diarrhoea, which has progressively worsened. She has also experienced a few episodes of faecal incontinence. Her past medical history includes gastric reflux disease, anxiety, and hypothyroidism. Her medications include sertraline, double-dose omeprazole for chronic dyspepsia, and levothyroxine. Apart from diarrhoea, she is well and has not lost any weight. She has not travelled abroad recently. Her thyroid function tests are normal.

What is the most appropriate action?
options_json: ["Colonoscopy and biopsy", "Faecal elastase", "Faecal occult blood test", "Reduce dose of levothyroxine", "Trial of mebeverine"]
explanation_text:
PPIs are a cause of microscopic colitis, which can present with chronic diarrhoea, colonoscopy and biopsy should be considered when patients present in this way and are taking a PPI

Colonoscopy and biopsy

is the correct answer. Microscopic colitis should be considered in patients with chronic diarrhoea, particularly those receiving PPI therapy. Suspected microscopic colitis should be evaluated with endoscopy and biopsies, as the macroscopic appearance of the colon is usually normal.

Faecal elastase

is incorrect. This is a test used in the diagnosis or exclusion of pancreatic exocrine insufficiency. Chronic pancreatitis is an unlikely diagnosis due to the lack of abdominal pain, nausea/vomiting, or weight loss.

Faecal occult blood test

is incorrect. Aside from diarrhoea, there are no other features to suggest gastrointestinal malignancy. There is no weight loss, and her diarrhoea is consistently non-bloody. A faecal occult blood test would add little to the diagnostic work-up of this patient.

Reduce dose of levothyroxine

is incorrect. Whilst it would be reasonable to check her thyroid function, it would not be appropriate to reduce her medication dose without doing so. Furthermore, the use of omeprazole alongside chronic diarrhoea in a middle-aged woman should raise the suspicion of microscopic colitis.

Trial of mebeverine

is incorrect. Certainly, patients with diarrhoea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome may present similarly to this woman, but you would also expect abdominal pain. Abdominal pain in IBS is classically related to defecation and is associated with a change in the frequency or consistency of stool.

question_text:
A 35-year-old female patient presents with persistent dyspepsia of 6 months duration. She failed multiple trials of conservative treatment by her GP, therefore, she was referred for the gastroenterologist for further review.

Investigations were done and her urea breath test was negative for Helicobacter pylori. Gastroscopy revealed multiple gastroduodenal ulcers. Fasting gastrin level was detected to be very high.

explanation_text:
Gastrin increases H+ secretion by gastric parietal cells

Gastrin hormone is secreted from the G cells in the antrum of the stomach and increases acid secretion from gastric parietal cells.

Chief cells secrete pepsin, a proteolytic enzyme.

D cells in the pancreas & stomach secrete somatostatin hormone.

G cells in the antrum of the stomach secrete gastrin hormone in response to distension of the stomach and vagal stimulation.

Goblet cells secrete an alkaline mucus that protects the epithelium against shear stress and acid.

options_json: ["Transferrin saturation + ferritin", "Haematocrit + ferritin", "Liver biopsy with Perl's stain", "Serum iron + ferritin", "Serum iron + haematocrit"]
explanation_text:
Screening for haemochromatosis

question_text: A 35-year-old former intravenous drug user is reviewed in the liver clinic. He has recently been diagnosed with hepatitis C after being found to have abnormal liver function tests. It is decided as part of his work-up that he should be assessed for liver cirrhosis. What is the most appropriate test to perform?
options_json: ["MRI liver", "Liver biopsy", "Urinary fibroblast quantification", "Endoscopic ultrasound", "Transient elastography"]
explanation_text:
Transient elastography may be useful for diagnosing and monitoring the severity of liver cirrhosis

The correct answer is

Transient elastography

. Transient elastography, also known as Fibroscan, is a non-invasive test that measures liver stiffness, which correlates with the degree of fibrosis or scarring within the liver. It has been validated for assessing liver fibrosis in chronic hepatitis C and is recommended by the National Institute for Health and Care Excellence (NICE) guidelines in the UK. The procedure involves placing an ultrasound probe on the skin overlying the liver, emitting a shear wave and measuring its speed to estimate tissue stiffness.

MRI liver

is not typically used as a first-line investigation for cirrhosis. While it can detect changes associated with cirrhosis and provide detailed images of the liver's structure, it lacks specificity in determining the stage of fibrosis compared to transient elastography.

Liver biopsy

, although traditionally considered the gold standard for diagnosing and staging cirrhosis, is invasive and carries risks such as bleeding and pain. It's also subject to sampling error because only a small part of the liver is examined. Due to these reasons, non-invasive tests like transient elastography are often preferred.

Urinary fibroblast quantification

does not exist as a diagnostic tool for assessing liver fibrosis or cirrhosis. It seems to be a distractor in this case.

Lastly,

Endoscopic ultrasound

might be useful in identifying complications related to cirrhosis like varices but it does not assess the severity of liver fibrosis directly. Therefore, while useful in managing patients with established cirrhosis, it would not be appropriate as an initial test to diagnose or stage hepatic fibrosis or cirrhosis.

question_text:
A 50-year-old presents with abdominal cramps and loose stools 8 weeks after being discharged from hospital following a chest infection.

His recent admission had been complicated as he developed diarrhoea as an inpatient with a stool sample testing positive for Clostridium difficile. He was managed successfully with first-line treatment and his symptoms resolved.

Today the patient appears clinically stable with all observations within in normal range. A stool sample is taken and again tests positive for C. difficile toxins.

What treatment course should the patient now be commenced on?
options_json: ["No treatment is required", "Oral fidaxomicin", "Oral metronidazole", "Oral vancomycin", "Oral vancomycin and IV metronidazole"]
explanation_text:
A recurrent episode of

Recurrent episodes of

C. difficile

are common affecting approximately 20% of patients after initial infection. The first-line treatment is oral vancomycin for 10 days. If recurrency occurs within 12 weeks of symptom resolution

oral fidaxomicin

should be commenced. Fidaxomicin is from the class of narrow-spectrum macrocyclic antibiotic drugs called tiacumicins and currently is only used in the management of

C. difficile

. If recurrence occurs beyond 12 weeks either oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin can be used for treatment.

This patient had a recent confirmed case of

C. difficile

which responded to management. Recurrent episodes are common and as the patient has re-developed symptoms he is at risk of complications (i.e. ileus or toxic megacolon).

No treatment

is therefore not an appropriate course of action.

IV metronidazole is used in combination with oral vancomycin for third-line or or life-threatening cases of

C. difficile

with

oral metronidazole

playing no role in treatment.

A

oral vancomycin

course can be trialled if a patient presents with a recurrent case of

C. difficile

over 12weeks after symptoms resolution only. As this patient has represented within 12 weeks oral fidaxomicin should be started.

Vancomycin and IV metronidazole

is normal reserved for third-line or life-threatening cases of

C. difficile

. This treatment regime should therefore only be used if oral fidaxomicin fails or if the patient has developed features of significant infection such as hypotension, ileus or toxic megacolon.

question_text:
A 65-year-old man presents to the emergency department with a two-week history of jaundice, dark urine, and pruritus. He also reports anorexia and an unintentional weight loss of 5 kg over the past two months. He has no significant past medical history, is a retired engineer, is an ex-smoker with a 10 pack-year history, and consumes 12 units of alcohol per week.

On abdominal examination, a mass is palpable in the epigastric region.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Cholangiocarcinoma", "Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC)", "Liver cirrhosis", "Pancreatic cancer", "Primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC)"]
explanation_text:
Pancreatic cancer classically presents as painless jaundice

The patient’s history of painless jaundice, anorexia, and weight loss is highly suggestive of

pancreatic cancer

, making this the correct answer. Pancreatic cancer commonly presents with obstructive jaundice when the tumour compresses or invades the bile duct. The presence of an epigastric mass in this patient further supports this diagnosis, making pancreatic cancer the most likely cause. Courvoisier’s sign—a palpable gallbladder in a jaundiced patient—may also be observed in cases of pancreatic head tumours causing biliary obstruction.

Cholangiocarcinoma

is a malignant tumour arising from the bile duct epithelium. It is classified anatomically as intrahepatic, perihilar (also known as klatskin tumours), or distal extrahepatic. When located distally, it can closely mimic pancreatic head cancer, as both may compress or invade the common bile duct, causing obstructive jaundice. Like pancreatic cancer, it typically presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, pale stools, pruritus, and weight loss. However, a palpable epigastric mass is uncommon and more indicative of pancreatic malignancy, making this the most likely diagnosis.

HCC

may also present with jaundice, weight loss, and constitutional symptoms, particularly in advanced stages. However, it more commonly causes right upper quadrant pain, hepatomegaly, ascites, and signs of chronic liver disease (e.g., cirrhosis). Large tumours, especially in the left lobe, may occasionally be palpable in the epigastrium, but this is uncommon and typically occurs only with significant enlargement. HCC usually arises in the setting of chronic liver disease, which is absent in this case, making it a less likely diagnosis, though it remains a consideration in older patients with systemic and liver-related symptoms.

Liver cirrhosis

is an unlikely diagnosis in this patient given several factors. Firstly, his alcohol intake is moderate (12 units per week), which is below the threshold typically associated with alcohol-related liver disease. Secondly, there is no clinical evidence of chronic liver disease, such as ascites, spider naevi, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, or splenomegaly. A palpable mass in this region more likely reflects a solid tumour, like pancreatic cancer. In the absence of risk factors or clinical stigmata, cirrhosis is an improbable primary diagnosis in this scenario.

PSC

is a chronic inflammatory and fibrosing disease affecting the intrahepatic and extrahepatic bile ducts. It is strongly associated with inflammatory bowel disease, especially ulcerative colitis. PSC typically presents with cholestatic features including jaundice, pruritus, dark urine, and pale stools. Patients may also experience constitutional symptoms like fatigue and weight loss. However, PSC would not explain an epigastric mass, and it most commonly presents in patients aged 30–50 years. Therefore, PSC is less likely in a 65-year-old male, particularly if an epigastric mass is present, where malignancy should be considered more strongly.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

question_text:
A 54-year-old woman presents with jaundice shortly after being discharged from hospital. Liver function tests are reported as follows:


Albumin	49 g/l
Bilirubin	89 µmol/l
Alanine transferase (ALT)	66 iu/l
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)	245 µmol/l
Gamma glutamyl transferase (yGT)	529 u/l

Which of the following antibiotics is she most likely to have received?
options_json: ["Flucloxacillin", "Gentamicin", "Ciprofloxacin", "Trimethoprim", "Ceftazidime"]
explanation_text:
Flucloxacillin is a well recognised cause of cholestasis

The correct answer in this case is

Flucloxacillin

. Flucloxacillin is a penicillinase-resistant penicillin used to treat Gram-positive bacterial infections, particularly those caused by

Staphylococcus aureus

. It has been associated with cholestatic hepatitis and jaundice, which can occur within days to weeks after starting the medication. The liver function tests of this patient show a predominantly cholestatic pattern, with elevated bilirubin, alkaline phosphatase (ALP), and gamma glutamyl transferase (yGT) levels.

Gentamicin

is an aminoglycoside antibiotic used to treat Gram-negative bacterial infections. While it can cause nephrotoxicity and ototoxicity, it is not commonly associated with hepatotoxicity or cholestasis. Therefore, it is less likely to be the cause of this patient's jaundice.

Ciprofloxacin

is a fluoroquinolone antibiotic used to treat a wide range of bacterial infections. Although rare cases of hepatotoxicity have been reported with ciprofloxacin use, it typically presents as acute hepatitis rather than cholestasis; thus, it is less likely to be the cause of this patient's jaundice.

Trimethoprim

, often combined with sulfamethoxazole (co-trimoxazole), is an antibiotic used primarily for urinary tract infections and respiratory infections. Hepatotoxicity related to trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole has been reported but is relatively rare compared to flucloxacillin-induced hepatotoxicity. Additionally, when trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole does cause liver injury, it usually presents as acute hepatitis rather than cholestasis.

Ceftazidime

is a third-generation cephalosporin used to treat Gram-negative bacterial infections. It is generally considered to have a low risk of hepatotoxicity, and when it does occur, it is usually in the form of acute hepatitis rather than cholestasis.

question_text: Which one of the following hormones is most responsible for the secretion of bicarbonate is the upper gastrointestinal tract?
options_json: ["Somatostatin", "Gastrin", "Secretin", "CCK", "Vasoactive intestinal peptide"]
explanation_text:
Secretin increases secretion of bicarbonate-rich fluid from pancreas and hepatic duct cells

The correct answer is

Secretin

. Secretin is a hormone that plays a crucial role in the regulation of gastrointestinal functions. It is released by the S cells of the duodenum in response to low pH (acidic chyme entering from the stomach). One of its main effects is stimulating the pancreas to secrete bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice into the duodenum. This bicarbonate helps to neutralise the acidic chyme, thereby protecting the intestinal mucosa and providing an optimal environment for pancreatic enzymes.

Somatostatin

, on the other hand, inhibits various endocrine and exocrine processes. It suppresses bicarbonate secretion by inhibiting secretin release, acting as a counter-regulatory hormone. Therefore, it does not promote bicarbonate secretion in the upper gastrointestinal tract.

Gastrin

is primarily responsible for stimulating acid secretion by parietal cells in the stomach, not bicarbonate secretion. Gastrin also stimulates the growth of gastric mucosa and increases gastric motility but it has no significant effect on pancreatic bicarbonate production.

CCK (Cholecystokinin)

mainly stimulates gallbladder contraction and pancreatic enzyme secretion into the small intestine following a meal. Its primary function is facilitating digestion within the small intestine by slowing gastric emptying and stimulating bile production. CCK does stimulate some bicarbonate secretion from the pancreas but this effect is less prominent than that of secretin.

Finally,

Vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP)

acts as a neurotransmitter as well as a local hormone in many parts of the human body including the gastrointestinal tract where it inhibits gastric acid secretion and absorption from the intestine while promoting smooth muscle relaxation and blood flow. However, VIP's role in regulating bicarbonate secretion is limited compared to secretin.

question_text:
A 64-year-old man with end-stage metastatic pancreatic cancer is admitted to a hospice for end-of-life care. He is receiving high-dose oral morphine for widespread metastatic bone pain and has developed severe opioid-induced constipation.

Despite trying multiple laxatives, his symptoms remain. The palliative care team recommend a laxative reserved for terminally ill patients due to the risk of potential carcinogenicity, and it is not prescribed outside of this setting.

What is the most likely laxative this patient will receive?
options_json: ["Bisacodyl", "Co-danthramer", "Dantron", "Phenolphthalein", "Sodium picosulfate"]
explanation_text:
Co-danthramer is genotoxic and should only be prescribed to palliative patients due to its carcinogenic potential

Co-danthramer

is the correct answer. This patient is receiving end-of-life care and has severe opioid-induced constipation that has not responded to multiple standard laxatives. Co-danthramer, which combines dantron with poloxamer, is a stimulant laxative specifically licensed for use in palliative care due to concerns about potential carcinogenicity. In the UK, it is only prescribed to terminally ill patients when the benefits of symptom control outweigh long-term risks. Dantron stimulates colonic motility, while poloxamer acts as a stool softener, providing effective relief in severe refractory constipation. This aligns with the patient’s presentation—advanced metastatic cancer, high-dose opioids, and ongoing symptoms despite standard treatment—making co-danthramer the most appropriate option.

Bisacodyl

is incorrect because it is a standard stimulant laxative that is not restricted only for palliative care, and it is likely to have already been tried in this patient. The scenario describes severe opioid-induced constipation unrelieved by multiple laxatives, indicating the need for a palliative-specific agent like co-danthramer.

Dantron

is incorrect because it is not used as a single agent and is only prescribed in combination with poloxamer as co-danthramer. The combination is required to provide both stool-softening and stimulant effects. In the scenario, the effective agent referred to is co-danthramer, not dantron alone.

Phenolphthalein

is incorrect as it has been withdrawn from clinical use in the UK due to its carcinogenic potential and serious adverse effects. It is no longer recommended in any setting, including palliative care. The scenario mentions a laxative reserved for terminally ill patients due to potential carcinogenicity, which refers to co-danthramer, not phenolphthalein, which is not used at all.

Sodium picosulfate

is incorrect because it is a commonly used stimulant laxative and not reserved only for end-of-life care. It is likely to have already been tried in this patient, who remains symptomatic despite multiple laxatives. In this context of refractory opioid-induced constipation in a terminally ill patient, a palliative-specific agent like co-danthramer is more appropriate.

question_text:
A 56-year-old Asian male is being consented for an endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP). He is very anxious about the procedure and requests for more information about the common complications of ERCP. He is concerned about peritonitis, which usually occurs secondary to a perforation of the bowel - a rare complication of ERCP. You reassure him that perforation of the bowel, although a very serious complication, is uncommon. However, they are other more common complications of ERCP that he should be aware of.

Which one of the following is the most common complication of ERCP?
options_json: ["Significant bleeding", "Cholangitis", "Infection", "Acute pancreatitis", "Intolerance to sedation"]
explanation_text:
Acute pancreatitis is the most common complication of ERCP

Acute pancreatitis due to irritation of the pancreatic duct by the X-ray contrast material or cannula is the most common complication of ERCP.

Although all the other options can be regarded as complications of ERCP, they are not as common as acute pancreatitis.

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman presents with jaundice. This has progressively worsened over the past 4 weeks. On examination, her abdomen is soft and non-tender, and there is no evidence of hepatosplenomegaly. You cannot identify any stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Blood results are as follows:


Bilirubin	84 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	832 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	224 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	962 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	35 g/L	(35 - 50)
Ferritin	4842 µg/L	(15 - 150)


Hepatitis B core antigen	Negative
Hepatitis B core antibody	Negative
Hepatitis B surface antibody	Positive


Anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA)	Strongly positive

What treatment is indicated?
options_json: ["Cholestyramine", "Peginterferon alfa-2a", "Prednisolone and azathioprine", "Ursodeoxycholic acid", "Venesection"]
explanation_text:
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis

Ursodeoxycholic acid

is correct.  The clinical features and positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA) favour a diagnosis of primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Ursodeoxycholic acid is the main treatment for PBC. It can help prevent or delay liver damage in the majority of patients.

Cholestyramine

is incorrect. Cholestyramine can be used to treat symptomatic itch in PBC however it does not prevent disease progression.

Peginterferon alfa-2a

is incorrect.  This drug can be used to treat hepatitis B. The hepatitis B serology suggests previous vaccination rather than active infection.

Prednisolone and azathioprine

is incorrect. This is the treatment choice for autoimmune hepatitis. This is a less likely diagnosis as this condition is often associated with anti-smooth muscle antibodies (SMA).

Venesection

is incorrect. Although the ferritin is significantly raised this is most certainly due to hepatic inflammation with subsequent release of ferritin from hepatocytes. Therefore haemochromatosis is a very unlikely diagnosis.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with sudden onset abdominal pain. He describes the pain as cramping, 6/10 in severity and all over his abdomen. He has a past medical history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. He is an ex smoker with a 40 pack year history.

Which part of the colon is most likely to be affected in this patient?
options_json: ["Ascending colon", "Hepatic flexure", "Transverse colon", "Splenic flexure", "Sigmoid colon"]
explanation_text:
The splenic flexure is the most commonly affected site in ischaemic colitis

The cramping, generalised abdominal pains, in conjunction with a history of smoking and hypertension, point to a diagnosis of ischaemic colitis.

The splenic flexure is a watershed area, at the border of the regions supplied by different arteries. This makes the area vulnerable to compromised blood supply.

The rectosigmoid junction is another watershed area, but is less commonly affected than the splenic flexure.

The other regions of the large bowel are less likely to be affected by ischaemic colitis.

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman presents with abdominal pain of the right upper quadrant, of several days' duration. She has a background of chronic knee pain, epilepsy, familial hypercholesterolaemia and a recent urinary tract infection. Her regular medications include sodium valproate, atorvastatin, paracetamol and the combined oral contraceptive pill. She is currently finishing a course of nitrofurantoin.

On examination, she has tenderness in the right upper quadrant and appears visibly jaundiced. Blood tests are shown below:


Bilirubin	68 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	494 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	82 u/L	(3 - 40)
Albumin	39 g/L	(35 - 50)

Which of her medications is most likely to have caused this?
options_json: ["Atorvastatin", "Combined oral contraceptive pill", "Nitrofurantoin", "Paracetamol", "Sodium valproate"]
explanation_text:
The oral contraceptive pill is associated with drug-induced cholestasis

An obstructive picture is seen here, much more indicative of cholestasis rather than hepatitis. As such, the correct answer is the combined oral contraceptive pill (COCP), which is known to cause cholestasis. Other drugs which may also cause cholestasis include antibiotics such as co-amoxiclav, phenothiazines, sulphonylureas, fibrates and anabolic steroids.

Atorvastatin is a statin. These drugs tend to cause more of a hepatocellular picture, rather than that of cholestasis.

Nitrofurantoin is an antibiotic commonly used in the treatment of urinary tract infections. This is also known to generally cause more of a hepatic picture, rather than cholestatic.

Paracetamol overuse tends to lead to hepatic injury, with ALT more elevated than alkaline phosphatase, and not so much of the cholestatic picture seen here.

Sodium valproate is an antiepileptic drug. It may also cause liver disease, although again tends to be a hepatocellular picture, rather than a cholestatic presentation.

question_text:
A 42-year-old man is diagnosed with hereditary haemochromatosis after genetic testing confirms homozygous C282Y mutation. He has no symptoms and his liver function tests are normal. Initial investigations show ferritin of 850 µg/L and transferrin saturation of 68%. He undergoes weekly venesection for 6 months. His latest results are shown below.


Ferritin	45 µg/L	(20-300)
Transferrin saturation	48%	(20-55%)

What is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Continue weekly venesection", "Reduce to monthly venesection", "Commence desferrioxamine", "Stop venesection and monitor in 6 months", "Perform liver MRI"]
explanation_text:
Ferritin and transferrin saturation are used to monitor treatment in haemochromatosis

Reduce to monthly venesection

is the correct management approach for this patient. The goal of therapy in hereditary haemochromatosis is to reduce iron stores to normal levels, typically indicated by a ferritin level below 50 µg/L and transferrin saturation below 50%. In this case, the patient's ferritin has successfully decreased from 850 µg/L to 45 µg/L, which is within the target range. However, his transferrin saturation remains slightly elevated at 48%, though it has improved significantly from the initial 68%. This indicates that while substantial progress has been made, some ongoing iron removal is still needed. Transitioning from weekly to monthly venesection is appropriate at this stage to maintain iron levels within the target range without causing iron deficiency. This maintenance phase typically continues lifelong to prevent reaccumulation of iron.

Continue weekly venesection

would be too aggressive at this point. The patient's ferritin is already at the lower end of the target range (45 µg/L), and continuing weekly venesection could lead to iron deficiency anaemia. Weekly venesection is typically used in the initial depletion phase of treatment, which this patient has already completed successfully as evidenced by his current ferritin level.

Commence desferrioxamine

is not appropriate. Desferrioxamine is an iron chelator used as second-line therapy in patients who cannot tolerate venesection or in cases of severe iron overload with cardiac involvement. This patient has responded well to venesection with no indication of intolerance or complications that would necessitate switching to chelation therapy.

Stop venesection and monitor in 6 months

would be premature. Although the patient's ferritin is now within target range, his transferrin saturation remains slightly elevated. Completely stopping therapy would likely result in reaccumulation of iron and progression of the disease. Maintenance therapy is essential in haemochromatosis management.

Perform liver MRI

is not indicated at this stage. Liver MRI is used to quantify hepatic iron stores and is typically performed during initial assessment or if there is concern about hepatic damage. This patient has responded well to treatment with normalising parameters and has normal liver function tests. There is no clinical indication for liver MRI at this point in his management.

question_text:
A 42-year-old man has acute jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, and confusion. He has a 6-year history of chronic alcohol excess, and admits to drinking alcohol heavily over the past month due to a recent separation from his partner.

He is afebrile and has marked hepatomegaly, jaundice, and ascites. His Glasgow Coma Score (GCS) is 14, and he has mild scleral icterus. His blood pressure is 110/70 mmHg, and his heart rate is 102 bpm.

Investigations:


Bilirubin	84 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	192 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	246 u/L	(3 - 40)
AST	496 u/L	(3 - 40)
Prothrombin time (PT)	27 s	(10 - 14)

Which option is the best next step?
options_json: ["Prescribe pentoxifylline", "Prescribe prednisolone", "Prescribe terlipressin and IV antibiotics, and refer for endoscopy", "Prescribe terlipressin and refer for endoscopy", "Refer for liver transplantation"]
explanation_text:
Corticosteroids are used in the management of severe alcoholic hepatitis

Prescribe prednisolone

is correct. This patient’s acute jaundice, right upper quadrant pain, ascites, confusion (GCS 14), hepatomegaly, and AST > ALT pattern strongly suggest severe alcoholic hepatitis, further supported by his heavy alcohol use and prolonged PT (27 s), indicating coagulopathy. Prednisolone can reduce hepatic inflammation in severe alcoholic hepatitis. The decision to prescribe it can be guided by Maddrey’s discriminant function, with values > 32 or signs of liver failure indicating severe hepatitis (this patient's value is around 64.7). Given his altered mental status and coagulopathy, he is at risk of further deterioration. Early corticosteroid therapy improves short-term survival in these cases by modulating the inflammatory response.

Prescribe pentoxifylline

is incorrect. Pentoxifylline is not first-line for severe alcoholic hepatitis, as steroids offer a superior survival benefit. It was historically considered in patients who cannot receive corticosteroids (e.g., those with active infection or gastrointestinal bleeding); however, the STOPAH trial found that pentoxifylline does not improve survival. Hence, it is no longer recommended.

Prescribe terlipressin and IV antibiotics, and refer for endoscopy

is incorrect. Terlipressin is used for variceal bleeding, which this patient does not have, as there is no evidence suggesting haematemesis or melaena. In this context, IV antibiotics are indicated for preventing spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. Endoscopy is used for variceal bleeding or gastric lesions, which are not suspected in this case.

Prescribe terlipressin and refer for endoscopy

is incorrect. Terlipressin and endoscopy are used in the management of acute variceal haemorrhage. In this scenario, this patient has no haematemesis or melaena. Even if this patient had variceal haemorrhage, treatment would also involve the use of antibiotics to reduce the risk of infection, such as spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

Refer for liver transplantation

is incorrect. Liver transplantation is contraindicated in active alcohol consumption without sustained abstinence. In very exceptional cases, after a multidisciplinary meeting, early liver transplantation may be considered if there is a low risk of relapse post-transplant and if strict abstinence and psychosocial criteria are met. However, this would be considered if the patient had failed to respond to medical therapy (e.g. corticosteroids), which is not the case here.

question_text:
A 50-year-old man presents with weakness and a change in skin colour. He describes the pain in both hands. He was previously fit and well.

On examination, he has ascites, hepatomegaly and his skin has a bronze tint. There is swelling and tenderness of the second and third metacarpophalangeal joints. Neurological examination and mini-mental exam are normal.

X-rays of the hands are requested, which show chondrocalcinosis. Blood tests are also requested:


Hb	162 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	304 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	7.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	5.6 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Glucose	11.2 mmol/L	(4.0 - 5.5)

Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most useful initial screening test?
options_json: ["Caeruloplasmin", "Ferritin", "Genetic testing", "Liver biopsy", "Transferrin saturation"]
explanation_text:
Screening for haemochromatosis

The correct answer is transferrin saturation. The diagnosis here is haemochromatosis, given the presentation and investigations - the bronze tint to the skin, chondrocalcinosis of the finger joints, raised glucose suggesting iron deposition in the pancreas, and liver disease suggesting iron deposition in the liver too. In the general population, transferrin saturation is considered the most useful marker initially. Ferritin is often also measured but is not as sensitive. If the transferrin saturation indicates a diagnosis of haemochromatosis, genetic testing may then be undertaken.

Caeruloplasmin is incorrect. This would be used to screen for Wilson's disease, a metabolic disorder involving the build-up of copper. While there are some similarities in presentation with haemochromatosis, like liver disease, Wilson's disease would present with neuropsychiatric signs and symptoms, too - whereas this patient's neurological and psychiatric examinations were normal.

Ferritin is also often used as an initial screening test. However, it is not as sensitive as transferrin saturation, which is thus more useful.

Genetic testing is the definitive test for haemochromatosis - looking for the C282Y and H63D mutations. However, the question asks about the most useful initial screening test. Genetic testing is also the test of choice for family members.

Liver biopsy is useful to determine liver iron content using Perl's stain. It is both sensitive and specific. It would not, however, be used initially.

question_text:
A 78-year-old woman presents with persistent diarrhoea. Her symptoms started around three months ago and she is now passing frequent 'mucous' like stools. There is no visible blood in the stool and her weight is stable. Bloods show the following:



Hb	11.6 g/dl
Platelets	222 * 109/l
WBC	7.8 * 109/l


Na+	144 mmol/l
K+	3.1 mmol/l
Urea	8.2 mmol/l
Creatinine	101 µmol/l

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Diverticular disease", "Angiodysplasia", "Tubular adenoma", "Colon cancer", "Villous adenoma"]
explanation_text:
Diarrhoea + hypokalaemia → villous adenoma

The correct answer is

villous adenoma

. A villous adenoma is a type of colonic polyp that characteristically presents with secretory diarrhoea containing mucus, leading to electrolyte disturbances - particularly hypokalaemia as seen in this case (K+ 3.1 mmol/L). The secretory nature of these tumors is due to their production of prostaglandin E2 which stimulates fluid and electrolyte secretion into the bowel lumen.

Diverticular disease

typically presents with left-sided abdominal pain and altered bowel habit. While it can cause diarrhoea, it would not typically cause the mucoid secretory diarrhoea with electrolyte disturbances seen here. Bleeding, when it occurs, is usually acute rather than chronic.

Angiodysplasia

is characterized by vascular malformations in the gastrointestinal tract. It typically presents with intermittent gastrointestinal bleeding rather than mucoid diarrhoea. It is more common in elderly patients with aortic stenosis or chronic kidney disease.

Tubular adenoma

is the most common type of colonic polyp but does not typically cause secretory diarrhoea or electrolyte disturbances. These polyps are usually asymptomatic and found incidentally during screening colonoscopy.

Colon cancer

typically presents with a change in bowel habit, weight loss, and often iron deficiency anaemia. While it can cause diarrhoea, it would not typically cause the secretory diarrhoea with electrolyte disturbances characteristic of villous adenomas. The stable weight in this case also makes cancer less likely.

question_text:
A 55-year-old female care worker presented to the general practitioner (GP) with a three-year history of persistent pruritus. She has a history of hypothyroidism which is treated adequately with levothyroxine. On examination, the GP notices widespread excoriation. The patient has been otherwise well apart from generalised lethargy.

Blood results reveal:


Bilirubin	150 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	330 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	36 u/L	(3 - 40)
AST	57 IU/L	(1-45)
INR	1.4	(<1.1)


Anti-mitochondrial antibody-M2 subtype	POSITIVE


What is the first-line treatment for the most likely condition?
options_json: ["Cholestyramine", "Malathion", "Obeticholic acid", "Topical emollients", "Ursodeoxycholic acid"]
explanation_text:
Ursodeoxycholic acid is the first-line medication for primary biliary cholangitis

This patient has primary biliary cholangitis. This is evidenced by the lethargy, pruritus and liver dysfunction. It is most commonly associated with the anti-mitochondrial antibody- M2 subtype and blood tests typically show cholestatic jaundice. The first-line treatment for this condition is ursodeoxycholic acid as this slows disease progression.

Cholestyramine can be used concomitantly with ursodeoxycholic acid. Cholestyramine is used for symptomatic treatment of pruritus but will not affect the disease progression.

Malathion is a treatment for scabies and whilst her occupation put her at increased risk of scabies, the pattern of liver dysfunction would fit with primary biliary cholangitis.

Obeticholic acid is a selective farnesoid X receptor agonist, which decreases circulating bile acid. It is used in combination with ursodeoxycholic acid only when the response to ursodeoxycholic acid is inadequate.

Topical emollients will aid with symptoms but are not a direct treatment of the condition.

question_text:
A 79-year-old woman has been admitted to the gastroenterology ward with abdominal pain.

She has a past medical history of dyslipidaemia, hypertension, bronchiectasis and glaucoma.

Her pain started two days ago but has been gradually becoming more severe. She has had a loss in appetite and diarrhoea. She is opening her bowels up to 5 times daily with some blood in the stool.

On examination, she has a mild tachycardia of 108 beats per minute, a blood pressure of 107/62 mmHg and pyrexia of 37.9 ºC.

Abdominal x-ray showed evidence of mucosal thickening of the large bowel with 'thumbprinting'.

Due to concerns for ischaemic colitis a CT abdomen with contrast is arranged which confirms the diagnosis.

Which part of the colon is most likely to have been affected?
options_json: ["Ascending colon", "Caecum", "Hepatic flexure", "Rectum", "Splenic flexure"]
explanation_text:
The splenic flexure is the most commonly affected site in ischaemic colitis

Given this woman's signs and symptoms along with 'thumbprinting' on her abdominal x-ray it is likely that she has ischaemic colitis.

Ischaemic colitis most commonly affects 'watershed' areas. These are areas at the very edges of the territory supplied by particular vessels where there are fewer collateral vessels. At times of hypoperfusion, these sections of bowel are at an increased risk of ischaemia.

The two most common 'watershed' areas in the large bowel are at the splenic flexure and the rectosigmoid junction.

The splenic flexure is at the 'watershed' area of the superior mesenteric artery and inferior mesenteric artery, whilst the rectosigmoid junction is at the boundary between the inferior mesenteric artery and hypogastric artery.

Given the above options, splenic flexure is the correct answer.

question_text:
A 52-year-old woman has 8 months of progressive fatigue, pruritus, and mild right upper quadrant discomfort. Her history includes Sjogren's syndrome, and she has never drunk alcohol or smoked.

She has mild scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and skin excoriations. Her abdomen is otherwise non-distended and soft.

Investigations:


Bilirubin	35 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	280 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	73 u/L	(3 - 40)
IgM	4.5 g/L	(0.4 - 2.5)
Anti-nuclear antibodies	positive
Anti-mitochondrial antibodies	positive

Which further test must be performed before a definitive diagnosis can be made?
options_json: ["Abdominal ultrasound", "CT abdomen with contrast", "Gallbladder biopsy", "Liver elastography (FibroScan)", "Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography"]
explanation_text:
Imaging is required before making a diagnosis of PBC to exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction

Abdominal ultrasound

is correct. This 52-year-old woman presents with fatigue, pruritus, scleral icterus, hepatomegaly, and a cholestatic liver profile (raised ALP and mildly raised ALT), all of which point toward primary biliary cholangitis (PBC). Her positive anti-mitochondrial antibodies, raised IgM, and history of Sjögren’s syndrome further support this diagnosis. However, before confirming PBC, it is essential to exclude extrahepatic causes of cholestasis such as gallstones, strictures, or malignancy. Abdominal ultrasound is the first-line investigation to evaluate the biliary tree and liver parenchyma because it is non-invasive, accessible, and effective in identifying biliary dilatation or obstructive pathology. If no obstruction is seen and suspicion for PBC remains, more specific imaging such as MRCP may follow.

CT abdomen with contrast

is incorrect because it is not the first-line test for suspected PBC. Although it can detect large lesions or masses causing biliary obstruction, it involves unnecessary radiation and is less sensitive than ultrasound or MRCP for detecting small duct abnormalities. In this patient with no signs of malignancy (e.g. weight loss or palpable mass), and a likely autoimmune cause given the AMA positivity and Sjögren’s history, an ultrasound is more appropriate. CT may be considered if imaging later suggests malignancy or if symptoms suggest an alternative cause, such as pancreatic or biliary cancer.

Gallbladder biopsy

is incorrect as it is not relevant to the diagnosis of PBC, which affects the intrahepatic bile ducts rather than the gallbladder. This invasive procedure is not part of routine workup and would not provide useful diagnostic information for PBC. It may be considered if imaging suggests gallbladder cancer or mass lesions causing biliary obstruction, which is not indicated in this case. Her symptoms and antibody profile instead point to an autoimmune cholestatic disease rather than gallbladder pathology.

Liver elastography (FibroScan)

is incorrect as it assesses the degree of liver fibrosis, not the cause of cholestasis. While useful in monitoring known liver diseases, it is not helpful in excluding extrahepatic obstruction, which must be ruled out before confirming PBC. Additionally, cholestasis can falsely elevate stiffness readings, making it unreliable during active disease. In this patient, who has not yet had biliary imaging, liver elastography is premature and not part of the initial diagnostic pathway.

Percutaneous transhepatic cholangiography

is incorrect as it is an invasive imaging test used for therapeutic or highly detailed diagnostic purposes when ultrasound and MRCP are inconclusive. It carries procedural risks such as bleeding or infection and is not indicated without prior imaging. In this patient with suspected PBC, non-invasive imaging such as ultrasound is preferred first. PTC may only be appropriate if there is confirmed or suspected obstruction not well visualised by other methods, or in cases requiring intervention, such as biliary drainage.

question_text: A 54-year-old man is investigated for dyspepsia. An endoscopy shows a gastric ulcer and a CLO test done during the procedure demonstrates H. pylori infection. A course of H. pylori eradication therapy is given. Six weeks later the patients comes for review. What is the most appropriate test to confirm eradication?
options_json: ["Culture of gastric biopsy", "H. pylori serology", "Hydrogen breath test", "Urea breath test", "Stool culture"]
explanation_text:
Urea breath test is the only test recommended for

The correct answer is

Urea breath test

. This is the recommended test to confirm eradication of

H. pylori

following treatment according to NICE guidelines. The test should be performed at least 4 weeks after completion of eradication therapy to ensure accurate results. The urea breath test works by detecting the presence of

H. pylori

urease activity. The patient ingests 13C-labelled urea, which is broken down by

H. pylori

urease if present, producing labelled CO2 that can be detected in exhaled breath. It is non-invasive, highly sensitive and specific, and provides real-time results.

Culture of gastric biopsy

is incorrect because it is an invasive test requiring endoscopy. While it is highly specific and can provide antibiotic sensitivity information, it is not recommended for routine post-treatment confirmation due to its invasive nature and the availability of equally effective non-invasive alternatives.

H. pylori serology

is incorrect because antibodies can remain positive for months or even years after successful eradication. Therefore, serology cannot reliably distinguish between current and past infection, making it unsuitable for confirming eradication.

Hydrogen breath test

is incorrect because this test is primarily used to diagnose small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) or lactose intolerance. It measures hydrogen produced by bacterial fermentation of carbohydrates and is not specific for

H. pylori

infection.

Stool culture

is incorrect because while stool antigen testing can be used to diagnose

H. pylori

, routine stool culture is not appropriate for

H. pylori

detection. The organism is difficult to culture from stool samples, and this method is not recommended for confirming eradication in clinical practice.

A 28-year-old man with known alcohol misuse disorder attends the Emergency Department with abdominal pain and vomiting. He describes that his abdominal pain has been present for six hours, and is concentrated in the epigastric region, with radiation through to the back.

Selected blood test results are as follows:


WBC	18.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)

Calcium	1.9 mmol/L	(2.0-2.5)
Glucose	14 mmol/L

Given the likely diagnosis, what statement most accurately describes the utility of measuring serum amylase in this condition?

answer_text: It is useful for diagnosis only
explanation_text:
While amylase is an important investigation in the diagnosis of pancreatitis, it does not offer prognostic value

The correct answer is

it is useful for diagnosis only

. This patient has a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. This is supported by his description of epigastric pain radiating through to his back, coupled with vomiting, a history of alcohol excess, and a markedly raised serum amylase. A raised serum amylase in this clinical context is strongly supportive of a diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. This diagnosis could be supported further with cross-sectional imaging.

It has both diagnostic and prognostic utility

is incorrect as although amylase is useful in diagnosing acute pancreatitis, the extent to which it is elevated is not prognostically informative. As such, serum amylase does not feature in prognostic scores for pancreatitis, such as the Glasgow-Imrie score.

It has neither diagnostic nor prognostic utility

is incorrect as serum amylase is a helpful diagnostic investigation when establishing whether undifferentiated abdominal pain could be due to acute pancreatitis.

It is the most sensitive diagnostic test

is incorrect as serum lipase is more sensitive than serum amylase in diagnosing acute pancreatitis, particularly in cases of pancreatitis due to alcohol excess.

It is the most specific diagnostic test

question_text:
A 42-year-old man presents to the general surgical clinic for a routine follow-up appointment. He has a longstanding diagnosis of Crohn's disease and underwent an ileal resection 4 months ago. Since the operation, he has experienced ongoing diarrhoea. He denies any blood or weight loss. He has no fevers and feels otherwise well in himself.

Examination and observations are all normal. Blood tests are performed:


Hb	146 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	256 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.7 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	138 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	6.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	89 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	<5 mg/L	(< 5)

What is the most appropriate treatment?
options_json: ["Budesonide", "Cholestyramine", "Loperamide", "Metronidazole", "Ursodeoxycholic acid"]
explanation_text:
Ongoing diarrhoea in Crohn's patient post-resection with normal CRP → cholestyramine

Ileal resection can pose symptomatic issues in patients with Crohn's disease. Specifically, the procedure leads to malabsorption of bile acid. The increased load of bile acid in the colon results in increased secretion of salt and water - hence the diarrhoea post-surgery. In the absence of any signs of a relapse, and with the CRP being reassuringly normal, it would be appropriate to commence

cholestyramine

. This drug binds to bile salts, reducing their effect on the colon and thus reducing diarrhoea.

Budesonide

, a steroid, may be used to induce remission in patients with primarily ileocaecal disease. This patient is not showing signs of active inflammation, and his CRP is normal, so this would not be appropriate.

Loperamide

is often used for the relief of diarrhoea in numerous situations. However, given the clinical picture presented here, cholestyramine would best tackle the root cause of the diarrhoea.

Metronidazole

may be used if an infection is suspected alongside a relapse of Crohn's disease. This patient is systemically well, and there are no signs of an active flare, so this is not appropriate.

Ursodeoxycholic acid

is used for a number of liver/gallbladder-related issues, including the reduction of pruritus. This is similar to cholestyramine, which may also be used for this purpose. However, in the context of post-resection diarrhoea in a patient with Crohn's, the latter is more appropriate.

question_text:
A 39-year-old man is admitted to hospital with decompensated liver disease of unknown aetiology. As part of a liver screen the following results are obtained:


Anti-HBs	Positive
Anti-HBc	Negative
HBs antigen	Negative

Anti-HBs = Hepatitis B Surface Antibody; Anti-HBc = Hepatitis B Core Antibody; HBs antigen = Hepatitis B Surface Antigen
What is this man's hepatitis B status?
options_json: ["Chronic hepatitis B - highly infectious", "Previous immunisation to hepatitis B", "Probable hepatitis D infection", "Acute hepatitis B infection", "Chronic hepatitis B - not infectious"]
explanation_text:
HBsAg negative, anti-HBs positive, IgG anti-HBc negative - previous immunisation

The correct answer is

Previous immunisation to hepatitis B

. The presence of positive Anti-HBs (Hepatitis B Surface Antibody) and negative Anti-HBc (Hepatitis B Core Antibody) and HBs antigen (Hepatitis B Surface Antigen) indicates that the patient has been previously immunised against hepatitis B. This is because the presence of Anti-HBs shows that the immune system has mounted a response against the virus, but the absence of Anti-HBc and HBs antigen suggests that there is no active infection or exposure to the virus.

Chronic hepatitis B - highly infectious

is incorrect because this would be indicated by a positive HBs antigen, which signifies an ongoing infection with hepatitis B. Additionally, in chronic infections, both Anti-HBs and Anti-HBc are usually positive.

Probable hepatitis D infection

is incorrect because hepatitis D infection occurs as a co-infection or superinfection with hepatitis B. Therefore, if there was a probable hepatitis D infection, we would expect to see evidence of active hepatitis B infection such as a positive HBs antigen.

Acute hepatitis B infection

is incorrect because during an acute infection, both HBs antigen and Anti-HBc would typically be positive. In this case, both are negative, indicating no current or past exposure to the virus.

Chronic hepatitis B - not infectious

is incorrect because this status would be characterized by a positive Anti-HBs along with positive Anti-HBc and negative HBs antigen. This indicates that although there was prior exposure to the virus leading to immunity development (positive Anti-HBs), there is no ongoing active infection (negative HBs antigen). However, in this patient's case, both HBs antigen and Anti-HBc are negative, pointing towards previous immunisation rather than past infection.

question_text:
You are asked to review a 55-year-old man in the haematology ward who has developed severe leg cramps. He started chemotherapy 3 days ago for treatment of Burkitt's lymphoma. Following chemotherapy, he has felt markedly better with an increased appetite. He takes regular omeprazole, vitamin D, furosemide, and allopurinol. On examination, he is cachectic with a BMI of 16.5 kg/m².

Blood results are as follows:


Na+	135 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	2.5 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Phosphate	0.22 mmol/L	(0.8-1.4)
Magnesium	0.65 mmol/L	(0.7-1.0)
Urea	2.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	42 µmol/L	(55 - 120)

What is the most likely cause of the electrolyte derangement?
options_json: ["Furosemide", "Omeprazole", "Refeeding syndrome", "Tumour lysis syndrome", "Vitamin D excess"]
explanation_text:
Hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are the characteristic electrolyte disturbances seen in patients with refeeding syndrome

Refeeding syndrome

is correct. The patient most likely has refeeding syndrome given his severely reduced BMI and the fact that he has had increased appetite levels since starting chemotherapy. The biochemical features of hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia are classic of this condition.

Furosemide

is incorrect. Although this drug can result in various biochemical abnormalities (including hypophosphataemia, hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia), the acute and profound abnormalities following increased dietary intake in a cachectic patient seen here favour a diagnosis of refeeding syndrome.

Omeprazole

is incorrect. This agent can result in hypomagnesaemia. Severe hypomagnesaemia may also result in hypocalcemia and hypokalemia. However, hypophosphataemia is not associated with omeprazole use.

Tumour lysis syndrome

is incorrect. The classical biochemical features associated with this syndrome are hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, and hypocalcemia.

Vitamin D excess

is incorrect. Hypercalcaemia and hypomagnesaemia can occur with vitamin D excess. However, hypokalaemia and hypophosphataemia are not associated with vitamin D excess.

The patient in this question has spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP). SBP presents with non-specific symptoms including nausea and vomiting, abdominal tenderness, fever and general malaise. Patients may also develop hepatic encephalopathy. The most common organism causing SBP is

E. coli

.

question_text:
A 70-year-old man has presented to the emergency department with increasing dyspepsia, odynophagia and progressive difficulty in swallowing solids. He has a past medical history of gastritis managed with maximal proton pump inhibitor therapy and hypertension managed with ramipril and amlodipine.

His general examination reveals epigastric tenderness. Observations and routine blood results are unremarkable.

He undergoes an upper gastrointestinal endoscopy within two weeks of this presentation.

What is the best imaging modality for assessing this type of tumour's depth?
options_json: ["CT scan", "Endoscopic ultrasound", "MRI scan", "Positron emission tomography (PET) CT scan", "Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy"]
explanation_text:
Oesophageal/Gastric Cancer - Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) is better than CT or MRI in assessing mural invasion

Endoscopic ultrasound is the correct option. This patient most likely has adenocarcinoma of the lower third of the oesophagus. The first-line investigation is upper gastrointestinal endoscopy; subsequently, an endoscopic ultrasound is the best imaging for mural invasion or tumour depth. This is because the local staging of cancer can be most accurately depicted by a local ultrasound rather than other imaging modalities.

An upper gastrointestinal endoscopy is an incorrect option as it does not measure tumour depth as accurately as the ultrasound wave modality.

CT scan is an incorrect option as this is less accurate for mural invasion. Instead, it the best initial investigation for staging oesophageal cancer in the chest, abdomen and pelvis.

PET CT scan is also incorrect as this option is reserved for those with oesophageal cancer in whom a peritoneal laparoscopy to search for peritoneal metastasis is negative. A PET CT scan is superior to a CT scan for this purpose due to the increase in uptake of the injected dye in areas of rapidly dividing metastatic cells.

MRI scan is incorrect because it has been found to be inferior at accurately measuring the mural invasion/tumour depth of oesophageal cancers compared to endoscopic ultrasound.

question_text:
A 35-year-old man is referred to the gastroenterology department due to dysphagia. He has trialled a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) with no improvement to his symptoms. His past medical history is of asthma and atopic dermatitis.

He undergoes an endoscopy which shows thick oesophageal mucosa with reduced vasculature. An oesophageal biopsy is taken.

What results would you expect from the endoscopic biopsy?
options_json: ["Adenocarcinoma", "CMV positive on H&E stain", "Pseudohyphae invading into mucosal cells", "Raised levels of eosinophils", "Squamous cell carcinoma"]
explanation_text:
Eosinophilic esophagitis typically presents in young men with symptoms of dysphagia and in patients with a history of food allergy, eczema and asthma

This man presents with typical features of eosinophilic oesophagitis with dysphagia not responding to PPIs and with a background of asthma and eczema. Diagnosis is made by histological analysis of an oesophageal biopsy which must show more than 15 eosinophils per high power microscopy field. Hence

raised levels of eosinophils

is the correct answer.

Adenocarcinoma

of the oesophagus is a cancer that usually occurs in the lower portion of the oesophagus. This is less likely in this patient given the lack of relevant findings on endoscopy. His medical history also points towards eosinophilic oesophagitis.

Squamous cell carcinoma

of the oesophagus is a cancer that usually occurs in the middle and upper portions of the oesophagus. This is less likely in this patient given the lack of relevant findings on endoscopy. His medical history also points towards eosinophilic oesophagitis.

CMV on H&E stain

would be seen in CMV oesophagitis, a condition most common in immunocompromised patients, most commonly in patients who are HIV positive. This patient's medical background of asthma and eczema makes eosinophilic esophagitis more likely given their links to this condition.

Pseudohyphae invading into mucosal cells

would be seen in cases of oesophageal candidiasis which again is more common in immunocompromised patients. With this patient's medical background of asthma and eczema, eosinophilic oesophagitis is more likely given their links with this condition.
