A 68-year-old man presents to the emergency department with left-sided abdominal pain and rectal bleeding. He has a past medical history of atrial fibrillation and is on apixaban. He does not smoke cigarettes or drink alcohol.

His observations are heart rate 111 beats per minute, blood pressure 101/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/minute, oxygen saturation 96% on room air and temperature 37.8ºC.

Abdominal examination reveals tenderness in the left lower quadrant. Bowel sounds are sluggish. Rectal examination demonstrates a small amount of fresh red blood but no mass lesions, haemorrhoids or fissures. His pulse is irregular. Chest auscultation is normal.

An ECG demonstrates atrial fibrillation.

Blood tests:



Hb	133 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	444 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	18.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	131 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	8.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	130 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	32 mg/L	(< 5)
Lactate	2.6 mmol/L	(0.0-2.0)

Plain radiography of the abdomen demonstrates 'thumbprinting' suggestive of mucosal oedema.

Given the presumed diagnosis, where is the likely site of pathology?
options_json: ["Caecum", "Hepatic flexure", "Recto-sigmoid junction", "Rectum", "Splenic flexure"]
explanation_text:
The splenic flexure is the most commonly affected site in ischaemic colitis

Splenic flexure is the correct answer. This patient has ischaemic colitis as evidenced by abdominal pain, rectal bleeding, raised WCC, raised lactate and abdominal radiography suggestive of mucosal oedema. He has a risk factor for this condition (i.e. atrial fibrillation). The most common site of pathology for ischaemic colitis is the splenic flexure, which is a watershed area where the blood supplies of the inferior mesenteric artery and superior mesenteric artery change.

The hepatic flexure is incorrect. This is less likely to be affected than the splenic flexure as it is not a watershed region.

Recto-sigmoid junction is incorrect. This is another watershed region that is susceptible to intestinal ischaemia but is less commonly affected than the splenic flexure.

The caecum is incorrect. Ischaemic colitis rarely affects this region.

The rectum is incorrect. This region has a rich vascular supply and receives blood from both the inferior mesenteric artery and internal iliac artery and so is rarely affected in ischaemic colitis.

question_text: A 32-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic with a 6-month history of intermittent diarrhoea, bloating and unexplained weight loss. She has a past medical history of type 1 diabetes mellitus. Her blood tests show iron deficiency anaemia. Upper GI endoscopy with duodenal biopsy confirms villous atrophy. Which genetic marker is most strongly associated with her condition?
options_json: ["HLA-B27", "HLA-DR4", "HLA-DQ2", "HLA-DR3", "HLA-DQ8"]
explanation_text:
Coeliac disease has a strong association with HLA-DQ2 (present in 95% of patients)

HLA-DQ2

is the genetic marker most strongly associated with coeliac disease, being present in approximately 95% of affected individuals in the UK. Its presence is not diagnostic as it also occurs in about 30% of the general population, but its absence makes coeliac disease highly unlikely. This strong association underpins its use in challenging diagnostic scenarios or when serology and histology are inconclusive.

HLA-B27

is primarily associated with spondyloarthropathies such as ankylosing spondylitis and reactive arthritis, not coeliac disease. Although HLA-B27 positivity can be seen in some gastrointestinal disorders (such as inflammatory bowel disease-associated arthropathy), it does not have a significant link to coeliac disease.

HLA-DR4

has been linked to several autoimmune conditions including rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes mellitus but does not have a strong association with coeliac disease. While both conditions may coexist due to shared autoimmune predisposition, DR4 itself is not a key marker for coeliac disease.

HLA-DR3

shows some association with autoimmune diseases such as type 1 diabetes and autoimmune hepatitis, which are themselves more common in patients with coeliac disease; however, DR3 is not the principal HLA haplotype implicated in coeliac pathogenesis.

HLA-DQ8

, while present in around 80% of patients who do not carry DQ2, remains less prevalent than DQ2 overall. It accounts for most remaining cases of genetically susceptible individuals but does not reach the same level of association as DQ2.

question_text:
A 71-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department with a four-hour history of haematemesis. He reports vomiting fresh red blood, with occasional clots. He reports not having opened his bowels for three days. He has a past medical history of type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, gout and non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. He has no known drug allergies.

On initial inspection, he appears unwell and agitated. Digital rectal examination reveals faecal impaction, with some black, foul-smelling stool left on the glove.

His observations are as follows: heart rate 103 beats per minute; respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute; blood pressure 88/58 mmHg; temperature 36.4ºC; and oxygen saturations 96% on air.

His blood test results are shown below:


Hb	73 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	180 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	13.0 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Na+	132 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.9 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	24 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	16.1 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	122 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	14 mg/L	(< 5)


Bilirubin	11 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	88 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	27 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	55 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	29 g/L	(35 - 50)

He is treated as a presumed upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, and undergoes urgent endoscopy. Due to persistent bleeding, he is referred for placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS).

This successfully stabilises the patient, and he is transferred to the Intensive Care Unit for monitoring. The following morning, he is difficult to rouse, and grossly disorientated. Neurological examination is unremarkable, with the exception of a bilateral, 3Hz hand tremor when his arms are fully extended.

Repeat blood tests are as follows:


Hb	88 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	140 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	10.5 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)


Na+	135 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	3.6 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Bicarbonate	27 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
Urea	11.5 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	100 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	11 mg/L	(< 5)

What is the most appropriate next intervention?
options_json: ["Request a non-contrast CT scan of the head", "Start intravenous piperacillin-tazobactam", "List for urgent repeat endoscopy", "Give a phosphate enema and commence regular laxatives", "Observe closely"]
answer_text: Give a phosphate enema and commence regular laxatives
explanation_text:
Transjugular Intrahepatic Portosystemic Shunt  commonly causes an exacerbation of hepatic encephalopathy

This patient has presented with an upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage in the context of decompensated non-alcoholic fatty liver disease. He has undergone placement of a transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPSS) as an emergency measure to stem variceal bleeding. This involves the formation of an artificial conduit between the hepatic portal vein and the hepatic vein. In cirrhotic patients, advanced liver fibrosis obstructs the flow of blood from the hepatic portal vein through the liver, causing the build-up of high portal venous pressures. Bypassing the liver with a TIPSS reduces the blood flow to the bleeding varix. However, as a consequence, nitrogenous waste products in the portal circulation are unable to be processed into urea by the liver, leading to the accumulation of ammonia, and the onset of hyperammonemic encephalopathy. This is the cause for this patient's new disorientation, and is characterised by asterixis (a 3-5Hz asterixis hand 'flap'). Hepatic encephalopathy is best treated with the removal of ammonifying gut bacteria, by ensuring regular bowel motions. The presence of faecal impaction on the patient's original rectal examination ensures that rectal evacuation with an enema plus regular laxatives is the most appropriate strategy to reverse his encephalopathy.

A non-contrast CT scan of the head would not reveal the diagnosis of hepatic encephalopathy (which is largely a clinical diagnosis). However, if his symptoms failed to resolve despite regular loose bowel motions, the diagnosis may need to be revisited, and a CT scan may become appropriate.

Although infection is a common cause of decompensation of liver disease, and hence encephalopathy, by far the most likely culprit here is the placement of a TIPSS. With improving inflammatory markers, there is little evidence for an intercurrent infection, and so piperacillin-tazobactam is unlikely to be of benefit. It is reasonable to argue that this patient should have been given prophylactic fluoroquinolones during the initial management of his upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, but broad spectrum antibiotics are not the most appropriate intervention at this stage.

A repeat endoscopy would be an appropriate intervention if there was suspicion of re-bleeding. However, his repeat blood tests show an improved haemoglobin and decreasing urea, and there is no mention of further haematemesis or new melaena, making this unlikely.

Hepatic encephalopathy secondary to TIPSS placement may resolve spontaneously. However, given the original examination findings of faecal impaction, it is preferable to expedite this with minimally invasive interventions such as an enema and regular laxatives, rather than simply observe the patient.

question_text:
A 27-year-old man presents with persistent pain upon defecation for the past 3 months. He has noticed small amounts of fresh blood when wiping. He is otherwise completely well in himself and denies any weight loss. He has no significant family history. Inspection of the anus confirms the diagnosis. Initial treatment with laxatives and dietary modification has been unsuccessful.

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options_json: ["Botulinum toxin injection", "Rubber band ligation", "Topical glyceryl trinitrate", "Topical hydrocortisone", "Topical zinc sulfate monohydrate"]
explanation_text:
Chronic anal fissure - topical glyceryl trinitrate

The correct answer is topical glyceryl trinitrate. The diagnosis here, given the acute pain upon defecation and fresh blood, is an anal fissure. Given the chronicity of its duration and failure to improve with conservative measures, including stool softeners and dietary advice, an appropriate step to take now is to trial topical glyceryl trinitrate.

Botox injection is incorrect. This would be further down the line if topical measures also failed to control symptoms.

Rubber band ligation would be used to treat haemorrhoids if initial measures were not successful. Haemorrhoids would present differently - generally painless unless thrombosed.

Topical hydrocortisone is another option to settle haemorrhoids, available in over-the-counter preparations. It is not used for anal fissures.

Topical zinc sulfate monohydrate is found in most over-the-counter preparations for haemorrhoids. It is not routinely used for anal fissures.

question_text:
A 25-year-old woman is referred by her GP to the gastroenterology clinic.

She has a background of type 1 diabetes mellitus and reports nine months of loose stools, abdominal cramps, and bloating. Her GP performed some initial investigations shown below.


Hb	131 g/L	(115 - 160)
Platelets	265 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	5.1 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
CRP	3 mg/L	(< 5)
Stool culture	Negative
Coeliac screen	Negative
Faecal calprotectin	Negative

You suspect she may have irritable bowel syndrome but given her diabetes you are also considering small bowel overgrowth syndrome.

What is the most appropriate initial test in this case?
options_json: ["Abdominal X-ray", "Capsule endoscopy", "Hydrogen breath test", "Small bowel aspiration and culture", "Urea breath test"]
explanation_text:
Hydrogen breath testing is an appropriate first line test for diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome

Small bowel overgrowth syndrome results from an excess of bacteria in the small bowel. It causes symptoms which overlap considerably with irritable bowel syndrome but should be considered particularly in patients with relevant risk factors, in this case diabetes.

The first-line test for the condition is the

hydrogen breath test

. In this test, a fasted patient is given a high glucose drink. Bacteria in the small bowel metabolise this glucose to hydrogen gas, which can be measured as exhaled hydrogen. The more bacteria there are in the small bowel, the more hydrogen will be exhaled and thus people with small bowel overgrowth syndrome will tend to have significantly higher rises in hydrogen gas over time than healthy controls.

Small bowel aspiration and culture

is another test that can be used for the diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome. It involves collecting a sample of fluid from the small intestine with endoscopy and culturing this sample for bacterial growth. As it is considerably more invasive than the hydrogen breath test, it is not used first-line.

Capsule endoscopy

is useful in examining the appearance of the small bowel which can be hard to visualise through traditional endoscopy procedures. It involves a patient swallowing a capsule containing a small wireless camera that records images as it passes through the digestive tract. It is useful for diagnosing conditions by appearance (e.g. malignancy, polyps, colitis) but at present it cannot be used to collect biopsies for culture and has no role in the diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome.

Abdominal x-ray

also has no role in the diagnosis of small bowel overgrowth syndrome as there are no specific changes associated with this condition with this imaging.

The

urea breath test

is used in the diagnosis of

Helicobacter pylori

infection.

question_text:
A 31-year-old man is referred to gastroenterology with dysphagia. He feels that food is getting stuck in his oesophagus when he tries to swallow. His weight is static. He also complains of some heartburn with some improvement with omeprazole prescribed by his GP.

He has a past medical history of asthma, eczema and coeliac disease.

An oesophagus-gastro-endoscopy is performed which shows oesophagitis. Biopsies show an increased number of eosinophils.

What is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Amoxicillin", "Dupilumab", "Fluticasone", "Metronidazole", "Prednisolone"]
explanation_text:
Dietary modification and topical steroids are used in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis

The biopsy and endoscopy findings are in keeping with a diagnosis of eosinophilic oesophagitis. Initial treatment options include dietary modification and/or pharmacological. Pharmacological options recommended by the British Society of Gastroenterology (BSG) include proton pump inhibitors or topical steroids.

Fluticasone

is one such steroid that can be used and so this is the correct answer. It is administered by using an inhaler to spray the medication into the mouth which is then swallowed, leading to a topical effect.

If a proton pump inhibitor is opted for, this should be taken for a minimum of 8-12 weeks prior to assessment of histological response.

Antibiotics do not play a role in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis and therefore

amoxicillin

is incorrect.

Dupilumab

is used in the United States for non-responders to conventional treatment. In the UK, its BNF-recommended uses are for eczema, asthma and rhinosinusitis.

Antibiotics do not play a role in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis and therefore

metronidazole

is incorrect.

Systemic steroids have limited use in eosinophilic oesophagitis, with a topical treatment being preferred. Therefore,

prednisolone

is incorrect.

question_text: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with non-alcoholic steatohepatitis following a liver biopsy. What is the single most important step to help prevent the progression of her disease?
options_json: ["Stop smoking", "Start statin therapy", "Eat more omega-3 fatty acids", "Start sulfonylurea therapy", "Weight loss"]
explanation_text:
Weight loss is the best first line management for NAFLD

The correct answer is

Weight loss

. Non-alcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH) is a progressive form of non-alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD), which can lead to cirrhosis, hepatocellular carcinoma and liver failure. The mainstay of treatment for NASH is lifestyle modification, with weight loss being the most effective intervention. According to UK guidelines, reducing body weight by 7-10% can lead to significant histological improvement in NASH.

Stop smoking

is an incorrect choice as while it's generally good advice for overall health and certain liver diseases such as primary biliary cirrhosis and alcoholic liver disease, there's no direct evidence that smoking cessation alone will prevent the progression of NASH.

Start statin therapy

would not be the single most important step in this case. While statins can lower cholesterol levels and reduce cardiovascular risk, they have not been proven to reverse or halt the progression of NASH specifically.

The option

Eat more omega-3 fatty acids

may provide some benefit for NAFLD patients due to their anti-inflammatory properties but again, they are not considered a primary treatment strategy according to UK guidelines. More research is needed in this area.

Finally,

Start sulfonylurea therapy

is also incorrect. Sulfonylureas are a class of medications used in type 2 diabetes management but they do not directly address the pathophysiology of NASH. In fact, these medications could potentially exacerbate weight gain which would be counterproductive in managing NASH.

question_text:

Ten days after admission urine output decreases significantly and blood tests reveal:

question_text:
A 28-year-old man with a history of coeliac disease and hay fever is referred to the acute medical assessment unit with a two-month history of dysphagia, odynophagia, and regurgitation. He describes pain when swallowing and the intermittent sensation of liquids and solids becoming stuck. He reports 4kg of weight loss over the two-month period.

An oesophagogastroduodenoscopy (OGD) is organised and performed as an outpatient. There are no gross abnormalities. Oesophageal biopsies show dense eosinophilic infiltration in the epithelium.

What is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options_json: ["Dietary modification", "Endoscopic surveillance", "Oesophageal dilatation", "Proton pump inhibitor", "Topical steroids"]
explanation_text:
Dietary modification and topical steroids are used in the management of eosinophilic oesophagitis

Dietary modification

is the correct answer. Eosinophilic infiltration is diagnostic for eosinophilic oesophagitis. This patient has coeliac disease and hay fever. A history of allergy is common in patients with eosinophilic oesophagitis. Additionally, eosinophilic oesophagitis tends to present in young men, such as this patient. Dietary modification is the first line treatment as the disease is thought to be an allergic reaction to ingested food.

Endoscopic surveillance

is the incorrect answer. Endoscopic surveillance might be required to monitor response to treatment (either dietary modification or topical steroids). However, this does not treat the underlying condition. Treatment should be initiated before making plans for surveillance.

Oesophageal dilatation

is the incorrect answer. Oesophageal dilatation is a treatment option for oesophageal strictures. Strictures are often seen in eosinophilic oesophagitis, but there was no evidence of strictures during this patient's OGD.

Proton-pump inhibitor

is the incorrect answer. A proton pump inhibitor (PPI) could be considered if the patient's symptoms were in keeping with simple gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (GORD). However, the dysphagia and weight loss suggest an alternative diagnosis. Occasionally, a failed trial of a PPI can be used to exclude GORD but given this patient has already had an OGD confirming the diagnosis, this would not be of diagnostic benefit.

Topical steroids

is the incorrect answer. Topical steroids are a treatment option for eosinophilic oesophagitis but are used second line after dietary modification.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man attends the acute medical unit with a 3-month history of progressively worsening diarrhoea. He states that it is foul-smelling and difficult to flush. On examination, he has a non-tender abdomen and a palpable mass in the right upper quadrant.

Blood results are as follows:


Bilirubin	64 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	246 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	42 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	364 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	34 g/L	(35 - 50)

What is the investigation of choice to confirm the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Abdominal ultrasound", "Abdominal x-ray", "CT pancreas", "Faecal elastase", "Serum amylase"]
explanation_text:
High-resolution CT scanning is the diagnostic investigation of choice for pancreatic cancer

The presence of painless obstructive jaundice and steatorrhoea is highly suggestive of pancreatic cancer.  The presence of a right upper quadrant mass is suggestive of a palpable gallbladder.  As per Courvoisier's law, this is unlikely to be due to gallstones.

CT pancreas

is correct. A high-resolution CT pancreas is the most sensitive investigation for identifying pancreatic cancer making this the investigation of choice.

Abdominal ultrasound

is incorrect. Although ultrasound can detect pancreatic cancer, it is less sensitive than CT.

Abdominal x-ray

is incorrect. An abdominal x-ray can detect features of chronic pancreatitis, however, the clinical features in this case are more in keeping with pancreatic cancer.

Faecal elastase

is incorrect. Functional tests (e.g. faecal elastase) can be used to assess pancreatic exocrine function, however, they are not useful in making the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.

Serum amylase

is incorrect. Serum amylase may be raised if the tumour obstructs the pancreatic ducts, however, it has no role in the diagnosis of pancreatic cancer.

question_text:
A 70-year-old man presents to the emergency department with fevers, lethargy and dysuria. He has advanced dementia and lives in a care home. Initial investigations were pointing to a urinary-tract infection and he was commenced on an oral antibiotic.

Several days into his treatment he developed yellowing of his sclera and blood tests were performed.


Bilirubin	30 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	300 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	60 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	80 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	30 g/L	(35 - 50)

What antibiotic is the most likely to have been prescribed?
options_json: ["Albendazole", "Amikacin", "Co-amoxiclav", "Doxycycline", "Nitrofurantoin"]
explanation_text:
Co-amoxiclav is a well recognised cause of cholestasis

Co-amoxiclav

is a well recognised cause of cholestasis. Cholestatic jaundice can occur either during or shortly after the use of co-amoxiclav. Cholestatic jaundice is more common in people above the age of 65 years and in men. The pathogenesis behind amoxicillin/clavulanate liver injury requires more studies; however, it is believed that immune allergic mechanisms are involved.

Amikacin

is a parenterally administered, broad-spectrum aminoglycoside antibiotic typically used for severe gram-negative infections. Despite widespread use, amikacin has not been associated with instances of acute liver injury.

Doxycycline

induced liver injury is a rare phenomenon, with an unclear clinical course and mechanism. It would not typically be indicated in treatment for a urinary tract infection and there is an incorrect answer here.

Nitrofurantoin

is a commonly prescribed antibiotic that can cause drug-induced liver injury, typically hepatocellular in nature. This scenario however shows a cholestatic picture in view of the raised alkaline phosphatase and jaundice.

Albendazole

is an anthelmintic agent used predominantly in the treatment of echinococcosis, a parasitic worm that causes cysts in the liver and lung. Therefore this would not be suitable in this scenario making it an incorrect option. Albendazole therapy is commonly associated with mild and transient serum enzyme elevations and rarely can lead to clinically apparent acute liver injury.

question_text: Which one of the following features is not seen in carcinoid syndrome?
options_json: ["Flushing", "Diarrhoea", "Bronchospasm", "Hypertension", "Pellagra"]
explanation_text:
Flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm, tricuspid stenosis, pellagra → carcinoid with liver mets - diagnosis: urinary 5-HIAA

The correct answer is

Hypertension

. Carcinoid syndrome is a paraneoplastic syndrome associated with carcinoid tumours, which are neuroendocrine tumours that secrete vasoactive substances such as serotonin. These substances can cause a range of symptoms including flushing, diarrhoea, bronchospasm and pellagra but not hypertension.

Let's now discuss each of the incorrect options:

Flushing

is one of the most common and characteristic symptoms of carcinoid syndrome. It occurs due to the vasodilatory effect of the substances secreted by the tumour, particularly serotonin.

Diarrhoea

is also a common symptom in carcinoid syndrome. This happens because serotonin stimulates intestinal motility and fluid secretion. Therefore, patients with carcinoid syndrome often present with watery diarrhoea.

Bronchospasm

can occur in carcinoid syndrome due to constriction of smooth muscle in the airways triggered by certain mediators released by the tumour, such as histamine and tachykinins.

Finally,

Pellagra

, which presents as dermatitis, dementia and diarrhoea (the three Ds), can be seen in carcinoid syndrome. This is because tryptophan, which would normally be converted into niacin (vitamin B3), gets diverted into producing excess serotonin in these patients. The resulting deficiency of niacin leads to pellagra.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman with a 5-year history of ulcerative colitis presents to the gastroenterology clinic. She has had three exacerbations in the past year requiring oral prednisolone. Her symptoms are currently well controlled on oral mesalazine. She is concerned about future flares and wants to discuss preventative options.

What is the most appropriate maintenance therapy?
options_json: ["Oral azathioprine", "Oral budesonide", "Oral methotrexate", "Rectal mesalazine", "Topical corticosteroid"]
explanation_text:
If a patient with ulcerative colitis has had a severe relapse or >=2 exacerbations in the past year they should be given either oral azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine to maintain remission

Oral azathioprine

is the most appropriate maintenance therapy for this patient. According to NICE guidelines, patients with ulcerative colitis who have had a severe relapse or two or more exacerbations in the past year should be offered either oral azathioprine or oral mercaptopurine to maintain remission. This patient has had three exacerbations in the past year requiring oral prednisolone, which indicates frequent disease activity despite being on mesalazine. Azathioprine is an immunomodulator that suppresses T-cell function and reduces inflammation in the bowel mucosa. It has been shown to be effective in maintaining remission and reducing steroid dependency in patients with frequently relapsing ulcerative colitis. The patient would need regular monitoring of full blood count and liver function tests while on this medication.

Oral budesonide

is not recommended as a maintenance therapy for ulcerative colitis. Corticosteroids, including budesonide, are effective for inducing remission in active disease but are not appropriate for long-term maintenance due to significant side effects with prolonged use, including osteoporosis, diabetes, hypertension, and adrenal suppression. Furthermore, there is no evidence supporting the efficacy of budesonide in maintaining remission in ulcerative colitis.

Oral methotrexate

is not recommended for the management of ulcerative colitis according to NICE guidelines. While methotrexate is used in Crohn's disease as a maintenance therapy, evidence for its efficacy in ulcerative colitis is limited and inconsistent. Therefore, it would not be an appropriate choice for this patient with frequently relapsing disease.

Rectal mesalazine

is an effective maintenance therapy for patients with distal disease (proctitis or proctosigmoiditis), either alone or in combination with oral aminosalicylates. However, for a patient with multiple exacerbations in the past year despite being on oral mesalazine, adding rectal mesalazine would be insufficient. The history of three exacerbations requiring systemic steroids indicates the need for more potent immunosuppression with azathioprine or mercaptopurine.

Topical corticosteroid

therapy, like systemic corticosteroids, is not appropriate for maintenance treatment in ulcerative colitis. Topical steroids are used for inducing remission in distal disease but are associated with local and systemic side effects if used long-term. They have not been shown to be effective in maintaining remission and would not address this patient's need for more effective prevention of frequent relapses.

question_text:
A 56-year-old-lady with no past medical history presents to the emergency department with a 12 hour history of severe abdominal pain and vomiting. On examination, she is tender in the epigastrium and has a low-grade pyrexia. An ultrasound of the abdomen is performed which shows gallstones but no evidence of cholecystitis. question_text:
A 56-year-old man presents to the emergency department with 4-months of abdominal pain and nausea. He has a background of alcohol excess. Eight years previously, the patient was admitted to intensive care with severe acute pancreatitis. On further questioning, he describes fatty stools that are difficult to flush.

Observations are normal. Examination reveals a mildly tender abdomen with no masses.

FBC, U&Es, CRP and amylase are all within the normal range.

What investigation should be requested to confirm the diagnosis?
options_json: ["Abdominal ultrasound", "CT pancreas", "Colonoscopy", "ERCP", "Faecal elastase"]
explanation_text:
CT pancreas is the preferred diagnostic test for chronic pancreatitis - looking for pancreatic calcification

The patient's history of chronic abdominal pain and steatorrhea on a background of alcohol excess and previous acute pancreatitis is most suggestive of chronic pancreatitis. A normal amylase and mildly raised CRP support this.

CT pancreas

is sensitive for features of chronic pancreatitis including pancreatic calcification, atrophy and pseudocysts. It is generally considered the imaging modality of choice for chronic pancreatitis.

Abdominal ultrasound

would be an appropriate first-line investigation for patients who present with obstructive jaundice. The LFTs in this case are normal.

Colonoscopy

is not required. This patient is describing steatorrhoea which is explained by exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. There are no other concerning features for GI malignancy or inflammatory bowel disease.

ERCP

is a cause of pancreatitis. It is not required to make a diagnosis of pancreatitis.

Faecal elastase

would be low in cases of chronic pancreatitis causing exocrine pancreatic insufficiency. It would be helpful in this case for confirming the cause of steatorrhoea but it would not enable a diagnosis of chronic pancreatitis.

Patients must eat gluten for at least 6 weeks before they are tested

Serological tests and jejunal biopsy may be negative if the patient is following a gluten-free diet. The patient should eat some gluten in more than one meal every day for at least 6 weeks before further testing.

question_text:
A 45-year-old with known alcohol dependence presents with central abdominal pain and steatorrhoea progressively increasing over the last few months. The patient denies any clear trigger to his symptoms.

The patient has been admitted several times in the past with acute pancreatitis.

Blood tests are shown below.


Hb	130g/L	130-180
WCC	5x109/L	4.5-11
Creatinine	100 µmol/L	53-106
AST	14 U/L	12-38
Bilirubin	16 µmol/L	2-17
Amylase	30 U/L	25-125

What is the preferred test to confirm the patient's suspected diagnosis?
options_json: ["Abdominal ultrasound", "CT pancreas", "Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)", "Faecal elastase", "Urine amylase"]
explanation_text:
CT pancreas is the preferred diagnostic test for chronic pancreatitis - looking for pancreatic calcification

This patient has a history of acute pancreatitis but has now presented with features and investigations in keeping with chronic pancreatitis. Chronic pancreatitis results from long-standing inflammation of the pancreas, commonly following several episodes of acute pancreatitis. Patients may present with a further episode of acute inflammation in a previously injured pancreas or with symptoms of persistent pain and malabsorption. The normal serum markers associated with acute presentations are often normal.

CT pancreas

is the diagnostic test of choice, detecting pancreatic calcification. CT has a higher sensitivity and specificity than other imaging modalities or serum tests and is readily available and therefore is the preferred diagnostic test.

Abdominal ultrasound

may show some signs in keeping with chronic pancreatitis such as calcification. However, it is not a suitably sensitive test when compared to CT.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)

is typically indicated to relieve biliary obstruction caused by stones, strictures or malignancy. It is not commonly used to diagnose chronic pancreatitis but is a well-recognised cause of acute pancreatitis. This procedure is also relatively timely, costly and invasive when compared to CT and therefore is not the diagnostic test of choice.

Faecal elastase

testing is used for the detection of exocrine pancreatic dysfunction and not to diagnose chronic pancreatitis.

Urine amylase

may be used in the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis. A raised level indicates damage and some research indicates that it may be more sensitive at detecting chronic pancreatitis than serum testing. However, its sensitivity is low.

question_text:
A 72-year-old man is found collapsed and unresponsive by his carers. He is unable to give any history. He is pale and cold peripherally. Observations and blood tests are as follows.


Respiratory rate 34 breaths per minute
Oxygen saturations 92% on air
Heart rate 126 beats per minute
Blood pressure 72/36 mmHg
Temperature 35.6ºC



Hb	51 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Platelets	220 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.6 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	137 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	18.7 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	97 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	8 mg/L	(< 5)

What investigation is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
options_json: ["Bone marrow biopsy", "CT mesenteric angiogram", "Colonoscopy", "Flexible sigmoidoscopy", "Upper GI endoscopy"]
explanation_text:
High urea levels can indicate an upper GI bleed versus lower GI bleed

The correct answer is

upper GI endoscopy

. The markedly low haemoglobin with no other cytopenia is suggestive of a bleeding cause. In the absence of witnessed bleeding, the urea is then the key clue - elevation of this suggests an upper GI bleed. Common causes of this include peptic ulcer disease and oesophageal varices. Upper GI endoscopy is the investigation of choice and will also allow therapeutic measures.

Bone marrow biopsy

is incorrect. This could be used to investigate haematological causes such as myelofibrosis. These often cause other cytopenias and would not explain the elevation in urea.

CT mesenteric angiogram

is incorrect. This is the investigation of choice for acute mesenteric ischaemia, which usually presents with abdominal pain and lactic acidosis. It is used in some cases of GI bleeding where the source is not clear, but usually must be performed at the time of active bleeding.

Colonoscopy

is incorrect. This would be used to investigate lower GI pathology which might cause bleeding such as polyps or malignancy. Lower GI bleeding tends to present with fresh red bleeding. In contrast to upper GI bleeding, it does not cause an elevation in the urea.

Flexible sigmoidoscopy

is incorrect. This is also used to investigate lower GI bleeding, particularly from distal pathology such as diverticular disease. Again, this would not cause an elevation in the urea.

question_text: A 36-year-old woman presents with flushing, diarrhoea and abdominal discomfort. She says these symptoms have come on over the last few months and do not appear to be getting better. You decide to run some tests. 24-hour urine 5-HIAA is elevated confirming your diagnosis of carcinoid syndrome. A scan is undertaken which localises the neoplastic lesion to the jejunum. You start her on octreotide to calm her symptoms whilst she awaits surgery. What cardiac abnormalities are associated with this conditions?
options_json: ["Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy", "Acquired ventricular septal defect", "Pulmonary stenosis and tricuspid insufficiency", "Aortic dissection", "Loeffler endocarditis"]
explanation_text:
Carcinoid syndrome can affect the right side of the heart. The valvular effects are tricuspid insufficiency and pulmonary stenosis

Carcinoid syndrome is a neuroendocrine tumour. There are many locations that they can occur in such as in the GI tract, in the respiratory tract and many other places. They can secrete serotonin which leads to many of the symptoms this patient suffers. The syndrome is associated with right-sided valvular pathology. The most common pathology is tricuspid insufficiency and pulmonary stenosis. The best way to remember is the acronym 'TIPS'.

HOCM is associated with inherited gene defects on the β-myosin heavy chain. This is not associated with carcinoid syndrome.

Acquired VSD would be associated with an MI and not carcinoid syndrome.

Aortic dissection is associated with hypertension and connective tissue disorder.

Loeffler endocarditis is endocarditis due to eosinophil proliferation in the heart. It is associated with helminthic infections and not carcinoid syndrome.

question_text:
A 36-year-old man presents with several months of fatigue. He denies weight loss or any other symptoms and is otherwise well in himself. He has a past medical history of asthma and well-controlled ulcerative colitis. Physical examination is unremarkable. He is referred for blood tests:


Hb	143 g/L	(135-180)
Platelets	356 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	6.5 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Bilirubin	21 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
ALP	755 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	154 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	121 u/L	(8 - 60)
Albumin	43 g/L	(35 - 50)

Given the likely diagnosis, what is the investigation of choice?
options_json: ["Abdominal ultrasound", "Liver biopsy", "Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography (MRCP)", "Serum MPO-anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies (MPO-ANCA)", "Serum anti-mitochondrial antibodies (AMA)"]
explanation_text:
MRCP is the investigations of choice in primary sclerosing cholangitis

This patient's presentation is suggestive of primary sclerosing cholangitis (PSC). This is a biliary disease of unknown aetiology that causes fibrosis and inflammation of both intra- and extra-hepatic bile ducts. It is strongly associated with ulcerative colitis (UC) - 80% of patients with PSC have UC (although only a minority of patients with UC will develop PSC). Around half of patients present symptomatically, with jaundice, pruritus, fatigue or right upper quadrant pain. Around half may present asymptomatically. ALP and bilirubin are typically deranged. The investigations of choice are

MRCP

and endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography (ERCP), as these will demonstrate biliary strictures with a 'beaded' appearance, confirming the diagnosis.

Abdominal ultrasound

is incorrect. Although useful in assessing liver disease, it does not adequately evaluate the biliary tree to diagnose or exclude PSC.

Liver biopsy

is incorrect. Fibrous, obliterative cholangitis may be seen, often described as an 'onion skin' appearance, although findings are generally non-specific.

MPO-ANCA

(also known as p-ANCA) is incorrect. Whilst this is associated with both UC and PSC, it is not specific to either condition and thus is not particularly useful diagnostically.

AMA

is incorrect. This is classically associated with primary biliary cholangitis (PBC), rather than PSC. PBC typically affects middle-aged women and is not associated with inflammatory bowel disease.

question_text:
A 68-year-old man is admitted to the surgical ward following a laparotomy for small bowel obstruction. He has been malnourished for several months due to poor oral intake. On day 3 post-operation, total parenteral nutrition (TPN) is started via a peripheral cannula in his left forearm. On day 5, he complains of pain and redness at the cannula site. On examination, there is a 5 cm area of erythema with tenderness and induration along the course of the vein. His temperature is 37.2°C.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Cellulitis", "Catheter-related bloodstream infection", "Superficial thrombophlebitis", "Extravasation injury", "Allergic reaction to TPN components"]
explanation_text:
Thrombophlebitis is a common side-effect of TPN, especially if given peripherally

Superficial thrombophlebitis

is the most likely diagnosis in this scenario. The patient has developed pain, erythema, tenderness and induration along the course of the vein where the peripheral cannula is sited for TPN administration. These are classic signs of thrombophlebitis, which is inflammation of a vein associated with thrombus formation. Thrombophlebitis is a common complication of peripheral TPN administration due to the hyperosmolar nature of TPN solutions, which are irritating to peripheral veins. The high osmolality and sometimes acidic pH of TPN solutions can cause chemical irritation of the vein endothelium, leading to inflammation and subsequent thrombus formation. This is why TPN is ideally administered via central venous access for longer-term use. The patient's symptoms developed after several days of peripheral TPN, which is a typical timeframe for this complication to manifest.

Cellulitis

is a bacterial infection of the skin and subcutaneous tissues, which can present with erythema, warmth, and tenderness. However, cellulitis typically presents as a more diffuse area of inflammation rather than following the linear course of a vein. While cellulitis can occur at cannula sites, the linear distribution of symptoms along the vein strongly suggests thrombophlebitis instead.

Catheter-related bloodstream infection

(CRBSI) is a serious complication of intravenous cannulation and TPN administration. However, patients with CRBSI typically present with systemic symptoms such as high fever, rigors, and signs of sepsis. This patient has only a minimal temperature elevation (37.2°C) and the inflammation is localised to the cannula site and along the vein, making CRBSI less likely than thrombophlebitis.

Extravasation injury

occurs when intravenous fluids or medications leak into the surrounding tissues rather than remaining in the vein. While extravasation of TPN can cause significant tissue damage and inflammation, it typically presents as a more localised area of swelling, pain and potentially tissue necrosis at the cannula site, rather than inflammation along the course of the vein as described in this case.

Allergic reaction to TPN components

is uncommon but can occur, particularly in response to lipid emulsions or certain additives. However, allergic reactions typically present with more generalised symptoms such as urticaria, pruritus, or in severe cases, anaphylaxis. The localised nature of this patient's symptoms along the vein makes an allergic reaction less likely than thrombophlebitis.

question_text:
A 48-year-old woman presents to the Emergency Department with colicky abdominal pain. She reports that for the last three months, she has experienced intermittent pain in the right upper quadrant, particularly after the ingestion of fatty foods.

What cells are responsible for producing the hormone implicated in this presentation?
options_json: ["B cells", "D cells", "G cells", "I cells", "S cells"]
explanation_text:
CCK - I cells in upper small intestine

The correct answer is

I cells

. This patient has presented with classic symptoms of biliary colic, which is caused by contraction of the gallbladder against an obstruction (i.e. usually a gallstone). It occurs preferentially after the ingestion of fatty foods, as fatty foods stimulate the production of cholecystokinin (CCK) from the I cells of the duodenum. CCK promotes gallbladder contractility, causing the release of bile into the small intestine to aid with lipid emulsification.

B cells

is incorrect, as these are cells involved in the adaptive immune response, with no known function in promoting gallbladder contractility.

D cells

is incorrect, as these are cells in the stomach, small intestine and pancreas which release somatostatin. This decreases insulin production rather than affecting gallbladder contractility.

G cells

is incorrect, as these are cells in the stomach that secrete gastrin to promote acid secretion by the stomach's parietal cells.

S cells

is incorrect, as these are intestinal cells that release secretin in response to stomach acid, to promote intestinal alkalinisation.

The Waterlow score is used to estimate the risk of a patient developing a pressure sore. Whilst this includes an assessment of malnutrition as one of it's components the Waterlow score is not designed to screen for malnutrition.

question_text:
A 45-year-old man presents to the emergency department complaining of fatigue, malaise and yellow eyes. He has no past medical history. He does not take any regular medications. He drinks approximately 80 units of alcohol a week.

On examination, he is jaundiced and there is tender hepatomegaly. There is no ascites. The Glasgow coma scale is 15/15.

Blood tests:


Hb	130 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	189 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	18.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	133 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	4.2 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	4.2 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	88 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
CRP	45 mg/L	(< 5)
Bilirubin	85 µmol/L	(3 - 17)
Bicarbonate	21 mmol/L	(22-26)
ALP	88 u/L	(30 - 100)
ALT	82 u/L	(3 - 40)
Î³GT	142 u/L	(8 - 60)
AST	165 u/L	(10-40)
Albumin	34 g/L	(35 - 50)
PT time	24.5 seconds	(9.5-13.5)

What is the most appropriate management?
options_json: ["Lactulose", "Liver transplant", "Pentoxifylline", "Prednisolone", "Rifaximin"]
explanation_text:
Corticosteroids are used in the management of severe alcoholic hepatitis

Prednisolone is correct. This patient presents with fatigue, malaise, jaundice in association with tender hepatomegaly on a background of fatty liver and alcohol excess. Together with supportive biochemistry (hyperbilirubinemia, transaminitis with AST > ALT, leucocytosis and raised CRP), this suggests a diagnosis of alcoholic hepatitis. Maddrey's discriminant score is used to guide whether prednisolone should be given in alcoholic hepatitis. A score > 32 is associated with a poor prognosis and prednisolone treatment is indicated in these cases. In this case, the score is 62.5 (based on a PT time of 24.5 seconds bilirubin of 85 µmol/L).

Lactulose is incorrect. This is used in patients with cirrhosis to ensure 2-3 loose stools a day and so treat and prevent cases of hepatic encephalopathy. This patient is not known to be cirrhotic and is not confused.

Pentoxifylline is incorrect. This can also be used to treat severe alcoholic hepatitis. However, in a head to head comparison it was inferior to prednisolone.

Rifaximin is incorrect. This is used to prevent hepatic encephalopathy, which is not present in this case.

Liver transplant is incorrect. The majority of cases of alcoholic hepatitis resolve with abstinence from alcohol +/- steroid treatment. Additionally, the need for a liver transplant in acute liver failure is typically indicated either by a pH < 7.3 after fluid resuscitation or all three of the following: creatinine > 300 umol/L, PT time > 100 seconds and grade III/IV encephalopathy. The bicarbonate is only very mildly low in this case (21) and we might expect this to improve with abstinence, fluid and treatment with steroids. Therefore, a liver transplant would not be the first intervention.

A 26-year-old female was been newly started on medication by her GP. Two weeks later she reported noticeable yellowing of her eyes and abdominal discomfort, particularly over the right upper quadrant.

On examination, she appeared icteric with tenderness on deep palpation over the right upper quadrant.

Urgent blood tests were performed which showed the following:

Drug-induced cholestasis may present as an acute illness that promptly subsides by withdrawing the offending agent. It may present with or without jaundice and abdominal pain.

The oral contraceptive pill is known to cause cholestatic liver injury with hyperbilirubinemia and elevation of alkaline phosphatase.

Amiodarone is known to cause a hepatocellular picture with a rise in alanine transaminase (ALT) to greater than two times the upper limit of normal, not seen in this case.

Methyldopa is known to cause a hepatocellular picture with a rise in alanine transaminase (ALT) to greater than two times the upper limit of normal, not seen in this case.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man attends the clinic with a 3-month history of profuse diarrhoea. He denies any melaena or fresh rectal bleeding. His weight is stable.

Blood results are as follows:


Hb	145 g/L	Male: (135-180)
Female: (115 - 160)
Platelets	360 * 109/L	(150 - 400)
WBC	9.2 * 109/L	(4.0 - 11.0)
Na+	135 mmol/L	(135 - 145)
K+	2.8 mmol/L	(3.5 - 5.0)
Urea	8.8 mmol/L	(2.0 - 7.0)
Creatinine	110 µmol/L	(55 - 120)
Bicarbonate	16 mmol/L	(22 - 29)
CRP	2 mg/L	(< 5)

A colonoscopy is arranged by the gastroenterologists:


Colonoscopy	Three large adenomas (>1cm) were identified in the descending colon, splenic flexure, and transverse colon

What is the most likely diagnosis?
options_json: ["Colorectal carcinoma", "Familial adenomatous polyposis", "Peutz-Jeghers syndrome", "Tubular adenoma", "Villous adenoma"]
explanation_text:
Diarrhoea + hypokalaemia → villous adenoma

Villous adenoma

is correct. Most secretory villous adenomas of the colon cause hyperchloremic metabolic acidosis with associated hypokalaemia because they produce large volumes of potassium, bicarbonate-rich fluid. The presence of adenomas, metabolic acidosis, and hypokalaemia favours this diagnosis.

Colorectal carcinoma

is incorrect. Although villous adenomas are premalignant, there is no evidence at the current time that they have transformed.

Familial adenomatous polyposis

is incorrect. Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is a rare inherited cancer predisposition syndrome characterised by hundreds to thousands of precancerous colorectal polyps (adenomatous polyps). If left untreated, affected individuals inevitably develop cancer of the colon and/or rectum at a relatively young age. In this case, only 3 polyps were identified making this an unlikely diagnosis.

Peutz-Jeghers syndrome

is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant genetic condition affecting around 1/50,000 and 1/200,000 individuals. Symptoms usually appear during the first decade of life and begin with spots of dark skin freckling (melanocytic macules) around the mouth, eyes, nostrils, and fingers as well as inside the mouth (oral mucosa) and around the anus (perianal). Multiple benign polyps called hamartomas also begin to grow in the gastrointestinal tract of affected individuals around that age. The presence of adenomas (as opposed to hamartomas) makes PJS an unlikely diagnosis.

Tubular adenoma

is incorrect. Tubular adenomas are rarely secretory and thus would not explain the biochemical results present in this case.

question_text: A 31-year-old woman presents with symptoms consistent with coeliac disease. Which one of the following tests should be used first-line when screening patients for coeliac disease?
options_json: ["Tissue transglutaminase antibodies", "Anti-endomyseal antibodies", "HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping", "Anti-gliadin antibodies", "Duodenal biopsy"]
explanation_text:
Coeliac disease - tissue transglutaminase antibodies are the first-line test

Tissue transglutaminase antibodies (TTG)

are the recommended first-line serological test for screening patients with suspected coeliac disease according to NICE guidelines. TTG antibodies have high sensitivity (around 93-97%) and specificity (around 95-99%) for coeliac disease, making them an excellent initial screening tool. These antibodies are produced when the immune system reacts to the tissue transglutaminase enzyme, which modifies gluten peptides in the small intestine, making them more immunogenic in susceptible individuals. TTG testing is widely available, relatively inexpensive, and has good reproducibility between laboratories. It's important to note that patients should be on a gluten-containing diet for at least 6 weeks prior to testing to avoid false negative results. If TTG is positive, further investigation with duodenal biopsy is required to confirm the diagnosis.

Anti-endomyseal antibodies

are highly specific for coeliac disease (specificity >99%) but are not recommended as the first-line test. They are more technically demanding, requiring indirect immunofluorescence on tissue substrates, making them more expensive and labour-intensive than TTG testing. Additionally, interpretation is subjective and requires experienced laboratory personnel. Anti-endomyseal antibody testing is typically used as a confirmatory test when TTG results are equivocal or to increase diagnostic certainty before proceeding to biopsy. Both TTG and endomyseal antibodies target the same antigen (tissue transglutaminase), but the testing methodologies differ.

HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping

is not appropriate as a first-line screening test for coeliac disease. While approximately 95% of coeliac patients carry HLA-DQ2 and most of the remainder carry HLA-DQ8, these genetic markers are also present in about 30-40% of the general population, most of whom will never develop coeliac disease. The main value of HLA typing is its negative predictive value – if a patient is negative for both HLA-DQ2 and DQ8, coeliac disease is highly unlikely. Therefore, HLA typing is more useful for excluding coeliac disease in specific situations, such as in patients already on a gluten-free diet or in first-degree relatives of coeliac patients, rather than as an initial screening tool.

Anti-gliadin antibodies

are no longer recommended for coeliac disease screening due to their lower sensitivity and specificity compared to TTG and endomyseal antibodies. These were among the first antibodies identified in coeliac disease and target gliadin, a component of gluten. However, they can be elevated in various other gastrointestinal disorders and even in some healthy individuals, leading to false positive results. Newer generation tests for deamidated gliadin peptide antibodies have improved performance but are still not recommended as first-line tests by NICE guidelines. Anti-gliadin antibodies have largely been replaced by TTG and endomyseal antibody testing in clinical practice.

Duodenal biopsy

is considered the gold standard for diagnosing coeliac disease but is not appropriate as a first-line screening test. Biopsy is an invasive procedure requiring endoscopy, which carries risks and is more resource-intensive than serological testing. The typical histological findings in coeliac disease include villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes. While biopsy is essential for confirming the diagnosis in patients with positive serology, it would be inappropriate and impractical to perform biopsies on all patients with suspected coeliac disease without first screening with serological tests. The recommended approach is to start with TTG antibody testing and proceed to biopsy for confirmation in those with positive or equivocal serological results.
